double quotation markI know Camden because I live it every day. I know the challenges facing our communities, our estates, our broken lifts, our unpicked bins, our unclean roads and endless housing register waiting list because these are the places I have grown up and continue to call home.

We don’t need another MP who arrives during an election campaign, puts out a few leaflets, makes a few promises and disappears once the votes are counted. We need an MP who is present, accessible and visibly part of the community all year round.

I am asking Green party members for the opportunity to represent your home truly and properly. I’m not asking you to vote for a politician you’ll only see on a leaflet. I’m asking you to choose someone who is already here.

The Sarah Jones statement about Portsmouth (see 1.18pm) will be the second of three ministerial statements this afternoon. There are no urgent questions.

At 3.30pm, before Jones, Angela Rayner, the communities secretary, will make a statement about local government reorganisation. That should last about an hour, and after Jones finishes, at about 5.30pm, Emma Reynolds, the chief secretary to the Treasury, will make a statement about economic growth.

At the Downing Street lobby briefing the PM’s spokesperson condemned the behaviour of anti-migrant protesters who blocked roads in Portsmouth yesterday. He said: “Thuggish behaviour is unacceptable, we condemn it unreservedly.”

This was stronger than the initial response released by the Home Office yesterday, but in line with what Emma Reynolds, the chief secretary to the Treasury, said in interviews this morning. (See 8.59am.)

Sarah Jones, the policing minister, will give a statement to MPs on the disruption later this afternoon.

Asked if the government regarded the protests as “far-right”, the PM’s spokesperson said that dealing with them was an operational matter for the police, but that “any behaviour that is intimidatory and a cause of disruption to passengers and travellers is unacceptable”.

At the weekend Mike Huckabee, the US ambassador to Israel, posted this on social media about the UK.

double quotation markThe Brits have lost it. The Jew hate of their government knows no boundaries and knows no facts

Huckabee was commenting on a tweet from the Israeli government criticising Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, for comments about Israel’s record in Gaza.

Asked about Huckabee’s comment at the Downing Street lobby briefing, the PM’s spokesperson said:

double quotation markWe completely reject that assertion. We’re committed to protecting Jewish communities in the UK and continue to engage with community leaders and groups.

The government is investing almost £380m over three years, to protect Jewish communities, crack down on antisemitic extremism and hostile state activity, and tackle antisemitism in schools, universities and local communities.

The spokesperson would not say if the government had formally complained to the US authorities about Huckabee’s remark.

Jaguar Land Rover has announced thousands of job cuts in a “body blow for workers” as it grapples with tough trading conditions, Donald Trump’s tariff wars and the fallout from a cyber-attack. Rob Davies and Alex Daniel have the story.

Asked about this at the No 10 lobby briefing, the PM’s spokesperson said:

double quotation markWe understand that this will be an uncertain and concerning time for affected workers, their families and the wider communities.

And we know that current market conditions are challenging for the automotive sector globally. That’s why we’ve taken significant action to back the UK’s automotive industry by lowering electricity bills for manufacturers, providing £4bn of capital R and D funding to manufacture zero-emission vehicles and launching a £2bn electric car grant to encourage people to buy Evs.

The business secretary [Jonathan Reynolds] is in close contact with JLR and he will be meeting them early this week.

The spokesperson also confirmed that Reynolds has been “clear on his ruling out of any form of bailout”.

Hamish Falconer, appointed by Andy Burnham as minister for EU relations, has had his first official meeting with his EU opposite number, Maroš Šefčovič. In a social media post, Falconer says he wants “a more ambitious partnership”.

Opposition parties have criticised John Healey for sounding too much like Rachel Reeves in his speech.

This is from Andrew Griffith, the new shadow chancellor.

double quotation markJohn Healey sounds increasingly like continuity Rachel Reeves. Warm words about growth will not make growth a reality or cover up the enormous damage Labour have done to businesses and family finances.

Healey failed to end uncertainty by ruling out more tax rises, failed to set out a serious plan to reform welfare, and failed to commit to funding defence properly – the very issue he resigned over as defence secretary. Even as Jaguar Land Rover cuts jobs, he offered no pause to Labour’s job-destroying employment red tape and no measures to get ruinously high energy bills down.

This is from Robert Jenrick, the Reform UK Treasury spokesperson.

double quotation markOn the day 4,000 people are losing their jobs, Healey gave a dire and dreary speech that will change absolutely nothing. John Healey is beginning to make even Rachel Reeves seem inspiring.

And this is from Ellie Chowns, the Green party’s Treasury spokesperson.

double quotation markOnce again Britain is promised a new economic vision for the future – and once again we are delivered more of the same, from another government unwilling to truly grasp the nettle on wealth inequality and deliver for our communities.

The Green party is clear that the biggest priority must be building economic prosperity that is sustainable, equitable, and genuinely meaningful – not simply chasing ever-more growth for its own sake, regardless of impact.

There is nothing unusual about a chancellor refusing to rule out tax rises before a budget. It is normal for a chancellor not to comment on what is in the budget until it is delivered (apart from when they do rule out specific measures in advance, which happens more often than you might think). But, in his column in the Sunday Times yesterday, Rishi Sunak, the Conservative former PM and chancellor, argued on this occasion John Healey should rule out tax cuts now. Sunak argued that the rise in government borrowing costs means that the government’s headroom has been slashed, that Healey already has to find £4.7bn to fund the defence investment plan, and that as a result the country faces weeks of speculation about possible tax rises.

double quotation markThe uncertainty will deter investment and chill economic activity, the last thing needed if we are to foster the sense of optimism that Burnham rightly wants and the growth the country so urgently needs.

Chancellors are loath to tie their hands before a budget. I spent weeks before each fiscal event answering almost every question with, “You wouldn’t expect me to comment on that ahead of the budget.”

Yet Healey should reject such reticence. He should make clear that he’ll not increase taxes in the budget and that if adjustments need to be made, he’ll cut spending. That would provide the certainty needed in an increasingly uncertain world. Research shows that improving the budgetary position by spending cuts rather than tax rises is both more durable and better for growth.

When Kemi Badenoch keeps challenging the government to rule out tax rises in the budget, she is trying to cause trouble by generating a negative headline for the PM when he ignores her. By contrast, in his column, Sunak sounded like someone trying to constructive advice based on what might be good for the country.

If so, Healey did not take it. To be fair, in his speech today the chancellor clearly signalled that he is not about to embark on a big, tax-raising spree. (See 9.57am.) This was consistent with the message the Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary (in the audience for the speech) gave in an interview on Sky News yesterday. “There is no taxation answer that will meet the British people’s expectations on social care or defense or public services,” Reynolds said. But a hint about controlling spending is not the same as a firm commitment not to put up tax, and so Healey’s refusal to rule out tax rises is a story. (It is already the lead on the Telegraph’s website.)

That would not matter much if there were other big stories in the speech. But there weren’t; it was quite dull, and while it conveyed seriousness, it did not project authority. Most of it not only could have been said by Rachel Reeves, the previous chancellor, but actually was said by her (in terms of the arguments being made, if not the words and phrases). As new PM, Burnham has successfully signalled that he is a change from his predecessor. Healey hasn’t.

In his speech, towards the end, John Healey gave a bit more detail of how he intends to cut the burden of business regulation by 25%. (See 10.25am.)

He said that, as well as taking forward the recommendations of the Fingleton review to speed up the construction of nuclear power stations, he would apply those findings to some other sectors. He said there would be a review of the costs involved in rail infrastructure projects.

And he said he wanted to “end the consultation culture at the Treasury and beyond” by getting ministers to speed up decision making. He said new guidance has gone out today to ministers on this from the Treasury and the attorney general, Ellie Reeves.

The Treasury has now published this guidance, which has been sent to ministers as a letter from Healey, Reeves and Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state. It is potentially quite radical.

It starts by saying that in the past “administrative frictions” have stopped the government acting on behalf of the British public.

double quotation markWe want to be clear that the government will act with the full agency that sits with the executive, and which flows from our command of a majority in the House of Commons … We are also determined to overcome the administrative frictions that past administrations have allowed to accumulate, often with good intentions but which have served to slow the work of government, and which we must not allow to frustrate the speed of change.

Healey, Reeves and Haigh then go on to propose three changes.

Ministers are being told to reduce the amount of consultations they hold before decisions are taken and implemented. The letter says that “habitual, box-ticking consultation” has become a problem, and it says that “thousands” of unnecessary consultation requirements should be scrapped. It also implies formal consultation should be the exception, rather than the norm.

double quotation markConsultation culture has turned a sensible mechanism for sourcing external input into an industry of dither and delay, which too often fails to hear from those whose perspectives are most relevant to the issue under consideration, and can drag policies to a lowest common denominator outcome.

We will end this trend by reasserting that there is no general duty of consultation, and that the default position should be that ministers reach decisions and proceed to act on them …

Habitual, box-ticking consultation does not serve people or business and is a distraction to government …

New general guidance will be circulated by officials and more detailed guidance on approaches to public participation will follow in due course. Within this parliament, we will then go further and seek to unwind the thousands of unnecessary consultation and reporting requirements that have come to litter the statute book.

Ministers are being told that a “high” risk of a policy being ruled unlawful should not necessarily stop a policy being implemented. The letter says No 10 wants ministers to feel that they are “trusted” to take decisions even when there is a legal risk, and advice to government lawyers is being changed accordingly. It says:

double quotation markIn support of this approach, we will this week update the legal risk guidance that is used by government lawyers, and which amongst other changes will be clear that it is wholly proper for ministers to take decisions where there is a tenable legal argument even where there is a high legal risk, as well as encouraging lawyers proactively to suggest alternative options where there is a significant barrier or risk to a proposed policy.

Ministers are being told that the government will extend the list of projects exempt from judicial review (JR), building on decisions already taken to stop infrastructure projects being blocked by JR.

The arguments in the letter echo complaints about Whitehall and the civil service more usually heard on the right. When Suella Braverman was attorney general, she also encouraged government lawyers to worry a bit less about the risk of government decisions being found unlawful in the courts. Braverman is now a Reform UK MP, and at its party conference last week Reform also suggested elected politicians were being obstructed by officials – but using much more extreme language.

Q: [From Katherine Forster from GB News] It sounds from what you are saying taxes are going to go up in the budget. And what do you think of the British Chambers of Commerce today saying the pension triple lock should be scrapped so that more money can be spent on Neets (young people not in education, employment or training)?

On tax, Healey said Labour would stick to the promises it made in its manifesto. He repeated his point about not wanting to fuel more speculation by commenting on the budget.

double quotation markI agree with them what they were saying about youth unemployment. You heard me talk about it today -a scar, a blight on the future of those million young people … It cannot be right that we write off a young generation in that way. And so Alan Milburn is doing important work. We’ll base our plans on his full recommendations. But as the prime minister has said, there is a need to bring down welfare costs.

Q: [From Helia Ebrahimi, Channel 4 News] How are you going to deliver change on defence, the cost of living and social care. And would you devolve responsibility for corporation tax to local government.

Healey say he won’s speculate on what will be in the budget.

Addressing Ebrahimi, and also Beth Rigby, given her question a moment ago, he says:

double quotation markIf I respond to speculation now, that will only fuel more speculation. And it’s quite right, and every chancellor would say, that’s for the budget.

I’ll set out my plans and the future route for government for this country at that budget.

Q: [From Sky’s Beth Rigby] The markets expect interest rates to go up. So is the government really turning the corner? And can you assure people you won’t put taxes up in the budget?

Healey says global problems are making “our task in government harder”.

double quotation markWhat I am doing today is setting out plans, a direction for growth … that will see growth in more places in future.

I want to be the chancellor that gets things done, and I want to see growth driven from more places across the UK.

I want to be the chancellor also that recognises, tough as it is, Britain has huge resilience, great latent potential and relative strengths in relation to the way that we are dealing with the fiscal challenges we face.

He does not address the tax question directly.

Healey says he wants to cut the burden of business regulation by 25%.

double quotation markI will take an axe to the thicket of consultation, litigation and administration that has a stranglehold too often on private investment.

So I confirm today my commitment to reducing the burden of business regulation by 25% by the end of this parliament.

And today I announce this [the extension of] the reforms of judicial review from energy to all major infrastructure so that vexatious legislation and vexatious litigation and challenge can’t block economic growth.

Healey says he will change the Treasury’s green book rules to enable to back more regional investement.

double quotation markInvestment has increased by 4.9% since the election alone.

But we need to do more. So first, I’m making changes to the Treasury green book, reducing the discount rate from 3.5% to 3%, and that will skew investment towards projects with more long-term potential, meaning that more places across the UK will get a fair hearing.

This builds on a process that started when Rachel Reeves was chancellor.

Healey says he is also announcing that the I’m announcing today that South Yorkshire and Liverpool cityregions, the North East England. region and the Cardiff Capital Region will all become the latest strategic partners of the National Wealth Fund.

Healey confirms he is announcing an allocation of £150m from the British Business Bank, £150 million for scale-ups in the north of England.

In its news release, the Treasury has given a bit more detail about what this will do.

double quotation markThe new fund, from money already allocated to the British Business Bank, will provide larger investments of between £5m and £15m and is expected to back university spinouts and other ambitious businesses across the North, from Liverpool and Manchester to Leeds, Sheffield, Hull and Newcastle.

The British Business Bank will commit up to £150m, with the proposed fund intended to attract additional private investment. By bringing public and private capital together, it will give some of the north’s most promising companies the backing to grow, create jobs and build their future in the communities where they started.

title: Beverly Vance calls daughter-in-law Usha humble: 'One of the nicest people I've ever met'
excerpt:
"She's one of the nicest people I've ever met"

Being front and center in the political sphere is certainly not for the thin-skinned, and no one knows that more than Vice President JD Vance's wife, Us...
body_text:
"She's one of the nicest people I've ever met"

Being front and center in the political sphere is certainly not for the thin-skinned, and no one knows that more than Vice President JD Vance's wife, Usha.

The second lady of the United States recently caught some flak on the internet for wearing an $8 maternity dress from Old Navy in a recent appearance with her husband.

One person who is squarely in Usha's corner defending her from the online criticism is none other than her mother-in-law, Beverly Vance.

SECOND LADY USHA VANCE GETS CANDID ABOUT NEW BABY, JUGGLING FOUR CHILDREN AND MOTHERHOOD

Vice President JD Vance celebrates his mother Beverly Aikins' decade of sobriety on Friday, April 4, 2025, at the White House. (White House press office)

Vance joined OutKick's very own Tomi Lahren on her show, "Tomi Lahren is Fearless," and when the subject of Usha's choice of dress was brought up, Beverly couldn't help but sing the praises of her daughter-in-law.

"She's very humble," Beverly revealed to Lahren. "I think she's one of the nicest people I've ever met... I love her like she's my own daughter."

SECOND LADY USHA VANCE SHARES FAMILY PHOTOS FEATURING NEWBORN WHO IS LESS THAN 1 WEEK OLD

For those of you who have in-laws, you know it can be a crapshoot as to whether you get along with them or not, so it's really comforting to see Beverly speak so highly of Usha.

Beverly would go on to describe Usha as "authentic" while listing off some of her most admirable qualities.

"She's very genuine, very authentic. She loves JD. She's a good mom," Beverly said. "I can't think of anything bad to say about her."

U.S. Second Lady Usha Vance attends the 2026 World Cup Group D match between Turkey and the United States at Los Angeles Stadium in Inglewood on June 25, 2026. (Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images)

As for the cultural side of things, although the two could not be more different, Beverly admits that she's a big fan Indian food.

"I have to admit, I don't think I could cook it," she said. "But it's pretty good."

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

As Lahren opines, the Vance family represents a good example of a modern American family dynamic, and that mix of cultures is part of what makes them so special.

Vice President JD Vance and his wife Usha Vance attend the Commander-in-Chief Ball on January 20, 2025 in Washington, DC. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

This won't be the last time Usha Vance faces criticism and trolls from the internet, that much is for sure.

But with a mother-in-law like Beverly Vance on her side, I doubt she will ever be too bothered by the noise.

title: Oasis recordings up for auction despite band’s objections
excerpt:
Archive documenting concerts, rehearsals, soundchecks and conversations estimated at up to £1.6m

An archive of more than 100 hours of Oasis recordings – including concerts, rehearsals and candid conv...
body_text:
Archive documenting concerts, rehearsals, soundchecks and conversations estimated at up to £1.6m

An archive of more than 100 hours of Oasis recordings – including concerts, rehearsals and candid conversations between Noel and Liam Gallagher – is to be auctioned for up to £1.6m despite objections from the band.

The collection was amassed by the band’s sound engineer Huw Richards, who worked with Oasis from the release of their 1994 debut album, Definitely Maybe, until 2001. It comprises 209 DAT tapes, 73 analogue cassettes and three MiniDiscs, and is being sold by Richards’s son, Owain.

Littleton Auctions in Evesham, Worcestershire, has given the archive a guide price of between £1.2m and £1.6m, with the sale due to take place on 3 October.

Ben Homer, the auction house’s managing director, said Oasis had expressed concerns about the sale.

“The Oasis camp is aware of the auction and has expressed concerns, which is entirely understandable given the scale and significance of the material,” he said in a statement to the Guardian.

Homer said the auction house was handling the sale through the appropriate legal process and the recordings were being offered with verified provenance. He said the archive would give collectors and institutions the opportunity to acquire material documenting an important period in British music.

The collection includes what is believed to be the only recording of Oasis’s 1996 concert on the banks of Loch Lomond in Scotland. It also contains recordings of numerous rehearsals and soundchecks, as well as informal conversations involving the Gallagher brothers and members of the touring crew.

Owain Richards, who is also a sound engineer, said he had previously been in discussions with Oasis’s management after the band sought some of the recordings.

He told the Times those discussions had ultimately “fizzled away” and that the band wanted the tapes returned rather than sold elsewhere.

Richards said his father had meticulously preserved the recordings, which date from a period when concertgoers were far less likely to make their own recordings on mobile phones. “It really is a piece of history,” he said.

Richards said the audio remained in sufficiently good condition to be mastered for a live album. The recordings cannot, however, simply be released by whoever buys them. Oasis retain the intellectual property rights, meaning the archive cannot be commercially exploited without the band’s cooperation.

Littleton Auctions has described the collection as a significant record of the band’s live career and said it could be of interest to collectors, scholars and museums.

The auction comes as interest in Oasis continues to grow since the band’s reunion last year, when Noel and Liam Gallagher returned to the stage together for the first time in 15 years.

Oasis became one of the biggest British rock bands of the 1990s, with albums including (What’s the Story) Morning Glory? and Be Here Now. Their career was marked by the fractious relationship between the Gallagher brothers, whose arguments eventually contributed to the band’s split in 2009.

The reunion saw Oasis play sold-out dates in Britain, North America, Australia and Asia. The brothers were also pictured together at the Venice film festival this weekend, where Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger, a film documenting their return, was premiered.

The Littleton auction will also feature other Oasis memorabilia, including a pair of Adidas Kegler Super Ostrich trainers given to Noel Gallagher. Oasis were approached for comment.

title: Merz says ‘shock’ AfD victory in key German state ‘is an election result we cannot simply move past’ – Europe live
excerpt:
German chancellor says vote for far-right party ‘will have repercussions’ across the country

Far-right AfD wins key German state election but falls just short of majority

Merz begins by saying “we a...
body_text:
German chancellor says vote for far-right party ‘will have repercussions’ across the country

Far-right AfD wins key German state election but falls just short of majority

Merz begins by saying “we are all deeply shocked” by the result in Saxony-Anchalt.

“We did not expect it to turn out this way,” he says.

He says the vote “will have repercussions” and says even a glance at who congratulated the AfD shows “the level of international attention this result has garnered.”

He says that “when nearly 60% of voters … cast their ballots for political parties that fundamentally call into question our country’s democratic institutions … it is an election result we cannot simply move past as if nothing happened.”

He concedes this is “the most severe election defeat the CDU has suffered in years, indeed in decades.”

A little more of European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen’s words in Greenland earlier here:

double quotation markGreenland can count on the EU. Territorial integrity sovereignty, the inviolability of borders, these are fundamental principles of international law. We want to be very clear and repeat again here that Greenland’s future is for the people of Greenland and Denmark to decide, no one else.

Meanwhile, EU’s Ursula von der Leyen, Greenland’s PM Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Denmark’s PM Mette Frederiksen are speaking in Nuuk, Greenland.

Their press conference is part of von der Leyen’s landmark visit to Greenland, during which she pledged €200m to invest in projects there focusing on energy, raw materials and connectivity there, AFP reported.

The new EU-Greenland Partnership Package is meant to strengthen the territory’s ties with the EU amid continuing interest from the US president, Donald Trump.

In a pointed remark, von der Leyen said the bloc “stands in full solidarity with Denmark and Greenland,” and Greenland’s future is only for the people of Greenland to decide.

Merz ends the presser with another defence of his time in the government, and saying he needs to get better at explaining his rationale and reforms to the public.

He concedes there is a problem, and he needs to address it.

And that’s where the press conference ends.

Merz also gets asked about Germany’s position on Russia and Ukraine given the high support for pro-Russian parties in Saxony-Anhalt.

He says it was 57.7% of the vote last night.

He says resolutely that he will “not deviate by even a millimeter from my fundamental conviction that we must defend our freedom, especially now, from Russia.”

“I will likely have to explain this much more frequently and much more intensively,” he concedes.

But he says the threat to Germany’s internal security “is not abstract; it is very concrete” and that “if we stop supporting Ukraine, things will not get better, but worse.”

“The goal of the Russian leadership is to destabilise the value system of what we used to call the West. And that value system is not up for negotiation.”

Merz gets asked about the concerns reported among some minorities in Saxony-Anhalt about what could happen if AfD came to power.

The Guardian’s Ashifa Kassam covered that extensively before the vote.

He says that all state governments have to abide by the constitution.

“That holds true today, and will hold true tomorrow.”

In a more direct question, Merz gets asked at what point he would be prepared to accept his approach is failing and conclude that he can no longer serve as the chancellor.

Could the two other upcoming state elections be his breaking point?

He says he is “thinking hard how we can find our way back to shared political success.”

He says he is “not the sort of person that wears their emotions on their sleeve every day,” but “giving up is not an option.”

Merz also gets asked about apparent differences of opinion within the coalition government with the SPD.

He says “we need to talk” between partners, but lists what he focuses on what he says are some of this government’s success stories.

He says more needs to be done to remove obstacles to competitiveness and reduce bureaucracy.

Saxony-Anhalt’s Schulze gets asked if he can see some CDU politicians defecting to AfD to give the party a majority in the state parliament.

He says the AfD previously said it would not want to talk to other parties. But he says he cannot see any members of the CDU faction leaving to join AfD.

Merz also broadly defends his government’s track record.

He says the government will need to “demonstrate that the path we chose last year … is the right one” to regain public trust.

Merz also gets asked about his personal responsibility for allowing the AfD to gain in strength.

He points to both international trends, and domestic reasons.

He says “reassessing this situation” is needed to respond to this crisis.

But he says any democratic government relies on compromises, and “perhaps we need to emphasise, explain, that point more.”

He says he “has been reflecting” on these issues for some time, but does not elaborate as to what he is actually planning to do about it - for now.

In further comments, Merz comes fairly close to drawing a link betweeen AfD and Russia, as he says “2,500 kilometres in the east, the election results were being celebrated.”

“That comes as no surprise, given who tried to foster and bring about this outcome. In that sense, we know exactly who we are dealing with here.”

Saxony-Anhalt’s outgoing premier Sven Schulze concedes the vote and says the party “no longer has a mandate to govern” and will be in the opposition.

“The mandate to govern now lies with the AfD,” he says.

He says the decisions on what’s next lie down with the elected members.

Merz says he wants to focus on this in the coming days and weeks, and says he is aware of “our shared responsibility for our country.”

“I am aware of my personal responsibility for our country. I am determined to live up to this responsibility,” he says, seemingly dismissing any talk he could choose to step down from the post.

Merz says Germany needs “fundamental reforms” in response to the result, a challenge he says he is ready to face.

“It is a matter of nothing less than the future of our country and the opportunities available to our children and grandchildren – opportunities we must not squander,” he says.

He says the government needs to get better at explaining its actions and rationale behind them.

Merz says it is “the very essence of democracy” that people’s attitudes shift, but he says “there is one thing that is not up for a vote: the rules by which we live together and the values enshrined” in the constitution.

He says Germany “bears a special responsibility due to its history,” and will “always uphold our political order.”

“We did not expect it to turn out this way,” he says.

He says the vote “will have repercussions” and says even a glance at who congratulated the AfD shows “the level of international attention this result has garnered.”

He says that “when nearly 60% of voters … cast their ballots for political parties that fundamentally call into question our country’s democratic institutions … it is an election result we cannot simply move past as if nothing happened.”

He concedes this is “the most severe election defeat the CDU has suffered in years, indeed in decades.”

Mainstream politicians around Europe have expressed alarm after the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) swept to a historic state election victory in Germany, while nationalist figures cheered the result as a mandate for change.

While falling just short of an absolute majority, the AfD surged into first place in the Saxony-Anhalt state election on Sunday, exit polls ⁠showed, putting the far right within reach ​of power at ‌the state level for ‌the first time since the second world war.

Back to Germany, we are expecting to hear from chancellor Friedrich Merz in the next half hour.

As reported earlier (11:22), he chaired a crisis meeting with his CDU colleagues this morning, and Bild reported that he said the AfD’s win in Saxony-Anhalt had shaken his ⁠CDU party ​to ‌its core ‌and signalled that a ‌major reckoning was needed.

“This ‌shakes our party to its ​very foundations. We cannot simply carry on as ⁠before, nor can ​I, ​nor can ​the federal government,” ​Merz ‌said, according ​to ​the newspaper.

Let’s see what he says in his first public comments since the election soon.

I will bring you his comments here live, obviously.

The funeral service has just concluded with the church bells marking the occasion, as can be heard on Tanjug news agency’s live stream, which shows thousands of Mladić’s supporters gathered in the area.

Mladić is expected to be buried at a cemetery nearby in the next hour or so.

title: Germany's far-right AfD says 'democracy demands' parties work with them after state election win
excerpt:
Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD's leader in Saxony-Anhalt, says the result is a "clear mandate to govern"

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is "very, very close" to taking power, its deputy parlia...
body_text:
Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD's leader in Saxony-Anhalt, says the result is a "clear mandate to govern"

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is "very, very close" to taking power, its deputy parliamentary leader has told the BBC, after a historic victory in elections for the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Sunday's preliminary results show it fell three seats short of an outright majority, with 43.8% of the vote. It is now seeking support from other parties or individuals in order to govern.

While most German political parties refuse to work with the AfD, Beatrix von Storch called for its opponents to enter talks and said: "You cannot say I do not accept the vote of the people".

Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he was "deeply shocked" by the result, describing it as "seismic... not just in the country but also in my own political party and I take that very seriously".

His party, the conservative CDU, saw its share of the vote almost halved to 17.2% in the state's preliminary results.

Merz said it was not possible to return to "business as usual", adding that the country needed "profound reforms" and the CDU needed to "reach people at an emotional level.

"This election result is a seismic result not just in the country but also in my own political party and I take that very seriously," he said.

No far-right party has controlled a German state since World War Two, and governing at state level would mean powers over policing and local education.

Von Storch said the state's results "were on the table and now democrats have to talk to [one] another. This is what democracy demands".

She added that if parties refused to work with the AfD, "then we might end up in severe chaos and maybe we have a new election".

Her comments were echoed by AfD's leader in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, who told a news conference on Monday that the party had won a "clear mandate to govern".

The state's defeated premier, the CDU's Sven Schulze, also said the mandate to govern Saxony-Anhalt "now lies with the AfD".

Saxony-Anhalt has a small population of 2.1 million and the AfD in the state is assessed by domestic intelligence as "right-wing extremist", a classification rejected by Siegmund, 35.

The party's plans for Saxony-Anhalt, which include segregating child refugees into special classes and setting up a task-force to help detain and deport migrants who no longer have the right to be in the state, are highly controversial within Germany.

Siegmund said discussions with other parties were initiated on Sunday night and could potentially take days or weeks to conclude.

"We reach out to everybody first, we will have consultations and then we'll see whether [there are] individual parliamentary groups or MPs who would be willing to help us," he added.

The AfD is currently heading for 39 seats in the 83-seat state parliament instead of the 42 needed for an outright majority, although the result has not yet been finalised.

Von Storch told the BBC the AfD was talking to individuals within the CDU group - the largest party in both the state's outgoing coalition and Germany's government - because they were "very, very unhappy with their own party".

One idea being floated is whether there could be informal deal whereby a small party - the BSW - could give their tacit support to allow the AfD to form a minority government.

The left-wing populist BSW, which is set to win five seats, is also tough on migration and backs importing Russian gas.

The AfD has signalled an openness to talk with other parties but all - apart from the BSW - refuse to co-operate with the far-right.

The AfD leads the opinion polls nationally, ahead of the ruling conservatives of Merz and the Social Democrats, but their heartland lies in the eastern states.

They also won the 2024 state election in neighbouring Thuringia, but failed to secure enough seats to win power.

Among the AfD's policies is a highly controversial plan for "remigration", which is widely understood to mean mass deportations of migrants, although the party says it refers to deporting criminals and those in the country illegally.

Commentators and political opponents called AfD's victory a watershed and break with the past.

"This isn't just about Saxony-Anhalt," Siegmund told supporters overnight. "It's a signal for the whole of Germany - a self-confident signal."

On Sunday, US President Donald Trump posted a screenshot of the state's projected results on his Truth Social platform. Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev then took a screengrab of Trump's post and praised a "historic win for the pragmatic AfD".

Dmitriev had earlier praised the Russia-friendly AfD as "the party of hope and reason, co-operation truth and hope for Germany". Ahead of Germany's federal election last year, US Vice-President JD Vance endorsed the party, in a move criticised in Germany as political interference.

Polish centre-right Prime Minister Donald Tusk saw the result very differently, saying "in Poland only idiots and traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD".

Asked about those who had expressed fears over the far-right party gaining power in the state, deputy parliamentary leader Beatrix von Storch told the BBC that its supporters were afraid of "losing our economy, they are afraid of losing our inner security".

She said conservative voters were turning to alternative political parties because they were not being listened to".

She added that the party's detractors should: "Wake up and realise what happened in several other European states... The conservative parties will disappear from the landscape as it happened in Italy, as it's about to happen in the UK, as it might also happen in France".

Germany's far-right AfD hails big victory in east, but falls short of majority

title: Italy women's basketball star tears into ref after missing game-tying shot vs US in Women's World Cup
excerpt: Riley Gaines and Louis Barker recap their Indiana Fever game experience and break down the WNBA conversation around Simone Biles, Sophie Cunningham, Caitlin Clark, and the fight to protect women’s spo...
body_text:
Riley Gaines and Louis Barker recap their Indiana Fever game experience and break down the WNBA conversation around Simone Biles, Sophie Cunningham, Caitlin Clark, and the fight to protect women’s sports.

Italian women’s basketball star Cecilia Zandalasini was irate with FIBA officials at the end of their loss to the U.S. on Sunday in their Women’s World Cup game.

Zandalasini was looking to tie the game with a 3-pointer in the closing moments of Italy’s 55-52 loss to the U.S. She was creating space while being guarded by Jackie Young. As she was dribbling, she reacted as though Young swiped her in the face.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Cecilia Zandalasini during the Women's FIBA World Cup 2026 between the USA and Italy on Sept. 6, 2026, in Berlin, Germany. (NurPhoto via Getty Images)

No foul was called and Zandalasini was forced to put up a contested shot. She missed and the game was over. However, Zandalasini was not finished with the officials.

She was seen yelling at them and needed to be held back by some staff members.

Zandalasini apologized for her outburst later.

Italy's Cecilia Zandalasini rebounds during the Women's Basketball World Cup match between the United States and Italy in Berlin on Sept. 6, 2026. (AP Photo/Ebrahim Noroozi)

"I would like to apologize for the way I reacted," she said in the postgame press conference. "It wasn’t sportsmanship at all. Yeah, just wanted to apologize to the team and the referee. When I wear this jersey, it’s just a different me I guess. I feel embarrassed. I just wanted to say that out loud and to whoever watches."

Zandalasini finished with 14 points and seven rebounds in 27 minutes.

Italy had the U.S. on the ropes the entire game before the Americans utilized their interior offense to draw fouls and grab free points at the foul line.

Paige Bueckers #4 of the USA Basketball Women's National Team plays defense during the 2026 FIBA World Cup Qualifying Tournament game against the Italy Women's National Team on Sept. 6, 2026, at Berlin Arena in Berlin, Germany. (NBAE via Getty Images)

Young led the way for the U.S. with 10 points, four rebounds and three assists. Angel Reese added eight points and three rebounds.

Ryan Gaydos is a senior editor for Fox News Digital.

title: Four arrested after baby dies on camping trip in Staffordshire
excerpt:
Two women and two men arrested on suspicion of murder after death of three-month-old girl near Great Wyrley

Four people have been arrested on suspicion of murder after a three-month-old girl died in ...
body_text:
Two women and two men arrested on suspicion of murder after death of three-month-old girl near Great Wyrley

Four people have been arrested on suspicion of murder after a three-month-old girl died in Staffordshire while camping with her family.

Officers said they were made aware of the death on Saturday at 8.45am after being called by paramedics from the West Midlands ambulance service, who were responding to a report of a child in cardiac arrest. An air ambulance was also sent but the child was pronounced dead at the scene.

Staffordshire police said they attended the scene in woodland off Strawberry Lane near Great Wyrley and arrested four people on suspicion of murder. This includes a 42-year-old man and 30-year-old woman from south Staffordshire, a 20-year-old woman from Wolverhampton and an 18-year-old man from Walsall.

Officers said all four had now been bailed with conditions while the investigation continued. DI Josh Lee, from Staffordshire police’s child protection team, said: “I want to assure the local community that we are working around the clock to investigate the circumstances of this tragic incident, which has understandably caused concern.

“While we can confirm that all four people have been arrested on suspicion of murder, we are still working hard to obtain further evidence and we are keeping an open mind as to the circumstances of the death at this very early stage, which we are treating as an isolated incident.

“All four people were arrested at the scene of the incident and have been released on bail.

“While we fully understand that speculation into the nature of this incident is likely to take place, we’d ask people to follow this page for factual, accurate updates as our investigation unfolds and to avoid sharing unconfirmed and speculative claims online.”

A spokesperson for West Midlands ambulance service said: “We were called to reports of a medical emergency near to Strawberry Lane at 8.39am on Saturday. Two ambulances, two paramedic officers and a helicopter from the Midlands air ambulance charity attended the scene.

“On arrival we discovered one patient, a female child. Ambulance staff immediately began administering advanced life support but sadly, despite their best efforts it became apparent nothing could be done to save her and she was confirmed dead at the scene.”

title: Tanzanian President Samia's husband dies in hospital
excerpt:
The Tanzanian president's (pictured above) husband, Hafidh Ameir Hassan, kept a low profile and was rarely pictured

The husband of Tanzania's President Samia Suluhu Hassan, Hafidh Ameir Hassan, has d...
body_text:
The Tanzanian president's (pictured above) husband, Hafidh Ameir Hassan, kept a low profile and was rarely pictured

The husband of Tanzania's President Samia Suluhu Hassan, Hafidh Ameir Hassan, has died while receiving treatment at a hospital in Zanzibar.

Vice-president Deogratius Ndejembi - who made the official announcement of Ameir's death - said he had been suffering from a heart condition.

Ndejembi added that funeral arrangements are under way in Kizimkazi, a village on the country's semi-autonomous island of Zanzibar.

Ameir was an agricultural academic who largely kept a low public profile. He became Tanzania's first First Gentleman after President Samia took office in 2021.

In his announcement, Ndejembi said Ameir died at 08:00 local time (06:00 GMT) on Monday at the Emilio Mzena Memorial Hospital.

The vice-president led tributes as he conveyed his condolences to Samia, as well as Ameir's family and friends.

Kenyan President William Ruto said he received the news of his passing with "deep sorrow".

"President Samia has lost a lifelong companion, her children a beloved father, and Tanzania a distinguished son," he wrote on social media.

Zambia's President Hakainde Hichilema also shared his condolences, saying that they "stand side by side" with the first family, and all of Tanzania during "this difficult time".

Similarly, Burundi's President Évariste Ndayishimiye paid his respects and prayed for Samia and her family to have "comfort and strength in this difficult moment".

"May he [God] grant eternal rest to the soul of Hafidh Ameir Hassan," he added.

The First Gentleman rarely appeared in public alongside the president. He was only occasionally seen with her at official events.

He married Samia in 1978, before she entered national politics. The couple had four children - three sons and a daughter - together.

Their daughter, Wanu Hafidh Ameir, is also a politician who currently serves in Zanzibar's House of Representatives in the National Assembly.

title: Legal veterans lead fightback against Trump’s ‘full-out assault on democracy’
excerpt:
Advocacy groups expand legal challenges and condemn president’s ‘self-serving attempts to take over midterms’

A cluster of advocacy groups that boast veteran lawyers, voting experts and ex-judges hav...
body_text:
Advocacy groups expand legal challenges and condemn president’s ‘self-serving attempts to take over midterms’

A cluster of advocacy groups that boast veteran lawyers, voting experts and ex-judges have expanded legal challenges to Donald Trump’s authoritarian executive orders on voting and other presidential actions they see as a “war” on the rule of law in the US.

Heavy legal opposition to Trump’s two executive orders on elections to curb voting rights and supplant the authority of states on election matters has come from the Democracy Defenders Fund, the Campaign Legal Center, the American Civil Liberties Union and kindred groups.

These legal outfits and like-minded allies have won key lawsuits on election issues, plus litigation thwarting Trump’s moves to end birthright citizenship and a $1.8bn slush fund that could have paid money to allies including January 6 rioters he deemed were unjustly charged.

Since Trump returned to power, for instance, Democracy Defenders Fund and the Campaign Legal Center have jointly filed lawsuits against Trump’s 2025 and 2026 executive orders on voting, challenging their constitutionality to set new voting rules that by law are run by the states.

Key legal briefs they filed together include an August one on behalf of several voting rights groups and local officials in two states to block Trump’s March 2026 executive order that would restrict voting by mail and authorize the US Postal Service to implement rules to that end.

Other groups that have accelerated their legal challenges to Trump’s moves to thwart voting rights and expand his executive powers in other ways, include the Brennan Center for Justice, Democracy Forward, the Democratic Attorneys General Association and the Washington Litigation Group.

Last month, for instance, 24 Democratic attorney generals and other plaintiffs filed suit to block USPS from moving forward with rules to curb mail voting and in late August won a temporary 14-day restraining order from federal judge Indira Talwani in Massachusetts.

In response, the DoJ’s solicitor general John Sauer on Thursday appealed to the supreme court to lift the injunction, arguing in heated words that the freeze would create “serious, irreparable harm on the federal government, the states themselves, and the voting public”.

On 4 September Talwani made her injunction permanent, writing that implementing Trump’s order so close to the election “threatens disenfranchisement of millions of United States citizens who seek to vote by mail.” She also stressed that “the record includes no evidence relating to fraudulent mail voting to support the rushed implementation.”

Sauer on 6 September responded with another emergency appeal to the high court urging it permit the new USPS rules to go into effect, claiming that it “does not seize control of states’ administration of elections — it simply imposes reasonable preparation requirements for certain election-related mail.”

In a related twist, a detailed whistleblower complaint that Democratic senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut released last week alleged that the USPS has been proceeding with a “secretive, rushed” effort to implement Trump’s order that could lead to “catastrophic failure” with this year’s mail-in voting.

About 50 million Americans, the majority of whom are Democrats, vote by mail, according to reports.

With the elections about two months away, the legal groups are stepping up efforts to thwart “self-serving attempts to take over the midterms”, said a former DoJ lawyer, which experts fear may create chaos and disenfranchise millions of voters.

Anna Baldwin, director of voting rights litigation at the Campaign Legal Center, told the Guardian: “The CLC and the DDF have worked closely together on two ongoing lawsuits challenging the president’s unlawful voting executive orders that attempt to dictate election rules. We’ve teamed up in the supreme court on a brief filed by former state and federal judges, including noted conservative judges, that emphasized just how unlawful and dangerous the president’s efforts to dictate election rules are.”

Baldwin, who spent 14 years in the justice department’s civil rights division, said the CLC and the DDF have also “worked together in federal cases filed in Oregon and California to make sure that the DoJ isn’t able to seize voters’ sensitive data by making false claims about non-citizen voting. In cases around the country, the Campaign Legal Center is pushing back on the DoJ’s lawless efforts to vacuum up and aggregate sensitive data to create a national voter file of some sort.”

Further, former ambassador Norm Eisen, the executive chair of the Democracy Defenders Fund, which he co-founded in 2023, told the Guardian that since its inception the DDF has been involved in more than 300 legal cases and matters in three primary areas: elections, the rule of law and anti-corruption.

Eisen said the group, whose board boasts former federal judge and conservative stalwart J Michael Luttig and liberal-leaning ex-federal judge Nancy Gertner, likes to work in conjunction on cases with other ideologically diverse and nonpartisan groups like the CLC and the WLG because “they both have strong bipartisan credibility. It’s a big-tent approach we’ve taken with our election work.”

Eisen said Luttig and Gertner were instrumental in helping recruit dozens of former judges with bipartisan credentials to file amicus briefs on multiple matters including an August one to the supreme court opposing Trump’s 2026 executive order to curb mail voting.

For its part, the WLG this summer hired about half a dozen new lawyers to handle election-related litigation. “As the midterms approach with growing concerns about potential federal interference in elections, we’ve brought on more attorneys to be even more prepared to litigate sensitive matters under acute time pressure,” said James Pearce, a principal with the WLG.

Elsewhere, Sophia Lin Lakin, who leads the ACLU Voting Rights Project, said the group had been “pushing back” on administration efforts to seize personal voting data from states, and said the ACLU has been involved in 26 of 30 legal challenges to the administration on the issue. To date, the administration has lost 23 cases where rulings have been made.

Critics say Trump, the DoJ, the USPS and the Department of Homeland Security seem to be laying the groundwork for further attacks on the nation’s election rules, citing Trump’s false claims about election fraud and his radical plans to change voting rules.

In July in a televised speech, Trump falsely portrayed the nation’s voting system as riddled with fraud and condemned voting by mail and non-citizen voting. “Mail-in ballots are inherently corrupt,” Trump claimed without evidence, even though he voted twice by mail this year.

Trump, who continues to blame voting fraud for his 2020 loss to Joe Biden, also charged that non-citizen voting, which is illegal and historically minuscule, poses a “crisis of election security”. Trump’s fixation on noncitizen voting is belied by a database from the rightwing Heritage Foundation that only cites 100 cases over a quarter-century.

But according to documents reviewed by the New York Times, hundreds of DHS agents have been engaged in a hunt to find noncitizens among registered voters. The chief of the DHS has said ICE agents could be sent to polling places “if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant”.

The DoJ has helped to amplify Trump’s bogus election claims with legal threats and actions.

In July, Harmeet Dhillon, who runs the department’s civil rights division, wrote to officials in 50 states warning that “any election officer, including the chief election officer of the state, who knowingly retains noncitizens on the state’s [voter list] or facilitates noncitizens in receiving and casting ballots could be subject to criminal liability”.

In August, the DoJ announced plans to send a larger-than-usual contingent of 1,000 lawyers to monitor voting nationwide, raising concerns that such large efforts could lead to voter intimidation.

And in a harbinger of coming legal fights, Trump announced on his Truth Social platform last month that the DoJ’s Ed Martin, a key election denialist in charge of pardons, was leaving to handle election-related litigation.

Former DoJ lawyers say administration threats to voting rights make opposition from legal advocates crucial.

Stacey Young, a lawyer who left the department at the start of 2025 after 18 years to found Justice Connection, a group of more than 3,000 ex-DoJ lawyers and other alumni, denounced Trump’s moves “to interfere” with elections.

“The constitution makes clear that the president has no authority over the administration of our elections, but that hasn’t stopped this president, or those he put in power at the justice department, from trying to interfere,” Young said in a statement. “We’re taking these threats seriously and leveraging our collective strengths to protect election integrity, which is key to maintaining a functioning democracy.”

Justice Connection is working with experts in its alumni network to engage with the media, Congress and the public to highlight the justice department’s traditional role in election security and ensuring compliance with federal voting laws.

Other DoJ alumni agree that opposition to Trump’s election agenda is critical.

“These organizations are doing critical work in protecting the ability of people to vote and make their voices heard – a cornerstone of democracy,” said Michael Bromwich, a former DoJ inspector general. “The full-out assault on democracy must be addressed through the courts because Congress has proven itself unwilling and unable to check the undemocratic steps taken by the administration.”

Barbara McQuade, a former US attorney for eastern Michigan who now teaches law at the University of Michigan, said: “Large law firms sent armies of young attorneys to our nation’s airports to represent individuals caught up in Trump’s travel ban. That is not happening any more because of the ‘deals’ they negotiated with the Trump administration in his second term to support his pet causes.

“Thank goodness for groups like the Democracy Defenders Fund, which are attracting top legal talent and challenging some of Trump’s lawless activities. Their work is protecting the rights of all Americans.”

Further, Nick Brown, Washington state’s attorney general, who chairs an election protection group for the Democratic Attorneys General Association, said it has teamed up with some legal advocacy groups such as the Brennan Center, States United and the DDF to hold “strategy sessions” to prepare for potential disruptive moves by the Trump administration in the November elections.

Brown also attacked the administration’s appeal to the supreme court to move forward with Trump’s executive order on voting by mail, despite Judge Talwani’s strong concerns and Daga’s litigation against it.

He said: “As the court said, states’ compliance with this illegal order would be ‘practically impossible’ before the November elections given the unprecedented demands it would put on state and local elections officials. The chaos that would cause is exactly what Trump wants. That’s why we continue to fight for a fair and properly administered election.”

Baldwin too raised strong concerns about the DoJ’s push to get the supreme court to issue a ruling that would expedite Trump’s executive order on voting by mail.

She said: “The DoJ’s slapdash effort at getting the supreme court’s blessing to turn the USPS into a gatekeeper for mail would be a farce, if it didn’t put our fundamental right to vote in the crosshairs. Given the importance of what is at stake, the DoJ’s continued efforts are nothing more than an attempt to foist chaos on the electoral process. But they will fail.”

Other lawyers engaged in key election legal battles and other litigation voice optimism they will prevail.

Tianna Mays, the legal director of the DDF, said: “The Trump administration has declared war on the rule of law, yet our democratic guardrails are still holding. We refuse to stand by idly while this administration flouts the constitution and attempts to eviscerate our institutions.”

title: Discovery beneath soccer field reveals massive medieval convent lost for centuries
excerpt:
SOLVA Archaeology Service in Belgium announced the recent discovery of ancient Roman artifacts and remains, including a well-preserved dog, in Velzeke. (Source: SOLVA Dienst Archeologie)

Researchers ...
body_text:
SOLVA Archaeology Service in Belgium announced the recent discovery of ancient Roman artifacts and remains, including a well-preserved dog, in Velzeke. (Source: SOLVA Dienst Archeologie)

Researchers recently uncovered a long-lost medieval convent in an unusual location in Denmark: a soccer field — with an expert sharing details with Fox News Digital about the "rare" find.

The discovery, made in Roskilde, was announced last month by ROMU, a state-recognized Danish museum organization.

St. Clare's Convent, which was built in the 13th century, was found through a ground-penetrating radar survey ahead of plans to build an underground parking facility.

FORBIDDEN PASSAGE? SECRET MEDIEVAL TUNNEL FOUND BENEATH ANCIENT PAGAN GRAVES, ARCHAEOLOGISTS SAY

"The survey revealed a well-preserved convent complex approximately one meter [three feet] below ground level," officials said in a press release.

The scans also "revealed traces of the convent’s buildings, including rooms, columns, cloisters and a church in the southern wing," officials said.

Researchers in Roskilde, Denmark, have discovered the remains of a long-lost medieval convent beneath a modern soccer field. (Nationalmuseet/NIKU; Jesper Langkilde/ROMU)

"The eastern wing, in particular, is exceptionally well-preserved, with clearly defined rooms and vault pillars," the statement said.

St. Clare's was one of five monastic sites in medieval Roskilde. Unlike the other four, it was not protected as an ancient monument because it was believed to have been lost.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNEARTH REMNANTS OF FORGOTTEN CITY 'MARKED BY CONFLICT' BURIED BELOW BUSTLING HUB

Researchers are working with the municipality on plans for trial excavations at the proposed parking site.

Excavations of monasteries and convents are "rare," said Jesper Langkilde, an archaeologist and museum curator at ROMU.

Langkilde told Fox News Digital he was "quite surprised" by the discovery.

St. Clare's Convent, built in the 13th century, was identified through a ground-penetrating radar survey in Roskilde. (Heritage Art/Heritage Images via Getty Images; Nationalmuseet / NIKU)

"I almost didn’t believe my own eyes that so much was still there, and that we got such a clear image of it," he said.

The convent was a large complex, measuring roughly 230 feet by 230 feet.

Although the convent was demolished in the 16th century and hundreds of thousands of its bricks were removed, much of its underground footprint survived.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER LOST MEDIEVAL CITY THAT VANISHED WITHOUT A TRACE: 'TRUE TIME CAPSULE'

Langkilde said the radar is detecting the lowest portions of the walls and foundations, which were made with large boulders that were often left in place when medieval buildings were torn down.

Historical records show that about 500,000 bricks were sold after the convent was demolished, but Langkilde said a complex of its size could easily have contained twice that number.

The newly identified convent complex measured roughly 230 feet by 230 feet before its demolition in the 16th century. (Nationalmuseet/NIKU)

Though there hasn't been an excavation of the site yet, Langkilde said archaeologists expect to find "quite a lot of artifacts," especially those from daily medieval life.

Excavators expect to find everything from "lots of pottery sherds and animal bones" to "religious objects, like pendant crosses, rosary beads and pilgrims' badges" and objects related to writing and books, he said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"The convents and monasteries were centers of literacy and had libraries and book production," added Langkilde, noting that book fittings, writing utensils and personal effects like combs and needles are also expected.

If organic remains are well-preserved, archaeologists could learn more about the nuns' diets and the plants grown in the convent gardens.

"[The discovery] is very significant, since we know very little of the monasteries in Roskilde from an archeological point of view."

Researchers also expect to find burials at the site, which "can tell us about who the nuns were and who else was buried at the convent," Langkilde said.

The discoveries could also reveal the convent's international connections. Its first nuns are believed to have come from a convent in Strasbourg, according to Langkilde.

"The convents were part of international networks, so it would be interesting to look for signs of international relations in the [material] from this site," he said.

"[The discovery] is very significant, since we know very little of the monasteries in Roskilde from an archaeological point of view," he said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The expert also called the discovery "a very big step forward for our knowledge of the medieval monasteries."

Archaeologist Jesper Langkilde, seen above, said he was surprised by how much of the medieval convent remained detectable beneath the ground. (Lene Steinbeck/ROMU)

"[They] played a key part in the development of Roskilde as one of the most important and wealthiest towns in medieval Denmark," he said.

Langkilde added, "It is an excellent example of how much archeological knowledge a geophysical survey can contribute — under the right circumstances — without even putting a shovel to the ground."

Andrea Margolis is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital and Fox Business. Readers can follow her on X at @andreamargs or send story tips to andrea.margolis@fox.com.

title: Indonesia volcano eruption leaves 270,000 stranded as airports extend closure
excerpt:
Watch: Lava fountain and ash cloud as Indonesia volcano erupts

Some 270,000 passengers have been left stranded across Indonesia after a volcanic eruption grounded more than 2,000 flights and forced a...
body_text:
Watch: Lava fountain and ash cloud as Indonesia volcano erupts

Some 270,000 passengers have been left stranded across Indonesia after a volcanic eruption grounded more than 2,000 flights and forced airports to suspend operations for a second day.

Anak Krakatau, located 150km (90mi) from Jakarta, began erupting late on Friday, producing lava fountains and sending volcanic ash into the capital and the Lampung province. It stayed seismically active throughout the weekend.

Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International and three other airports have extended closures till 18:00 local time on Monday after volcanic ash was detected in airspaces near them.

Schools in the region moved classes online while some shipping operations were also disrupted.

Snaking queues formed at the departure halls in Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport on Monday as stranded passengers sought refunds and tried to get updates on when they would be able to fly.

Finna, who was supposed to fly home to Jakarta from Malang, a city in East Java, on Sunday morning, described the frezny at the airport as flights got repeatedly rescheduled.

"It was very crowded because passengers from the morning flights had piled up, while those scheduled for later departures still didn't know what would happen," the 46-year-old told BBC Indonesian.

"We were all glued to the flight information screens."

Not wanting to deal with the uncertainty, Finna eventually spent the night on two intercity trains before arriving in Jakarta at 03:00 on Monday.

"Everyone seems to be racking their brains [figuring alternative transportation options]", said Jo Shaw, who was visiting Indonesia with members of her conservation charity Save the Rhino International.

Shaw's team had axed their plans to camp out at Java's Ujung Kulon National Park after authorities raised its alert level for the Anak Krakatau volcano.

"Being stranded in an airport hotel is a relatively minor inconvenience to be resolved in a few days hopefully," Shaw said, adding that she was more concerned about the teams working on the ground with the rhinos under such environmental conditions.

A newly wed Malaysian couple who had just spent a week in Bali said they were told that the next flight back to Kuala Lumpur wouldn't be until 11 September.

"What are we going to do here for another five days? We only prepared enough money for our honeymoon and [were supposed] to go home yesterday," Amir Hamzah told Malaysia's national news agency Bernama.

"We thought we would just sleep at the airport for a few hours and then take the morning flight home [on Monday]. We never thought we would end up being stuck here for days," the 29-year-old said.

On Monday, Indonesia's Geological Agency warned that "the probability of further eruptions in the coming periods remains high".

Volcanic ash reached as high as 6,000m on the Java side of the volcano and 15,000m on the Sumatra side and in some parts of Java's westernmost province Banten, the meteorological agency BMKG said.

Anak Krakatau sits on the Sunda Strait about midway between the islands of Java and Sumatra.

The most recent eruption occurred at 20:23 on Sunday, according to the agency.

"We ‌cannot ascertain when this ‌will end due to the dynamic weather," Transport Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said in relation to the temporary closures of the affected airports.

Dudy said on Sunday that authorities across the airports have been conducting tests every 30 minutes "to anticipate whether the ash spread is widening or subsiding".

Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International and three other airports have extended closures till 18:00 on Monday

Authorities have warned against approaching or engaging in activities within a 3km radius from the active crater, while ships passing through the Sunda Strait have also been prohibited from entering an exclusion zone of 3km radius from it.

Authorities have also confirmed there is no tsunami warning linked to the recent activity of the volcano.

Anak Krakatau, which means Child of Krakatoa, has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of last century in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa.

The volcano collapsed in December 2018 triggering a huge tsunami which killed over 400 people, and displaced and injured thousands more on the nearby coastlines of Sumatra and Java.

Scientists found that some of the chunks of rock that slid from the volcano when it collapsed were about 70-90m high.

The Pacific Ring of Fire refers to a string of volcanoes, earthquake sites and tectonic plates around the Pacific. It spreads across 40,000km (25,000 miles) from the southern tip of South America all the way to New Zealand.

Roughly 90% of all earthquakes occur along the area and the ring is dotted with 75% of all active volcanoes on Earth, that's 452 individual active volcanoes.

With reporting by Farida Susanty in Jakarta and Koh Ewe in Singapore
