title: What the US militarisation of Latin America could look like
excerpt: Latin America is seeing growing military activity by the United States. Under the umbrella of the Americas Counter-Cartel Coalition (ACCC), launched by President Donald Trump in March, US forces are c...
body_text:
Latin America is seeing growing military activity by the United States. Under the umbrella of the Americas Counter-Cartel Coalition (ACCC), launched by President Donald Trump in March, US forces are carrying out strikes on vessels suspected of drug trafficking, while US officials are deepening ties and cooperation with Latin American militaries.

This reflects the growing push from Washington towards militarisation of the region, as left-wing politics decline. For Latin America, this may spell the return of coercive US policies.

The projection of US military power, whether through coordinated operations, US boots on the ground or the use of regional bases, will not help improve regional security and fight crime. If anything, it could undermine democracy and usher in more violence and instability.

Apart from the US, the ACCC includes 17 Latin American and Caribbean nations: Argentina, Bahamas, Belize, Bolivia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Guyana, Guatemala, Paraguay, Jamaica, Panama, Trinidad and Tobago, Honduras, El Salvador, the Dominican Republic, Colombia and Peru.

Although Venezuela is not officially part of the coalition, it appears it has opened up its territory for US operations. With its informal participation, the ACCC is able to complete the “Andean arc”, which accounts for the entirety of the cocaine production distributed and sold in the US and Europe. This is also where many of the region’s organised crime groups operate.

But the coalition appears to be about more than just narcotics. Trump has said that the ACCC’s mandate is to counter “malign foreign influences from outside the Western Hemisphere” – a veiled reference to China.

The fact that the ACCC was created in Florida just two months after the US army had carried out a ground operation in Venezuela and deposed its president, Nicolas Maduro, was also significant.

Another step in that direction came on August 4 , when the US Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) announced the creation of the Western Hemisphere Joint Task Force, which will “synchronise U.S. military operations with allies and partners to counter threats, strengthen regional security and respond rapidly to crises across the Western Hemisphere”. The new task force will integrate command and control of the 18 members of the ACCC.

Washington is clearly seeking to reassert coercive hegemony over the region. It wants to exert greater influence and control over security and defence decisions in the region, in what appears to be a resurrection of the 1823 Monroe Doctrine, now renamed the Trump Corollary.

Recent operations in the region have shed light on what a renewed US force projection might look like. In June, Trump revealed on Truth Social that the US army, acting in coordination with Venezuelan authorities, carried out an air strike targeting Hector Guerrero Flores, leader of the criminal gang, Tren de Aragua, in Bolivar state. In a statement, the Venezuelan government later acknowledged the joint action by both countries.

In late August and early September, the newly created Western Hemisphere Joint Task Force attacked several suspected vessels, killing at least two people. This was a continuation of the “Southern Spear” operation, which to date has killed at least 220 people with no investigation launched into whether they were all indeed involved in drug trafficking.

Added to this is the announcement made by Secretary of Defence, Pete Hegseth, that newly inaugurated Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has authorised the US to conduct military operations in Colombia “to combat narco-terrorism”.

All of this means, the US is seeking greater military reach in Latin America, whether in the form of bilateral cooperation through joint operations or unilateral action involving overflights of the countries’ territories and even access to national military bases. There will likely be US troops on the ground involved in operations to neutralise whatever activities the US perceives as a threat.

Latin America is not new to US military intervention. During the Cold War, Washington was extensively involved in mostly covert activity in the region, but there were also overt operations, such as the invasion of the Bay of Pigs in Cuba and of the island nation of Grenada. In many cases, the civilian population faced violence as a result of the US interventions.

After the Cold War, US involvement took the shape of anti-drug campaigns, which similarly did not produce positive outcomes for local communities. Take the example of Plan Colombia (2000-2015), which was meant to combat drug trafficking and leftist insurgent groups.

Although it contributed to the weakening of insurgent organisations, it also produced a lot of violence, including by the US-trained Colombian military, which was accused of killing thousands of civilians and claiming they were rebels to “show results”. US troops stationed in Colombia as part of training programmes were also accused of raping dozens of Colombian women and girls and smuggling drugs and weapons.

Plan Colombia, which received $10bn in US funding, ended up militarising Colombia’s security agenda, intensifying armed conflicts and cartel violence, as well as the persecution of union leaders, peasants and the civilian population. It failed to stop the proliferation of coca plantations.

Given the past historical record, the US push for the militarisation of Latin American states and a greater military presence in the region is unlikely to bring more security.

The effect of greater US military engagement in the region will not be limited to the security sector only.

Washington has made clear that membership in the ACCC should translate into greater national spending on defence. That means national budgets will be thrown out of balance and resources will be diverted away from vital sectors such as education, health care, housing and social security. Worsening social services provision will likely lead to more public discontent.

Then there is the question of sovereignty. The US will seek to influence the design of security and defence policies—particularly with regard to maintaining internal security and the scope of military cooperation. Washington can and will put pressure on governments and legislatures to align with its agenda.

The fact that US officials have insisted that ACCC member countries withdraw from the International Criminal Court does not bode well for transparency and accountability. Clearly, the aim is to ensure impunity for US armed forces and their allies.

It is highly likely that a lack of transparency and accountability will exacerbate the authoritarian trend that has been emerging in Latin American politics, with well-known consequences: weakening of institutions, increased discretionary power, the erosion of the rule of law, and, consequently, a decline in citizens’ quality of life.

For the Trump administration, the ACCC may be an important foreign policy win. But for Latin American societies, it is yet another threat to their fragile democratic institutions.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

title: Dozens feared trapped in collapsed building in Delhi
excerpt:
Rescuers race to free people trapped after building collapse in Delhi

A residential building in the Indian capital Delhi has collapsed with dozens of students feared trapped inside.

Eyewitnesses tol...
body_text:
Rescuers race to free people trapped after building collapse in Delhi

A residential building in the Indian capital Delhi has collapsed with dozens of students feared trapped inside.

Eyewitnesses told local media that as many as 50 people were inside the five-storey building in the Satya Niketan neighbourhood of south-west Delhi when it came down around 13:30 local time (08:00 GMT) on Sunday.

At least one person was killed and two others are in a critical condition, NDTV reports, citing local police. Six people were said to have been rescued so far.

There had been construction work going on in the basement of the building, Hostel Daze, which sits a short distance from the Delhi University campus.

Many of the students staying there were thought to be in their rooms at the time of the collapse as there were no lessons on Sunday.

A legislative assembly member said at the scene that some of the trapped students had been making calls from under the rubble.

Eyewitnesses told local media that another building beside the hostel had also collapsed.

Chief Minister of Delhi Rekha Gupta said an adjacent building had been evacuated "as a precautionary measure".

"Every possible effort is being made to safely rescue those trapped," she added.

Delhi Police said the building had only been 40 or 50 years old.

The owner of a nearby shop told news agency ANI that it was under a 100-year lease and that the leaseholder had undertaken excavation work in the basement to increase their income.

"They strengthened the upper building, but the pillars below were weak," he said, noting that the construction workers had also been buried.

The National Students' Union of India called on the government to investigate the cause of the collapse and hold anyone found responsible to account.

"Negligence with the safety of students and common people will not be tolerated at any cost," it said.

Police are searching for the owner of the building, Times of India reports.

title: Reform UK says Britain is broken. Birmingham tells another story
excerpt: This week, Reform UK gathered thousands of supporters at Birmingham’s National Exhibition Centre to present itself as a government-in-waiting. This was not a sudden interest in Britain’s second-bigges...
body_text:
This week, Reform UK gathered thousands of supporters at Birmingham’s National Exhibition Centre to present itself as a government-in-waiting. This was not a sudden interest in Britain’s second-biggest city: Reform has repeatedly used Birmingham for national campaign launches and conferences, committing considerable resources to making it a showcase for its advance.

Birmingham – young, working-class, multiracial and almost evenly divided between residents recorded as white and those from Black, Asian, mixed and other ethnic groups – is precisely the kind of city Reform leader Nigel Farage’s politics portrays as a warning: a place where an older Britain has supposedly been displaced by an alien new one.

In May’s local elections, Reform became the largest single group on the Birmingham City Council, winning 23 of 101 seats.

The party’s growing presence in Birmingham, however, is not proof that multiculturalism has failed. It is a warning about the feeling of abandonment spreading across Britain.

Reform’s gains in the city demand serious attention. They should neither be minimised by those repelled by its politics nor inflated into a popular mandate the party did not win.

Birmingham is not one electoral community. It is a mosaic of neighbourhoods with different histories, class compositions and political instincts. According to an analysis of the 2021 census, 48.6 percent of residents identified within the broad white category and 51.4 percent within Black, Asian, mixed or other ethnic categories. But citywide diversity does not mean every ward is equally diverse, or that ethnicity is the only lens through which people vote.

Reform’s strongest performances were concentrated in particular outer-city wards which are poor and less diverse. Meanwhile, the Green Party won the largest number of votes across the city, but due to Britain’s first-past-the-post system, got only 19 seats. Labour collapsed to 17 seats (down from 65), the Conservative Party got 16, the Liberal Democrats 12, and 14 went to independent groups and candidates. The overall result of the election was fragmentation, not a far-right conversion.

Being the largest group in the council has not translated into power for Reform either. The party has found no partners. The city is now run by a collaborative minority administration of Liberal Democrats, Greens and the “Better Birmingham” Independents group, with a Liberal Democrat leader and Green deputy.

Reform has neither won Birmingham nor governs it. It has a foothold.

This matters because too much national commentary treats disillusionment with Labour as if it can travel in only one direction. It is benefitting Reform, but it is also creating space for a progressive challenge.

Under their leader Zack Polanski, the Greens have offered a clearer language of economic justice, public investment and opposition to racism. Nationally, they won the Gorton and Denton by-election in February, cementing their position as a credible progressive electoral option, leading to unprecedented council gains, took control of councils, won mayorships, and broke new ground in the Scottish and Welsh parliaments

The result has exposed Labour’s twin vulnerability: voters are moving to the right, but also to a left that has rejected the premise that Farage speaks for everyone left behind.

What Reform and other parties are doing is occupying a political vacuum left by failed centrist politics.

In Birmingham, it is hardly surprising that Labour is being abandoned. For years, residents were told to absorb decline as though it were unavoidable weather. The Labour-controlled council effectively declared bankruptcy in 2023 after historic equal-pay liabilities, a disastrous IT programme and the long erosion of local government funding.

Services were cut, council tax rose, youth provision disappeared and a prolonged refuse strike left rubbish in the streets. The cost-of-living crisis struck communities already weakened by low pay, insecure work and threadbare services.

The social conditions behind the anger are stark. Recent local data show that more than half of Birmingham’s neighbourhoods fall within England’s most deprived fifth. Official estimates put 44.4 percent of the city’s children in poverty.

Until recently, I served as associate director of health inequalities across Birmingham and Solihull’s NHS system. I saw how those pressures enter the body and the mind. Poverty becomes ill health long before a patient reaches a clinic: through cold or overcrowded housing, insecure work, unaffordable food, chronic stress, poor air quality and the practical barriers that make prevention and treatment harder to access. A city cannot remove the conditions for a healthy life and then be surprised when both illness and anger deepen.

That pain is real. Reform’s explanation for it is a fraud.

Reform offers false nostalgia: the promise of return to a secure, culturally uniform Britain that never existed for millions of working-class people. It replaces history with a comforting myth, then names migrants and minorities as the thieves of an imagined inheritance.

But simply denouncing Reform voters as racists is morally lazy and politically useless. Racism exists, and some voters are attracted precisely because Reform licenses prejudice. Others vote from fury, alienation or the desire to punish every party that has governed them. The task is to distinguish between the legitimate wound and the poisonous diagnosis offered for it.

Scapegoating is not an accidental excess of Reform’s politics. It is the mechanism that allows anger to be directed sideways and downwards rather than upwards at the people and institutions that hold economic power. It deflects from Reform’s own sources of financial support.

The party poses as an insurgency against the establishment while drawing extraordinary support from the super-rich. An analysis of Electoral Commission records found that Reform received almost 15 million pounds ($20m) in large donations in the first half of 2026, overwhelmingly from a small group of high-value donors in cryptocurrency and finance.

A party funded by millionaires and billionaires, while proposing sweeping cuts that would fall hardest on poorer households, does not threaten oligarchic power. It protects it by turning its own economic victims against one another.

What Reform’s strategy misses is that ethnic-minority communities are not adjacent to the working class; they are part of it. The Pakistani care worker, Black graduate, white pensioner and former Longbridge factory worker have more in common than their differences: they share an interest in decent wages, homes, services and democratic power.

As a former Birmingham councillor, I have seen abstract differences recede when people organise around a threatened school, poor housing or a missing bus route. Solidarity does not erase racism or difference. It refuses the lie that security for one community requires insecurity for another.

Reform chose Birmingham to claim that even this city has turned against the Britain it represents. The result says something more urgent: a minority embraced Reform, while many more abandoned parties that had abandoned them.

In the end, Birmingham is Britain: diverse, unequal, wounded, creative and capable of solidarity. Its history and its present both point to the same answers – individual rights, community and public power, economic justice and common purpose – not division and scapegoating.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

title: Angry locals block famous beach as mass tourism protests escalate at vacation hot spot
excerpt: Viral video from Positano shows tourists packed onto a tight cliffside path with little room to move, drawing backlash online as experts say tour groups, day-trippers and social media are fueling over...
body_text:
Viral video from Positano shows tourists packed onto a tight cliffside path with little room to move, drawing backlash online as experts say tour groups, day-trippers and social media are fueling overwhelming crowds.

Some 100 residents staged an occupation of a beach in Ibiza recently to protest overtourism amid growing frustration over mass tourism in Spain — and more action is apparently planned.

The group gathered at Cala Saladeta, a popular tourist beach, last week, according to Balearic public broadcaster IB3.

The protest was organized by the Ibiza Youth Association, a local youth group.

INFLUENCERS REACHING PEAK BACKLASH AFTER SUMMER OF RUINED DESTINATIONS AND EXPERIENCES FOR AMERICANS

Ibiza is one of Spain's Balearic Islands in the Mediterranean Sea.

The island is visited by many tourists, with its population swelling during the summer months.

Around 100 residents staged an occupation of a popular Ibiza beach to protest overtourism and tourist crowds on the Spanish island. (Instagram/Associació de Joves d'Eivissa)

Known to locals as Eivissa, Ibiza received nearly 1.2 million tourists in the second quarter of 2025, according to data from the Balearic Islands Statistics Institute.

Organizers rallied "against tourist overcrowding," IB3 reported, and activists handed out watermelon as part of a demand "that residents be able to enjoy the island's public spaces."

CRUISE SHIP CRACKDOWN HITS TOURIST HOT SPOT AS CITY FAST-TRACKS NEW VISITOR TAX

The group said in its manifesto that "our land and our culture are being directly pushed out of public spaces, and increasingly out of private spaces, as well, displayed solely as tourist attractions," according to local outlet CadeNA SER.

Residents gathered at Cala Saladeta in Ibiza as frustration over mass tourism continues to fuel demonstrations across Spain. (Instagram/Associació de Joves d'Eivissa)

The manifesto also decried a tourism model catering to "wealthy foreigners and famous partygoers," while arguing that housing, food and other living costs have become unaffordable for residents.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"[Young people are] fed up with not being able to enjoy [the island] as tourists do, because we believe we can no longer continue giving up spaces to the visitors brought by this extractive tourism model, which makes our lives in Ibiza more precarious," the manifesto added, per Cadena SER.

Residents of Ibiza have raised concerns about tourist overcrowding and access to public spaces during the busy summer months. (German Lama/Europa Press via Getty Images)

The island's coves, which attract tourists during the busy summer season, were also a focus of the group's manifesto.

The coves "should become our coves again, clean and peaceful," the manifesto said.

"We want to reclaim places of tranquility."

"We have decided that we want to reclaim places of tranquility, including during the summer," the statement added.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

In response to the recent protests, Ibiza Island Council President Vicent Marí said the island has been a "pioneer" in combating tourist overcrowding, according to Cadena SER.

The Ibiza demonstration comes amid broader tensions surrounding mass tourism across Spain.

Ibiza is a popular Spanish island in the Mediterranean Sea and one of the country's Balearic Islands. (German Lama/Europa Press via Getty Images)

In recent years, Barcelona residents have taken to the streets to protest mass tourism, with some demonstrators spraying visitors with water guns.

On Mallorca, another of Spain's Balearic Islands, viral videos showed pickpockets targeting tourists near the island's capital of Palma.

Andrea Margolis is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital and Fox Business. Readers can follow her on X at @andreamargs or send story tips to andrea.margolis@fox.com.

title: How Charlie Kirk inspired his mentor's fight to defend reality
excerpt:
Author Frank Turek, a spiritual mentor to the late Charlie Kirk, opens up about carrying on his friend's legacy in new book, 
"The War on Reality."

For decades, author Frank Turek has defended the id...
body_text:
Author Frank Turek, a spiritual mentor to the late Charlie Kirk, opens up about carrying on his friend's legacy in new book, 
"The War on Reality."

For decades, author Frank Turek has defended the idea that a Christian worldview offers the truest explanation of reality. The murder of his close friend, Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk one year ago, only reinforced that conviction.

Now, Turek is sharing those beliefs in his new book, "The War on Reality: Recovering Truth in a World that Celebrates Lies," co-authored with Phoenix Hayes. The book argues that popular culture views about the family, gender, education and politics defy logic and aims to equip Christians to challenge these beliefs.

Kirk's wife, Erika, wrote the foreword for the book, in which Turek says she reveals the source of her late husband's quiet confidence during hostile debates on college campuses.

Charlie Kirk appears at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025 in Orem, Utah. Kirk, founder of Turning Point USA, was speaking during his "American Comeback Tour" when he was shot later that day and killed. (Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune/Getty Images)

BENNY JOHNSON RECALLS HOW CHARLIE KIRK HELPED HIS FAMILY AFTER ARSON DESTROYED THEIR DC HOME

"She writes that the reason Charlie would go to college campuses and not get flustered is because he knew that the foundation of his belief was true — that there is a God, he is not Him," Turek told Fox News Digital.

"He has put us on this earth to know him and to make him known through Jesus," Turek said. "And everything else is really just details. And so he could stand firm on a college campus despite any kind of threat or despite any question that might come his way. But he knew he had to be prepared to answer those questions."

As an example of this "war on reality," Turek pointed to the debate over transgender issues, which he argued has caused immeasurable harm to women and children.

"It's a contradictory worldview that tragically is hurting children the most, because we have people now, politicians and mostly Democrats saying... what we ought to do is transition children that are confused about their sexuality," Turek said. "This is not care, this is child abuse. It's a war on women, by the way, because now women aren't protected in women's sports or in women's changing facilities."

Turek mentored Kirk on applying strategies he discusses in the book, such as employing the laws of logic and identifying fallacies when responding to polarizing cultural topics.

Their friendship began in 2020 after Kirk asked Turek to mentor him in Christian apologetics, which is the practice of defending Christianity with evidence and reasoning. Turek said their bond deepened over time until he came to view Kirk as a son.

Frank Turek, who was feet away when Kirk was fatally shot at Utah Valley University, says his new book carries on Kirk's legacy. (Daniel Cole/Reuters)

BILL MAHER TO APPEAR IN CHARLIE KIRK DOCUMENTARY, REMEMBERS LOVING HIS INTERVIEW WITH THE TPUSA LEADER

"Charlie was the same person offstage that he was onstage. He was somebody that was always trying to learn," Turek told Fox News Digital. "It can be hard to mentor somebody smarter than you, but not with Charlie, because the only thing that exceeded his intellect was his humility. The few things that I knew that he wanted to know, he asked me to tell him. So we would get together and discuss questions he might get on a college campus, because I've been presenting on college campuses for about 20 years. And we would sharpen one another."

Turek was standing just feet away when Kirk was shot and killed Sept. 10 at Utah Valley University during the first stop of TPUSA’s "The American Comeback Tour."

At Kirk's memorial service weeks later, Turek reflected on his friend's faith.

Charlie Kirk's assassination was one year ago this week. (Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune/Getty Images)

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"Now, I want you to know that Charlie, right now, is in heaven," Turek said at the service. "Not because he was a great husband and father, not because he saved millions of kids out of darkness on college campuses, not because he changed minds and chased votes to save the country, not because he sacrificed himself for his Savior. Charlie Kirk is in heaven because his Savior sacrificed himself for Charlie Kirk."

Ultimately, Turek hopes his book encourages Christians and churches to speak out boldly in the public square and to carry on Kirk's legacy.

"I hear from pastors all the time, 'I don't get involved in politics, I just preach the gospel,' to which I say to them, 'I guess you don't think the gospel is very important then.' And they say, 'Well, what do you mean?' And I say, 'Because the laws that are made politically can affect your ability to preach and live the gospel'... So for no other reason, Christians have to be involved in politics to protect our ability to preach and live the gospel, to have religious freedom," Turek said.

"The second reason, major reason, is because we're called to love one another. And God set up governments to protect innocent people from evil. According to Romans 13, the government is supposed to punish wrongdoers. Why will we not put laws in place as Christians to punish people who are doing evil. We should," Turek said.

Kristine Parks is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Read more.

title: Mysterious settlement discovered after residents seemingly packed up and vanished
excerpt:
London researchers have reconstructed a large Roman wall plaster collection, revealing 1,800-year-old frescoes that decorated a high-status building. (Source: MOLA)

Archaeologists recently uncovered ...
body_text:
London researchers have reconstructed a large Roman wall plaster collection, revealing 1,800-year-old frescoes that decorated a high-status building. (Source: MOLA)

Archaeologists recently uncovered the remains of a medieval village that was mysteriously abandoned in Germany — raising questions about why its residents packed up and left.

The excavation at the Am Frevelgraben site in Halberstadt, in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt, revealed numerous traces of a medieval settlement, including parts of a multi-tiered ditch system.

The State Office for Monument Preservation and Archaeology Saxony-Anhalt announced the findings on Aug. 24.

UNEXPECTED ANCIENT COMPLEX EMERGES NEAR BIBLICAL CITY LINKED TO JONAH AND ST PETER

Archaeologists began excavating the site in March ahead of the development of a nearby industrial park, officials said.

Historical maps suggest the settlement may be the remains of a medieval village known as Kühlingen.

Archaeologists uncovered the remains of a medieval settlement at the Am Frevelgraben site in Halberstadt, Germany. (State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology Saxony-Anhalt, Klaus Bentele; Print Collector/Getty Images)

Archaeologists documented rows of pit houses, settlement pits and two wells at the site, while other traces suggest residents also made extensive use of the nearby riverbank.

Overlapping features and houses built directly next to one another indicate the settlement developed in two phases, officials said — with its footprint shifting as new homes were constructed.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER 1,700-YEAR-OLD CHRISTIAN CITY HIDDEN BENEATH EGYPT'S DESERT

Despite the well-preserved remains, however, archaeologists found surprisingly few artifacts — a detail officials found remarkable.

"A few scattered ceramic shards and a handful of metal finds, including, for example, a bronze tap, fittings, and belt buckets, certainly represent only a fraction of the former possessions of the inhabitants," the release said.

Archaeologists found no evidence of destruction or fire at the site; the reason behind the abandonment "remains a mystery at this time." (State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology Saxony-Anhalt, Klaus Bentele)

The settlement was abandoned "in a highly orderly fashion," Oliver Dietrich, a spokesperson for the State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology Saxony-Anhalt, told Fox News Digital.

"It was indeed striking how few artifacts were left behind," he said. "Medieval deserted villages typically yield a wealth of artifacts."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Dietrich said archaeologists found no evidence of destruction or fire at the site, and said the reason behind the abandonment "remains a mystery at this time."

"Further analysis will produce further insights into the abandonment process," he said.

Archaeologists found surprisingly few artifacts despite the well-preserved remains uncovered at the medieval settlement in Halberstadt. (Prisma/UIG/Getty Images; State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology Saxony-Anhalt, Klaus Bentele)

The settlement is "clearly medieval," though researchers are not sure precisely when it was abandoned, Dietrich added.

"Because of the scarcity of finds, radiocarbon analyses of selected animal bones are expected to provide a precise date," he said.

As fascinating as it is, the expert added that Am Frevelgraben is one of hundreds of deserted medieval villages in Germany.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"The most drastic period of abandonment was during the 14th and 15th centuries," Dietrich said, citing the Black Death, migration and climate change.

Often these villages "had too few resources to sustain the people," he said.

Further analysis of the remains is expected to offer additional insight into the mysterious abandonment of the medieval settlement, officials said. (State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology Saxony-Anhalt, Klaus Bentele)

The find follows a similar discovery made recently in neighboring Poland.

Earlier this year, archaeologists uncovered another abandoned medieval settlement, Stolzenberg, which had remained hidden in a remote forest for centuries.

Andrea Margolis is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital and Fox Business. Readers can follow her on X at @andreamargs or send story tips to andrea.margolis@fox.com.

title: Letitia James’ Times Square shooting probe draws GOP criticism over New York’s mental health crisis
excerpt: Republican Attorney General hopeful Saritha Komatireddy says James "told you exactly who she is" and vows to launch an Office of Civil Commitment which will pair cops and doctors to get known dangerou...
body_text:
Republican Attorney General hopeful Saritha Komatireddy says James "told you exactly who she is" and vows to launch an Office of Civil Commitment which will pair cops and doctors to get known dangerous people off the streets and into treatment.

New York Attorney General Letitia James is facing scrutiny after opening up a legally required investigation into the police shooting of a woman who fatally stabbed Erin Piacenti, Bank of America executive and a new mother in her first week back to work from maternity leave, in Times Square.

James' office announced on Wednesday that it will be investigating Pamela Cisneros' death, who was wielding two large knives in each hand when officers confronted her following the fatal stabbing. She was ordered to drop the weapons but did not comply and was shot when she moved toward the officers.

Under state law, the Attorney General's Office of Special Investigation is mandated to investigate all deaths that were caused by police officers. However, Attorney General Republican candidate Saritha Komatireddy is pushing that the Attorney General's office take more concrete steps to ensure that another tragic killing or attack caused by a mentally unstable person doesn't happen again. She argued that an investigation into police conduct fails to address the real problem at hand.

"The problem is that we have people who are known dangerous individuals, people with documented mental illness," Komatireddy told Fox News Digital. "They've been in the courts before, or they've been to the hospitals before. The police know exactly who they are, but we have no ability to take care of them."

REPUBLICANS GET 'AGGRESSIVE' IN FIGHT TO WIN TOP COP SPOTS IN BATTLEGROUND STATES

A split of Erin Piacenti and the Times Square crime scene where she was tragically stabbed and killed on Aug. 31, 2026. (Getty ; Facebook)

A campaign spokesperson for James accused Komatireddy of seeking to "score cheap political points off of a tragedy."

"Saritha Komatireddy wants to be Attorney General but doesn’t understand the law," a spokesperson said in an email to Fox News Digital. "Under New York’s Executive Law, the Office of the Attorney General’s Office of Special Investigation is required to investigate any incident where a police officer’s actions may have caused a death, including this one."

However, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has a history of anti-police rhetoric, applauded the officers who stopped Cisneros.

"I want to thank the NYPD officers who stepped in and prevented a horrific attack from becoming even worse," Mamdani said at a news conference.

PARENTS IN BRONX NEIGHBORHOOD PLEAD FOR NYPD GUARD AS MAMDANI CUTS COPS, HALTS HIRES: 'HORRIBLE SITUATION'

New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch shared that while Cisneros, who lived in Queens, didn't have an arrest record in the city, there were two times police responded to calls concerning her suffering a mental health crisis.

In March 2019, Cisneros attempted suicide by jumping onto the tracks of the E train and was removed and later hospitalized. In March 2018, police found her in Midtown, where she was screaming, acting belligerent and intoxicated.

If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

Under the state's Mental Hygiene Law, police and doctors can take a person to the hospital for a psychological hold if they are deemed to be a risk to themselves or others, or they can not meet their basic needs — but often times those with severe mental illnesses are released by the hospital back onto the streets hours after being brought in.

LETITIA JAMES FACES SCRUTINY AFTER NEW YORK CITY SPENDS $81,700 PER HOMELESS PERSON AMID SHELTER SCANDALS

Letitia James, New York's attorney general, speaks outside federal court in Norfolk, Va., on Friday, Oct. 24, 2025. (Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"I was there in Times Square — just a couple of days after this fatal stabbing — and I was walking around and saw severely mentally ill people on the street," Komatireddy told Fox News Digital. "It's still happening every day, and we need someone who's actually going to propose a real solution and way forward."

TRUMP WANTS TO HELP 146,000 MENTALLY ILL WHO ARE HOMELESS. DEMOCRATS WANT TO STOP HIM

The New York State Office of Mental Health is tasked with overseeing the state's mental health system, which includes 23 psychiatric centers and 6,500 programs overseen by local governments and nonprofits, but Komatireddy said, if elected, she'd create a new office known as the Office of Civil Commitment which would target and keep tabs on people who are at most risk.

"The Office of Civil Commitment that I'm going to launch will be staffed with both law enforcement personnel and also physicians, and you need both because, under state law, the law requires that physicians certify that someone has the mental state required for involuntary civil commitment," Komatireddy told Fox News Digital. "So there's nothing like that right now in New York State. There's no office that has both law enforcement and physicians who can work together to get these people off the streets."

Erin Piacenti, the Bank of America Vice President who was tragically killed in a stabbing attack in New York City's Times Square on Monday Aug. 31, 2026, on her wedding day. (Facebook/Erin Piacenti)

Greene County Sheriff Peter Kusminsky told Fox News Digital that his deputies are not trained to handle psychiatric crises — and that the county has nowhere to send people who need real care. Deputies are constantly pulled off patrol for mental-health calls, he said, then left to put those in crisis in hotels because there aren't enough hospital beds available.

"Additionally, we really struggle when we have people in custody who we aren't equipped to handle, and secure beds are even harder to find," Kusminsky said. "It sometimes takes weeks or months to locate once and when we do, they are maybe on the other side of the state and at an exorbitant cost."

"Hotels and motels don’t have doctors, don’t have medicine, don’t have therapy," Komatireddy said. "The state needs to step in."

Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: WWE Sunday Night's Main Event match card, predictions and more

body_text:
WWE NXT women's champion Kelani Jordan talks to OutKick about her title win at Heatwave, her match against Kendal Grey and more.

For at least one night, WWE’s Saturday Night’s Main Event will transform into Sunday Night’s Main Event as the showcase will take place in Atlanta on Labor Day weekend.

There are only four matches on the card, but each comes with heightened stakes.

Sunday Night’s Main Event is also set to feature a live performance from hip-hop artist Quavo, who will debut an unreleased track from his forthcoming album "QROMELIFE."

COMPLETE PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE ON OUTKICK

Read below for the match card and predictions on what will happen at the State Farm Arena on Sunday night. The event begins at 8 p.m. ET and can be seen on Peacock.

Tatum Paxley makes her entrance with Alexa Bliss and Charlotte Flair during SmackDown at Canadian Tire Centre in Ottawa, Ontario, on Aug. 28, 2026. (WWE via Getty Images)

A six-woman tag team match will take place to add to the longstanding feud among Charlotte Flair, Alexa Bliss and Tatum Paxley and Jade Cargill, Michin and B-Fab. It feels as though these women have been battling for months. Paxley was added to the fray when she made her SmackDown debut to back up Flair and Bliss. But Cargill, Michin and B-Fab have continuously been scrapping with Flair, Bliss and Paxley with Cargill and Flair seemingly fighting for the top contender spot to Chelsea Green’s women’s title.

Prediction: Flair, Bliss and Paxley put away Cargill, Michin and B-Fab.

Lil Yachty faces Baron Corbin during SmackDown at TD Garden in Boston, Mass., on Aug. 14, 2026. (WWE via Getty Images)

Baron Corbin returned to WWE and made an immediate impact. He earned a United States Championship shot at SummerSlam and defeated Trick Williams to win the title. Williams has been clawing his way back to the top, eyeing a title return. But he hasn’t been the only who has messed with Corbin. Lil Yachty, Williams’ valet, has kept nipping at Corbin’s heels. He’ll have a chance to help Williams in his match against Corbin. If Lil Yachty lasts at least five minutes in the ring with Corbin, Williams will get a rematch for the U.S. title. Expect some kind of shenanigans to take place in this match.

Prediction: Lil Yachty holds out for as long as he can against Corbin

Randy Orton and Cody Rhodes speak during SmackDown at Canadian Tire Centre in Ottawa, Ontario, on Aug. 28, 2026. (WWE via Getty Images)

It’s the long-awaited grudge match between WWE superstars Cody Rhodes and Randy Orton. Rhodes owes Orton another lick after getting punted in the head following their WrestleMania 42 Night 1 main event brawl. Rhodes won that match to retain the Undisputed WWE Championship. Orton got the last word with the kick that left Rhodes’ eye swollen. Since Orton’s return, the two have brawled constantly. Rhodes even went for a kill shot at one point. It caused SmackDown GM Nick Aldis to tell them if they continued to fight each other, they would never get a shot at a WWE championship again. It led to some harsh words from Orton, trying to coax Rhodes into hitting him. It didn’t work, but you could feel the tension between the two men building. This match will turn into a good ol’ fashioned slobber knocker.

Prediction: Cody Rhodes comes out on top in this one.

Bron Breakker and Oba Femi face off during Monday Night Raw at KeyBank Center in Buffalo, N.Y., on Aug. 17, 2026. (WWE via Getty Images)

There’s no tangible title on the line in this one – there’s only perception. Who is the future of WWE? Bron Breakker has been inside his own head for weeks as he grappled with Oba Femi’s rise in WWE. Breakker was on the mend as Femi defeated Brock Lesnar at WrestleMania 42, won the King of the Ring Tournament and seemingly ended Lesnar’s career at SummerSlam. Breakker failed to dispatch Seth Rollins and only became a tag team champion after Logan Paul got hurt. Breakker has shown that he still has that dog in him but Femi’s rule over the Raw roster has been cataclysmic for his opponents. Both men could very well be champions in the future, but for now, they fight to be the face of what is to come down the road.

Prediction: Breakker needs a win here to go back to the days in which he was considered the man with the loudest bark and the biggest bite. Breakker wins in what might be an upset.

Ryan Gaydos is a senior editor for Fox News Digital.

title: How significant are the Yemeni government’s military gains against Houthis?
excerpt:
Yemen’s internationally recognised government says its forces have made significant gains against the Houthis as fighting has escalated in recent weeks, raising fears of a return to full-scale war.

T...
body_text:
Yemen’s internationally recognised government says its forces have made significant gains against the Houthis as fighting has escalated in recent weeks, raising fears of a return to full-scale war.

The government forces on Saturday said they had recaptured strategically located territory in Hodeidah province under Houthi control and advanced in western Taiz.

However, the latest gains do not yet amount to a decisive shift in Yemen’s long-running war.

The Iran-aligned Houthis still control the capital, Sanaa, and several other cities, and have themselves recently advanced around Taiz as they seek to threaten the government-held port of al-Makha (Mocha) and move towards areas bordering the strategically vital Bab al-Mandeb strait, the chokepoint that connects the Red Sea to the Arabian Sea.

The fighting comes amid a wider regional conflict involving Saudi Arabia, which is a key backer of the Yemeni government.

Riyadh has carried out air strikes against positions recently captured by the Houthis, as the battle increasingly focuses on territory leading towards one of the world’s most important shipping routes.

The government forces have been fighting the Houthis across several fronts, with some of the heaviest clashes in Taiz and Hodeidah provinces, and along the western Red Sea coast.

The SABA news agency, controlled by Yemen’s internationally recognised government, reported on Saturday that the Yemeni military had taken control of Hais district in Hodeidah, citing an unidentified military source.

Hais is strategically located at the junction of Hodeidah, Taiz and Ibb provinces. The Houthis have yet to comment on this latest development.

The source also said government forces have regained areas around the al-Barh junction in western Taiz and advanced towards Houthi positions. Taiz is divided between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.

Fayad al-Numan, a Yemeni Information Ministry official, said government forces had also captured dozens of Houthi fighters during clashes in al-Jarahi district in southern Hodeidah.

Clashes in Taiz killed more than 60 people, including civilians, on Saturday, the AFP news agency reported.

On Thursday, fighting erupted as Houthi forces launched a major offensive along front lines in western Taiz and southern Hodeidah, using ballistic missiles, drones and artillery as ground forces attempted to advance towards government-held territory along the Red Sea coast.

The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said that about 1,800 families have been displaced over the past two days as fighting escalated in Taiz.

Fighting renewed in early August after months of calm when Yemeni government forces launched attacks on Houthi positions across multiple front lines.

The Yemeni government re-established control over major southern and eastern territories following a Saudi-backed counteroffensive and the subsequent dissolution of the UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council (STC) in January.

They now aim to unite Yemen after bringing the areas under Houthi control under one administration.

But the Houthis have pushed towards government-held areas near al-Makha and territory bordering the Bab al-Mandeb strait amid reinforcements and counteroffensives from the government forces.

The latest escalation follows a period of relative calm in Yemen that had largely held since a UN-brokered truce in April 2022. The ceasefire brought an end to major fighting since the Houthis’ capture of much of the country, including Sanaa, in 2014.

But Thursday’s attacks hint at a return to large-scale conflict.

The capture of Hais could be significant because of its position linking Hodeidah, Taiz and Ibb, while advances around al-Barh could help government forces push back against Houthi forces in western Taiz.

Presidential Leadership Council chairman Rashad al-Alimi said Yemen’s armed forces were capable of restoring control over the entire country and warned that Houthi “miscalculations” would lead to their “complete collapse”.

However, it is too early to describe the developments as a significant shift in control.

The Houthis had themselves seized positions near Taiz shortly before the government counteroffensive, according to an AFP news agency citing a military officer.

Houthi forces have also been attempting to cut off the government-held port of al-Makha, and advance towards areas bordering the Bab al-Mandeb strait.

The scale of government losses also shows how contested the battlefield remains. Twenty-six government soldiers were killed in several hours of fighting on Saturday alone, according to AFP’s military sources.

The escalation is also increasingly intertwined with the wider regional conflict linked to the US-Israel war on Iran.

The Iran-backed Houthis announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia in July and began targeting Saudi ships and territory, while Saudi Arabia has carried out air strikes against Houthi positions in Taiz.

Bab al-Mandeb has become particularly important after Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping. The Hormuz blockade has triggered a global energy crisis and is pushing the global economy into turbulence.

The waterway is a key transit route for Saudi oil, one of only two exit-entry points to the Red Sea, the other being the Suez Canal, raising the stakes as Houthi forces attempt to advance towards areas bordering the strait.

In July, Saudi Arabia announced a mission to form an international alliance to guard the Red Sea from attacks on shipping by Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.

title: No bailouts for Jaguar Land Rover amid reports of thousands of job cuts, says minister
excerpt:
Carmaker, which is battling Trump tariffs and Chinese competitors, faces talks with union leaders and government

The government has signalled that it will not invest taxpayers’ money to limit job los...
body_text:
Carmaker, which is battling Trump tariffs and Chinese competitors, faces talks with union leaders and government

The government has signalled that it will not invest taxpayers’ money to limit job losses at Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), after it emerged that the UK’s biggest carmaker is planning up to 4,000 redundancies.

Before crunch talks on Tuesday between JLR, union leaders and government officials, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said it was not his job to “intervene and run businesses”.

JLR, owned by the Indian conglomerate Tata Motors, told staff on Friday to expect a voluntary redundancy programme, as it tries to shore itself up against tough conditions with £1.7bn in cuts over two years.

The Coventry-based company is expected to provide further details on job cuts as soon as Monday, which could include an admission that compulsory job losses are possible.

The expected cuts, which represent almost 12% of JLR’s 34,000-strong UK workforce, threaten to provide an early reality check on Andy Burnham’s pledge to “reindustrialise” Britain.

Sources said they expect the redundancies, first reported in the Sunday Times, to be weighted towards more senior roles in management and research and development rather than shop floor production workers.

JLR is understood to be responding to pressure from Tata to offset a slump in sales, exacerbated by the fallout from last year’s cyber-attack and the impact of Donald Trump’s tariff wars.

Speaking on the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg show on Sunday, Reynolds signalled that the government was unwilling to put money into the business to limit job losses.

Asked if there could be financial support to protect the jobs, he said: “Not if it’s to bail people out.

“If this is about making sure over time that workforce is right to make the business as ⁠competitive as possible, that’s the conversation we need to have,” Reynolds said, referring to the wider “challenging” environment for the auto sector.

“We need to adapt to evolving global market conditions,” a spokesperson for JLR, which has its largest plant in Solihull in the West Midlands, said.

Reynolds is expected to come under pressure to help staunch the number of job cuts from the Unite general secretary, Sharon Graham, during crunch talks with the JLR chief executive, PB Balaji, scheduled for Tuesday. Union officials will push for JLR to swerve compulsory job losses in favour of retraining or voluntary redundancy where possible.

While Reynolds indicated that no bailout would be available, he hinted at other options to support carmakers.

He refused to rule out watering down government targets for UK automakers to reach 80% zero-emission car sales by 2030, which would lead to a ban on the sale of new petrol and diesel cars by 2035, pointing to an open consultation on the issue.

Carmakers and unions have lobbied hard for a slower transition, saying the targets outpace actual customer demand.

Reynolds also said that the government was sometimes prepared to invest “alongside” industry.

In 2024, the new Labour government under Keir Starmer agreed to invest £500m in another Tata business, the Port Talbot steelworks, to build greener electric arc furnaces. However, the investment did not prevent 2,500 job losses at the south Wales site.

The prospect of a jobs purge at JLR poses a challenge for Burnham, who has placed plans to “reindustrialise” Britain at the heart of his offer to voters since taking office less than two months ago.

Last year, after JLR suffered the crippling cyber-attack, the government agreed to provide the company with a guaranteed loan facility of £1.5bn to help battle the impact on its supply chains and production. None of the loan has been drawn down.

As well as the cyber-attack, which halted production for several weeks and dented the UK economy, JLR has suffered the fallout from tariffs imposed by Trump, affecting the key American market for models such as the Range Rover and Defender.

Trump initially slapped tariffs of 27.5% on British cars before reducing the figure to 10% as part of a US-UK trade deal unveiled by Starmer to great fanfare at a press conference held at JLR’s Solihull plant in May last year.

Competition from Chinese models such as ​the Jaecoo 7 – ​ranked third among Britain’s top-selling cars – ​has also eaten into sales at JLR, which makes more than 400,000 vehicles a year.

JLR is not alone in being affected by these external factors. The German carmaker Volkswagen said last week it plans to cut a further 50,000 jobs as part of its turnaround plan as it faces US tariffs and Chinese competition.

The Guardian has approached the department for business and trade for comment.

title: German startup sends first commercial rocket into space from Europe
excerpt:
Isar Aerospace plans rapid expansion amid race to capitalise on expanding satellite-launch market

A German startup has launched the first commercial rocket to reach orbit from continental Europe, a m...
body_text:
Isar Aerospace plans rapid expansion amid race to capitalise on expanding satellite-launch market

A German startup has launched the first commercial rocket to reach orbit from continental Europe, a milestone for Europe’s efforts to secure independent access to space.

Isar Aerospace said on Sunday that it would rapidly ⁠expand satellite deployments after the ⁠first orbital launch of ​its uncrewed Spectrum rocket from Arctic Norway, marking a ⁠breakthrough for a region where several countries are seeking a foothold in the fast-growing market for satellite launches.

“Launch capability is right now the biggest bottleneck in the entire industry,” Isar co-founder and CEO Daniel Metzler told reporters.

Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor, hailed Saturday’s launch in a ​statement, calling it “the beginning of a new era”.

Merz visited Isar’s ‌launch site in March, underscoring Europe’s ‌efforts to establish greater autonomy as the global order once championed by the US is shifting under the administration of country’s president, Donald Trump.

The EU defence and space commissioner, Andrius Kubilius, wrote on the social media platform X: “Europe’s independent access to space just got a major boost.”

Blasting off from Andøya Spaceport, Spectrum carried five small satellites along with an in-flight technology experiment.

It was Isar’s second launch, coming 18 months after the company’s first rocket plunged into the sea and exploded in a fiery spectacle shortly after takeoff from the same site.

Isar has said it already has five more rockets in production and is now focused on scaling up operations to meet rising demand, with a long-term goal of conducting about 40 launches a year.

The German company ​is developing a second launch site in Nova Scotia in eastern Canada.

Global players ⁠in the satellite launch market include Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which launches from the US, and the French firm ArianeGroup, ​a joint venture between Airbus and Safran ​that uses a spaceport in French Guiana, South America.

title: Undercover report on donations ‘looks bad’ for Reform, admits Nigel Farage – UK politics live

In an interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg, Nigel Farage acknowledged...
body_text:
The Reform UK leader is under pressure after senior aides appeared to plot how to bypass electoral laws on foreign donations

In an interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg, Nigel Farage acknowledged that the comments by James Orr and Dan Jukes were “injudicious at best” and admitted that the optics of the undercover filming don’t look good for his party.

“This looks bad, as does the sale of peerages, as does government contracts for donations. We are not the first people to be involved in a row over donations,” he said.

The BBC aired the full interview during its politics show on Sunday, having released an excerpt of it on Saturday.

In an earlier post, we mentioned that thousands of jobs are to be cut at Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) as the British carmaker slashes costs after a slump in sales. My colleague Angus Thomson has more details about the expected job cuts in this story. Here is an extract from the report:

double quotation markJLR informed workers and their union on Saturday that the company would be opening a voluntary redundancy programme for salaried and management team members, the BBC and Sunday Times reported.

As many as 4,000 jobs would be cut over two years, the Times reported. JLR told the BBC it was yet to confirm the number but the company, which is owned by the Indian conglomerate Tata Motors, needed to save about £1.7bn over the next two years.

Unite’s general secretary, Sharon Graham, told the BBC she and the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, would meet JLR’s chief executive, PB Balaji, next week, after a weekend of intensive talks to mitigate job losses.

About 30,000 of the company’s 44,000 employees are based in the UK. Most of them work at 14 plants across the West Midlands, where the company is one of the region’s largest employers.

Sagal Abdi-Wali arrived in Camden as a child refugee from Somalia. She has worked for more than a decade as a volunteer and trustee for local charities and is a governor of two schools in the borough, according to Labour.

She was first elected as a councillor in 2022 and became the leader of the council in May, when she said: “Camden has been my home for 35 years. It is the place that gave my family sanctuary, that welcomed us, and that has shaped so much of who I am, what I stand for and what inspired my commitment to public service and to working for the community that welcomed us.”

Labour is expected to announce its candidate for the Holborn and St Pancras byelection by Wednesday. It faces a battle against the Green party to retain the seat as Zack Polanski, its leader in England and Wales, is expected to be confirmed as its candidate.

Zia Yusuf, Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson, has been accused of “pretty straightforward racism” by a Cabinet minister over comments about a potential Labour byelection candidate who was born in Somalia.

Yusuf has been criticised for a tweet about Sagal Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee and the leader of Camden council, who has been tipped as a favourite to stand for Labour in the Holborn and St Pancras contest triggered by former prime minister Keir Starmer’s resignation as an MP.

Yusuf wrote on X last week: “The front runner being foisted on the people of Holborn by Labour to replace the former Prime Minister Keir Starmer in our Parliament was born in Somalia. Do you understand what’s happening?”

The business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, was asked what he thought of Yusuf’s tweet during an interview with Jon Sopel on Sky News this morning.

“Pretty straightforward racism, isn’t it?” Reynolds said, adding that the potential Labour candidate had “spent decades in this country” and made a “huge contribution to her local community”.

Robert Jenrick, Reform’s economic spokesperson, later denied his colleague’s comments were racist and suggested it was legitimate to question the loyalties of foreign-born candidates.

“I don’t know this person, so I’m not here to cast aspersions upon her, but I do want people to sit in our parliament who are entirely committed to our country,” Jenrick said.

Javier Milei’s threats to the Falkland Islands make it even more important that Andy Burnham increase defence spending immediately, according to the Labour chair of the defence committee.

Tan Dhesi said the comments by the Argentinian president this week show why the government should raise military spending to 3% of GDP by 2030.

But he said Burnham’s plans remain mired in confusion after the prime minister appeared to reassure him that the 2030 target would be hit, only for Downing Street to later retreat.

“It’s important the prime minister and the chancellor don’t defer those decisions to next year,” Dhesi told the Guardian.

“We’ve seen Germany publicly expose Russia for the drone incident [in Leipzig]. Now we’ve got a threat from Argentina saying they are looking to take over the Falklands. We owe it to the Falklands – they say it’s their right to self-determination. It’s important that we also defend them from this threat.”

Reform UK’s Robert Jenrick also condemned the disruption of the Port of Dover by masked demonstrators – but said he understood the frustration with small boats crossing the Channel. Speaking to Sky News’ Sunday Morning programme, Reform’s economic spokesperson said:

double quotation markI absolutely do. I’ve always hated people obstructing other people doing their daily life, whether it’s Just Stop Oil or whatever.

And I don’t like people going around in balaclavas, which is obviously very intimidating. In fact, our party’s policy is to ban face coverings like that.

But do I understand why people are extremely frustrated? Yes, absolutely. This needs to end. This farce of the small boats has been going on for far too long.

And in fact you saw at our conference Nigel Farage and (National Rally president) Jordan Bardella, the likely next prime minister of France, signing an agreement which has the prospect of ending this once and for all.

Channel crossings are down about 40% compared to last year, with the number of crossings this summer at their lowest level since 2019. Home Office data shows people in small boats overwhelmingly come from war and conflict zones.

Reform UK’s Nigel Farage has agreed a deal with France’s hard-right National Rally party on returning migrants who try to cross the Channel in small boats, if both parties achieve power. A Labour party spokesperson said the proposal “is a meaningless document packed with daft and dangerous ideas, signed by an increasingly disgraced Reform leader and an opposition politician. It is nothing more than pointless posturing.”

The business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, went on to condemn the hundreds of masked protesters who prevented traffic from coming in and out of the port of Dover yesterday. In the interview with the BBC, he praised the police for effectively dealing with the “intimidatory behaviour” and said he had sympathy for the “people around Dover” and those disrupted by the delays.

A group called Patriot Platform, which styles itself as having “a fierce love for our homeland”, claimed responsibility for the blockade, as my colleagues note in this story.

The far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, reposted videos of the blockade, highlighting a live stream of the protest that directed viewers towards Patriot Platform.

Thousands of workers at Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) will be offered redundancies with job losses reported to be spread over two years. The job cuts will be unwelcome news for Andy Burnham, who has vowed to “safeguard sovereign manufacturing” and reindustrialise Britain.

When asked if the government would be willing to protect the jobs, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said it is not for him to “intervene” as he isn’t responsible for running JLR’s business.

“They need to know what the right footprint for them going forward is. I want to talk to them about the numbers,” Reynolds told the BBC, adding there could be financial support for long-term investment but not for a taxpayer-funded bailout.

Farage claims that he faces a disproportionate level of scrutiny compared to the other parties. When Laura Kuenssberg gave the Reform leader a series of examples of investigations faced by other party leaders, Farage responded:

double quotation markI don’t think the others have been de-banked. I don’t think the others have been kicked out by their pension provider. I don’t think the others have literally had an attempt to wipe them out of society, oh and their families as well.

There is no doubt there is huge political prejudice against Reform right across the corporate world and right across the establishment. And that is a simple fact of life – and why? Because we are the disrupters and that’s the way it works.

Farage told the Daily T podcast last month that he had received about 400 death threats in the last seven weeks, and as a high-profile, extremely divisive politician, it is argued that he needs a high level of security.

The claim that Reform is fighting the establishment is undermined by the fact that many of his senior figures, including treasury spokesperson Robert Jenrick and the MP for Fareham and Waterlooville, Suella Braverman, are former Conservative cabinet ministers who were at the heart of the same political establishment Farage is railing against.

In an interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg, Nigel Farage acknowledged that the comments by James Orr and Dan Jukes were “injudicious at best” and admitted that the optics of the undercover filming don’t look good for his party.

“This looks bad, as does the sale of peerages, as does government contracts for donations. We are not the first people to be involved in a row over donations,” he said.

The BBC aired the full interview during its politics show on Sunday, having released an excerpt of it on Saturday.

The Guardian’s city editor, Anna Isaac, is sitting on the panel on Laura Kuenssberg’s show alongside broadcaster Jeremy Vine and political scientist Francis Fukuyama.

Her revelation that Nigel Farage received a £5m gift from the Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne shortly before announcing he would stand in the 2024 British general election has dogged the Reform leader ever since she broke the story in April.

Farage, who has given different explanations as to why he accepted the gift, has argued he did not need to declare the money because he received it before he was elected as Clacton MP and it “wasn’t political in any sense at all”.

The parliamentary standards commissioner is investigating whether he broke the rules.

Isaac’s report came before a series of other stories raising questions about Reform’s finances, some of which you can read here. Isaac was among the journalists who have reported critically on Reform who were banned from the party’s annual conference this year.

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of UK politics. The Reform UK party leader, Nigel Farage, is scheduled to appear in an interview on Laura Kuenssberg’s Sunday politics programme at 9am, where he will likely be asked more about an undercover investigation broadcast by Channel 4 News which showed two of his senior aides appearing to plot to get around electoral laws on foreign donations.

Accepting donations from a foreign company, including donations in kind such as polling, could constitute a criminal offence and the party has been reported to the police.

Senior aide Dan Jukes and Reform’s head of policy James Orr have both stood down pending the outcome of an internal party investigation.

As my colleagues note in the story, Farage himself remains under pressure over a separate clip in which he was heard saying “it’s all above board” after one of the reporters who was posing as the UK-based son of a wealthy US backer told the Reform leader he had been in discussions with Jukes and Orr for some time.

“I’ll be the registered donor,” the son says. “But then dad will send the money to me, and then as soon as that’s done and all those conversations are had the money is available.”

On Saturday, during the party’s conference in Birmingham, Farage continued to bat away suggestions of impropriety. “I’m not a compliance officer,” he told the BBC. “I frankly wasn’t even listening,” he said in reference to the meeting with the undercover reporters in Clacton.

Farage has framed the investigation, carried out by Verbatim Investigations, which was founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting, as another example of an establishment stitch up, and has denied any wrongdoing, as have Orr and Jukes.

title: Farage says overseas donation row ‘looks bad’ but denies Reform breached electoral law
excerpt:
Robert Jenrick says party has followed legal protocol ‘at all times’ as Met police consider launching investigation

Nigel Farage has acknowledged the overseas donation row engulfing Reform UK “looks ...
body_text:
Robert Jenrick says party has followed legal protocol ‘at all times’ as Met police consider launching investigation

Nigel Farage has acknowledged the overseas donation row engulfing Reform UK “looks bad” for his party but denied it had ever taken foreign money in breach of electoral law.

The Reform leader, who is battling to contain the fallout from the allegations, was asked to categorically rule out that foreign money had ever been funnelled to his party. He replied: “I can … never happened.”

Farage was forced to suspend his close aide Dan Jukes and Reform’s head of policy, James Orr, on Friday after they were filmed in an undercover investigation apparently plotting to get around electoral laws on foreign donations.

In an interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg, Farage described their comments as “injudicious at best” and admitted the optics of the undercover filming were problematic for his party, which has in the past tried to suggest it would do politics differently.

“This looks bad, as does the sale of peerages, as does government contracts for donations,” he said. “We are not the first people to be involved in a row over donations.”

The Metropolitan police are now assessing the evidence after a complaint that Farage and his aides have broken political funding laws, with sources suggesting a full investigation is expected to be launched. They all deny wrongdoing.

Scotland Yard could extend an existing investigation into whether Reform took donations channelled through an intermediary from potentially impermissible sources, which the party and donors deny.

Farage is already facing intense scrutiny about Reform’s finances, as well as a £5m gift by a crypto billionaire shortly before announcing he would stand in the 2024 general election, which he has since said was intended to pay for security.

In an earlier extract of the BBC interview, Farage also claimed he “wasn’t even listening” during the meeting at the centre of the controversy, and that he knew donation law “better than anybody”, as he sought to limit the damage caused by the allegations.

Robert Jenrick, Reform’s Treasury spokesperson, said on Sunday that he had seen legal advice that the party had not in fact broken electoral law over foreign donations but that lessons would be learned from the episode.

“We’re going to investigate exactly what happened,” Jenrick told Sky News. “It’s right to have due process. But this is not the way that Reform conducts itself.

“Like any political party, we seek to abide by the law at all times, and we believe we have in this case. In fact, I’ve reviewed the legal advice from the KC who’s advised the party in the last 48 hours, and it shows that, yeah, we did.

“But do we want for the best version of ourselves? Yes, absolutely. And no doubt there will be lessons to be learnt from this.”

Speaking after the BBC interview, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said: “For a political party that don’t like foreigners much they do seem to have a soft spot for foreign cash. We have rules in this country about how our democracy works and everyone has to stick to them.”

He added: “I think you see someone struggling to decide whether they’re really serious about trying to run for power or want to keep the protest going.”

‘My View with Lara Trump’ host Lara Trump discusses the Democratic Party’s progressive shift, their use of social media to target young voters and more on ‘Fox & Friends Weekend.’

Democrats have made summer pilgrimages to Nantucket, tapping the wealthy Massachusetts island’s donor class as candidates and party leaders stockpile campaign cash ahead of November.

Nantucket and neighboring Martha’s Vineyard have long been magnets for political fundraising, and Democrats are again tapping the islands’ deep-pocketed donor networks as candidates and party leaders build their war chests ahead of November’s midterm elections.

As of June 30, the Democratic National Committee, Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee had about $136 million in combined cash on hand, compared with roughly $277 million held by their Republican counterparts, according to federal filings.

This summer, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., Texas Senate candidate James Talarico, Rep. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., and others have been spotted on the island for fundraising events.

FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: AS DEMOCRATS TURN LEFT, BLACK VOTERS TAP THE BRAKES

To salvage the annual event, another church on the island, St. Paul’s Episcopal Church, announced it would read the Declaration of Independence and the Bill of Rights. (Ashley J. DiMella/Fox News Digital)

Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., reportedly went to Nantucket for an Aug. 29 fundraiser hosted by Democratic heavyweight Elizabeth Frawley Bagley, a Biden-appointed U.S. ambassador to Brazil who previously served as ambassador to Portugal under President Bill Clinton, according to the Boston Globe.

The Democratic fundraising circuit extends to neighboring Martha's Vineyard, another exclusive Massachusetts vacation destination.

Former President Barack Obama visited Martha's Vineyard on Aug. 31 for an event hosted by former Attorney General Eric Holder benefiting the National Democratic Redistricting Committee.

Wes Moore, a possible 2028 presidential contender, was on Martha’s Vineyard the weekend of Aug. 8 for a DNC fundraiser with DNC Chair Ken Martin.

"Where was Wes Moore last weekend? Not campaigning in Maryland or solving our problems in Annapolis, but speaking at a national Democrat event in Martha’s Vineyard. Wes Moore's priority isn’t Maryland, and it will never be Maryland. His only focus is growing his national profile and running for President in 2028. Elect Dan Cox for a Governor who will put Maryland and the needs of Marylanders first," wrote Maryland GOP at the time.

Iowa state Rep. Josh Turek, a Democratic nominee for the open Senate seat held by retiring Republican Sen. Joni Ernst, was spotted on Nantucket while the Iowa State Fair was still underway. Turek, had appeared at the fair earlier in the week, did not answer a reporter’s questions about his fundraising stop, according to videos on social media.

Democratic donors Frank Herron and Sandra Urie, who previously hosted then-first lady Jill Biden for a 2022 Democratic National Committee fundraiser at their Nantucket home, hosted Moulton for a Nantucket fundraising brunch on August 2, according to local paper Nantucket Current.

JON OSSOFF DODGES ON WHY HE INVOKED TRUMP AIDE'S NAME DURING GEORGIA CAMPAIGN RALLY

Shot of Jeep with Trump sticker outside of rose covered cottage on Sconset, Nantucket. (Ashley J. DiMella/Fox News Digital)

Michelle Obama was also on the island, on Aug. 23, but was there to promote her book, "The Look," at two sold-out conversations at the Performing Arts Center in Oak Bluffs. The Obama's have had a vacation house on the Vineyard since 2019.

Nantucket has long been a destination for prominent Democrats as well as celebrities, millionaires and billionaires.

Former President Joe Biden and his family have traveled to the island for decades to celebrate Thanksgiving.

Former first lady Jill Biden was also spotted on the island in July to promote her new book, "View From the East Wing: A Memoir."

DEM ATTORNEY BACKS GOP HOPEFUL IN MICHIGAN RACE AGAINST EL-SAYED, 'JUMPING SHIP' FROM HIS PARTY'S 'LUNATICS'

Republicans have also tapped Nantucket’s deep-pocketed donor circuit. Back in 2022, when Vice President JD Vance was running for Senate, he appeared alongside Florida Senator Rick Scott and fellow Senate candidates Ted Budd, Dr. Mehmet Oz and Herschel Walker for another fundraising jaunt on the affluent island.

The NDRC is focusing on key battlegrounds including Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas and Wisconsin.
