title: Andy Burnham pressed on borrowing costs and spending at first PMQs – UK politics live
excerpt:
Burnham faced questions from Kemi Badenoch and other MPs amid speculation over budget

Kemi Badenoch starts by congratulating the PM “on his stamina – three hours”. (That generates some laughter.) She...
body_text:
Burnham faced questions from Kemi Badenoch and other MPs amid speculation over budget

Kemi Badenoch starts by congratulating the PM “on his stamina – three hours”. (That generates some laughter.) She asks if Burnham can name a single spending request to which he said no.

Burnham says he was clear about the need to get welfare spending down.

It is not right to have so many young people on benefits. He wants to invest in their success.

This is an area where both parties can engage “in problem solving, not point scoring’.

So much for the talk of a new-look PMQs. (See 11.12am.) Although Andy Burnham and his team have spoken about adopting a new approach to the traditional Commons joust with the leader of the opposition, in the end this felt much like business as usual. Burnham was more willing to engage with Kemi Badenoch’s questions than Keir Starmer was (certainly in the late Starmer phase), and he did make a point of stressing several times his desire to work with opposition parties. But, although he has made “problem-solving, not point-scoring” his mantra, Burnham was quite happy to resort to point-scoring. His main blast was directed at Andrew Griffith, the new shadow chancellor, and his role in the Liz Truss mini-budget.

Burnham may not have been particularly innovative, but he was good; confident, plausible, quite funny. In the exchanges with Badenoch, there was no obvious winner, but he had the best single put-down. That came when Badenoch asked:

double quotation markThe prime minister told the house that his summer of promises would be paid for by reprioritize within government. So what exactly has he cut?

Burnham replied: “In terms of what has he cut? Tax is the simple answer.” This was a reference to the point he made yesterday about how his early announcements included two tax cuts in his first week.

While Burnham and Badenoch will both be fairly happy with how the exchanges went, one person less pleased will be the PM’s diary secretary. Burnham did seem to agree to a lot of meetings with MPs wanting to discuss this, that or the other. (Starmer would have fobbed them off with a meeting with a minister, which is what Burnham himself will probably be doing before too long.) And this did seem to confirm Badenoch’s point about Burnham being a people pleaser. (See 12.09pm.) She claimed that, in response to 125 questions yesterday, Burnham did not once say no to a spending request. It is a fair line of attack, although probably not one that will be available for long because Burnham will soon discover that he cannot do this job without having to disappoint.

Just Stop Oil protesters are blockading the road outside parliament, Kate Ferguson from the Sun on Sunday reports.

During PMQs Tan Dhesi, the Labour chair of the Commons defence committee, asked Burnham if he would commit to raising defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030.

double quotation markIt is imperative that we invest in our armed forces in the here and now, rather than be sorry later. Indeed, defence is definitely one area where vibes alone just isn’t going to be enough.

So rather than kick the can down the road waiting for a fiscal event in the future, will the prime minister urgently commit to charting a pathway to reach 3% of GDP spend on defence by 2030, which, as his chancellor rightly noted, is critical to keep our country safe.

John Healey resigned as defence secretary when Keir Starmer was PM because Starmer would not commit to raising defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030. He is now chancellor, but has not publicly committed to reaching the 3% target he insisted was essential by 2030.

double quotation markI’ve made that commitment, made it very clear, and I have done for a considerable period of time. And I was in Ukraine last week for a very specific reason to repeat it on the world stage. There [Dhesi] can be absolutely sure of that.

This sounded like a clear commitment to 3% by 2030.

But there was some doubt about his intention because earlier during the exchanges, when Kemi Badenoch said that the armed forces needed a plan to hit 3% now, Burnham in reply just repeated the commitment to get defence spending up to 3.5% by 2035. (See 12.18pm.)

Samantha Niblett (Lab) tells Burnham that this is her first question at a PMQs too. Niblett is the MP who made headlines with her “summer of sex” campaign, and she says he has had a tremendous response to it. She says:

double quotation markI have discovered that shame, guilt and embarrassment around talking about sex and body parts like penis and vagina is even leading to late diagnosis of health conditions and illnesses such as cancer.

She asks if Burnham will meet her to discuss her campaign.

Burnham says he will. He says Niblett has been raising important issues, and he jokes that her summer sounds as if it was more exciting than his.

And that is the end of Burnham’s first PMQs.

Jack Rankin, who has just been appointed as Kemi Badenoch’s PPS, says Burnham did not answer any of Badenoch’s questions. He asks if Burnham can say what the fiscal rules are, and categorically say he will stick to them.

double quotation markNo borrowing to fund day to day spending, debt falling as a percentage of GDP by the end of the parliament. And yes, we will.

Danny Kruger (Reform UK) says youth unemployment in Manchester got worse when Burnham was mayor. He says the solution is tax cuts for business.

Burnham says Kruger should look again at the figures. He says he delivered a huge increase in apprenticeships, and Neet numbers went down.

But he offers to work with other parties on youth unemployment.

Helena Dollimore, the Labour MP for Hastings and Rye, welcomes a scheme that will ensure that young people from her constituency get access to the Bayeaux Tapestry exhibition.

Burnham praises Dollimore for her campaigning on this. He says he would like all young people to be able to see the tapestry that they learn about at school.

Andrew George (Lib Dem) asks if Burnham will back his private members’ bill to give local communities more power over housing. He says this is a particularly issue in Cornwall.

Burnham says he will meet George to discuss this.

Burnham says he wants more defence spending going into supporting British industries.

Liz Saville Roberts, the Plaid Cymru leader at Westminster, asks Burnham to give the Welsh government control over policing.

Burnham says he will give this proposal a fair hearing.

Kim Leadbeater (Lab) asks what Burnham will do to help people suffering from loneliness, or anti-social behaviour.

Burnham thanks Leadbeater for raising these issues. He raised them in the Makerfield byelection, he says. On antisocial behaviour, he says he accepts the broken windows theory – that small acts of criminality should not be ignored.

Bradley Thomas (Con) asks if Burnham will meet him to discuss a new approach to protecting the green belt.

Burnham says as mayor of Greater Manchester he adopted a brownfield first approach. But there is a balance to be struck, he says. He says the Tories should not turn their back on the need for more homes.

Sorcha Eastwood (Alliance) says the Northern Ireland executive cannot function properly under the rules it has to follow (for cross-community government, giving nationalists and unionists in effect a veto over any decisions). She asks if Burnham will reform the situation.

double quotation markOur first responsibility is to get Stormont government up and running and functioning properly with a budget. I’ve empowered the Northern Ireland secretary to go into talks to, to resolve that issue and the broader issues about reform.

Lindsay Hoyle, the Speaker, accepts Burnham is trying to answer questions, but says he is taking too long. At this rate, they won’t get through all the questions, he says,

Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, says Burnham was right yesterday to blame Brexit for the UK’s lack of growth. The answer to the problem is staring us in the face, he says – join the single market.

Burnham says he is glad Davey accepts his analysis. He says he wants a closer relationship with the EU, building on the work of Keir Starmer. The EU’s “Made in Europe” plan could pose real problems for British steelmakers.

Davey says he hopes Burnham will rejoin the single market.

He says in North Devon a maternity unit has been closed, meaning women have to travel two hours to give birth. They are being taught how to give birth in cars. This is “unthinktable”, he says. Will he commit to reopening the maternity unit within days?

Burnham says he will commit to reopening it – but not within days.

He says there are structural problems with maternity units in the country.

title: Site where Jesus was crucified and buried reveals new evidence that backs biblical account
excerpt: Douglas Estes, an early Christianity scholar, told Fox News Digital that findings from completed excavations beneath Jerusalem's Church of the Holy Sepulchre add archaeological support to details desc...
body_text:
Douglas Estes, an early Christianity scholar, told Fox News Digital that findings from completed excavations beneath Jerusalem's Church of the Holy Sepulchre add archaeological support to details described in the Gospel of John.

Archaeologists have completed an excavation beneath one of Christianity's holiest sites, revealing a fuller picture of the ancient landscape where Jesus Christ was crucified and buried and providing support for scripture — something an early Christianity expert said he found very compelling.

Francesca Stasolla, an archaeology professor at the Sapienza University of Rome, led the excavation in 2025, which focused on the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem.

The findings were recently published in Liber Annuus, the archaeological journal of Jerusalem's Studium Biblicum Franciscanum, in a 98-page preliminary report on the campaign.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER MYSTERIOUS FACE HIDDEN FOR CENTURIES IN BOOK OF REVELATION CITY

The report follows findings noted by Fox News Digital last year.

At the time, Stasolla confirmed that her team had uncovered ancient seeds and pollen in layers dating between the site's use as a quarry and its later Roman occupation.

Archaeologists have completed an excavation beneath Jerusalem's Church of the Holy Sepulchre, one of the holiest sites of Christianity. (LTL/Heritage Images via Getty Images; Heritage Art/Heritage Images via Getty Images)

The evidence is consistent with John 19:41 in the New Testament: "Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid."

The pollen and seeds date to "between the use of the quarry and the Roman age, when the area had a funerary use," Stasolla told Fox News Digital in 2025.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER MASSIVE ARTIFACT DEPICTING PHARAOH THOUGHT TO HAVE CHALLENGED MOSES IN EXODUS

"The quarry had to be gradually abandoned and as the stone extraction ended, it was used for agricultural areas and tombs," Stasolla said.

"This must have been what it looked like in the first century A.D."

Recent archaeological findings are helping researchers reconstruct the ancient landscape around the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem. (Archivio Università di Roma Sapienza)

The church was identified as Jesus' burial place during the reign of Roman Emperor Constantine in the fourth century, when the first church was built there.

Though it has been a Christian pilgrimage site for nearly 1,700 years, archaeologists are now reconstructing what the area may have looked like around the time of Jesus.

LOST PAGES WITH 'GHOST' TEXT RECOVERED FROM ONE OF THE WORLD'S MOST IMPORTANT NEW TESTAMENT MANUSCRIPTS

Fox News Digital reached out to Stasolla for additional comment.

The findings add archaeological support to details described in the Gospel of John, said Douglas Estes, associate professor of religion at New College of Florida.

The findings are consistent with the Gospel of John's description of a garden near the place where Jesus was crucified. (Fine Art Images/Heritage Images/Getty Images)

Estes, who specializes in early Christianity and was not involved in the research, told Fox News Digital that the Book of John is often dismissed by skeptics as exaggerated.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Archaeology has "over time, confirmed, again and again, details from the Gospel of John," he said — even though critics consider John's writings less accurate than the Gospels of Matthew, Mark and Luke.

He added, "For example, in the 19th century, scholars questioned whether or not there could be five colonnades [at the Pool of Bethesda in Jerusalem], as John 5 describes. Later archeological discoveries have found that, yes, there were five colonnades there."

The Church of the Holy Sepulchre, seen here, was identified as Jesus' burial place during the reign of Roman Emperor Constantine. (AP Photo/Mahmoud Illean)

He said that "in the same way, scholars have largely doubted whether or not Jesus would have been buried in an orchard.

"But instead we find confirmed that there was a garden there — and so the Gospel of John has been proven to be accurate again in the details."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The professor said he was personally excited by the recent discoveries and that he has "a lot of hope that archaeology will continue to reveal significant finds about the life of Jesus."

Archaeological evidence is helping researchers reconstruct the Jerusalem landscape around the site associated with Jesus Christ's crucifixion. (Planet One Images/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

"It's an exciting time to be alive, to be able to experience everything from the Dead Sea Scrolls all the way to the discovery of this funerary landscape," he said.

"These great archeological discoveries are great for those of us who want to learn more about first-century Judaism, first-century Christianity and the life of Jesus," he added.

Andrea Margolis is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital and Fox Business. Readers can follow her on X at @andreamargs or send story tips to andrea.margolis@fox.com.

title: Killing at Sea
excerpt:
Three families, two bombings and a hidden war: uncovering the lives behind Operation Southern Spear’s dead.

Since September 2025, the US military has carried out more than 60 strikes on suspected dru...
body_text:
Three families, two bombings and a hidden war: uncovering the lives behind Operation Southern Spear’s dead.

Since September 2025, the US military has carried out more than 60 strikes on suspected drug-trafficking boats in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific, killing more than 220 people.

In a military campaign called Operation Southern Spear, President Donald Trump’s administration has claimed to wage war against “narcoterrorism”. Yet the government has released little information about who was killed, the evidence against them or how targets were selected.

In Killing at Sea, Fault Lines investigates the administration’s claims about Operation Southern Spear by uncovering the stories of those targeted and the evidence used to justify lethal military force.

Through the stories of families left searching for answers, alongside witness accounts, physical evidence and interviews with legal experts, Fault Lines asks whether the strikes are lawful, whether they have disrupted the drug trade and what accountability exists for those killed.

From fishing communities in the Caribbean to Washington, DC, Killing at Sea examines a military campaign conducted largely beyond public view—and asks who is being killed in the US’s new war at sea, and why.

title: China has found a new illicit drug market. America must shut it down
excerpt:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick discusses the importance of manufacturing drugs in the U.S.

China has found another vulnerability in America’s borders and supply chain - and it's being exploited.

...
body_text:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick discusses the importance of manufacturing drugs in the U.S.

China has found another vulnerability in America’s borders and supply chain - and it's being exploited.

An illicit pipeline is bringing an experimental injectable drug from Chinese chemical manufacturers directly into American homes. The drug is retatrutide, commonly called "reta," and is in clinical trials as a potential treatment for obesity and type 2 diabetes. This means there is no FDA-approved version, no lawful generic and it’s illegal to sell to patients.

But the national security concern goes far beyond one drug.

JILLIAN MICHAELS EXPOSES DANGERS OF SELF-DOSING ILLEGAL 'GRAY MARKET' WEIGHT LOSS DRUGS

What we are witnessing is an illegal international supply chain that begins with chemical suppliers in Communist China, moves through customs fraud and concealed shipments, is relabeled by American middlemen and ends with an unapproved injectable drug in an American home.

CLOSE THE BACKDOOR DRUG PIPELINE THAT’S EMBOLDENING ENEMIES AND HARMING THE PUBLIC

For years, Chinese chemical companies have supplied precursor chemicals used by cartels to make fentanyl. Now there is evidence that elements of this same infrastructure are being used for another lucrative American market: people looking for weight-loss drugs.

Blockchain researchers at Chainalysis were able to track proceeds from U.S. peptide sales flowing back to China-based chemical manufacturers that have produced synthetic opioids, such as fentanyl. TRM Labs has similarly detected a pattern of Chinese chemical companies that produce fentanyl precursors turning to the "peptide business."

EXPERT WARNS CHINA ALREADY WAGING ‘UNRESTRICTED WARFARE’ AGAINST US THROUGH FENTANYL, ESPIONAGE AND SABOTAGE

This should set off alarm bells across Washington.

The fentanyl crisis demonstrated what happens when foreign chemical suppliers, transnational criminal organizations and illicit financial networks exploit weaknesses in America’s borders and supply chains. We cannot make the same mistake twice by waiting until another illicit market becomes a full-blown crisis before confronting it.

FORMER TOP COP WARNS OF LOOPHOLE EXPLOITED BY ILLICIT CHINESE VAPE COMPANIES 'TARGETING OUR YOUTH'

The methods being used should also sound familiar.

Reta and other GLP-1 ingredients are being shipped to the United States under false descriptions that conceal what is actually inside the package and there is no reliable way for patients to verify the identity, purity, potency or sterility of what they are injecting into themselves. Once regulators have identified sellers engaged in this illegal behavior, the sellers then make changes needed to adapt.

‘WILD WEST’ PEPTIDE CRAZE SURGES BEYOND GLP-1S AS FDA FACES PRESSURE TO EASE ACCESS

Some vendors use coded names such as "GLP-3 RT." One vendor even distributed a "peptide cheat sheet" explaining that "GLP-3 RT" meant retatrutide and providing weekly dosing instructions. To further obscure their activity, sellers stamp packages "for research use only" while providing customers with dosing instructions, syringes and videos showing them how to prepare the drug for injection.

In this photo provided by the New York City Police Department, narcotics, including fentanyl, and drug paraphernalia lie stored in the floor of a day care center, Sept. 21, 2023, in New York.  (Courtesy NYPD via AP, File)

This is not simply skirting U.S. law. It is intentional evasion.

CBP OFFICERS SEIZE $67 MILLION IN ILLEGAL DRUGS AT SAN DIEGO BORDER PORTS, DHS SAYS

In one operation, Customs and Border Protection officers in Cincinnati uncovered more than 300 master cartons from China containing roughly 5,000 individual peptide shipments. Reta was among the cache of chemicals seized.

CHINA, RUSSIA, IRAN AND NORTH KOREA FORM 'AXIS OF AGGRESSORS' THAT COULD OVERWHELM US, BOOK WARNS

This raises a larger question: if foreign chemical manufacturers can conceal thousands of unapproved injectable products in ordinary commerce and deliver them directly to Americans, what else can these networks move into the country?

That is why this must be treated as more than a pharmaceutical issue. This is a national security issue.

The immediate danger to consumers is also real. Products manufactured and distributed outside America’s safeguards leave buyers with no reliable way to know what they are injecting. There is no legitimate supply chain to inspect and no reliable mechanism to recall a dangerous batch.

President Donald Trump has correctly made securing our border and supply chains, fighting the illegal entry of drugs and confronting China’s economic aggression central priorities of his administration.

Now these principles must be applied to this emerging threat.

The Department of Homeland Security, Department of Justice, FDA, as well as state law enforcement should coordinate an aggressive enforcement strategy aimed at the entire network, from foreign manufacturers and deceptive importers to domestic distributors and the financial networks that profit from the trade.

Unlike many other policy challenges, the federal government already has many of the authorities it needs. What is missing is the muscular enforcement needed to combat the problem.

The private sector must also do its part. American tech companies, social giants, online platforms, payment processors and shipping companies cannot be idle bystanders while their platforms and services facilitate illicit commerce.

When sellers advertise unapproved injectable under coded names, provide dosing instructions and pay influencers a commission for each sale, it’s not difficult to understand what is happening.

If tech companies can identify copyrighted music, political content and alleged "misinformation" within seconds, then they should be able to identify an illegal injectable drug.

The lesson from the fentanyl crisis could not be clearer: America cannot afford to ignore foreign chemical supply chains until Americans begin to pay the price.

Today, the product is Reta. Tomorrow, it will be something else. The drug is the warning. The pipeline is the treat.

Chad F. Wolf served as acting Secretary of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security during President Trump’s first term.

title: ‘It always comes around’: fans react to conviction in Tupac Shakur’s murder 30 years later
excerpt:
Rapper’s supporters reflect on ‘astonishing’ events leading to Duane Davis being found guilty over 1996 fatal shooting

A criminal conviction this week in the murder of Tupac Shakur, the first since t...
body_text:
Rapper’s supporters reflect on ‘astonishing’ events leading to Duane Davis being found guilty over 1996 fatal shooting

A criminal conviction this week in the murder of Tupac Shakur, the first since the rapper was gunned down in 1996, sent shockwaves through his sea of fans who have waited three decades for answers.

Duane “Keffe D” Davis, a former California gang leader, was found guilty of murder on Monday for the role he played in orchestrating the fatal shooting of Shakur.

The case relied on several confessions from Davis, including his 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend, in which he described the events of 7 September 1996. Davis said he came up with a plan to retaliate against Shakur after the rapper’s entourage attacked Davis’s nephew in the lobby of the MGM Grand hotel.

Some of Shakur’s legions of fans reflected on what the artist meant to them while expressing bittersweet joy about the long-awaited moment.

As a teenager, Kelly Wilson, 48, was enamored with hip-hop’s boy wonder. (Shakur was just 25 years old when he died.) “There was a lot of depth to him that I just didn’t hear elsewhere,” the Seattle area resident said on Tuesday.

During his life, Shakur faced blowback over lyrics his detractors regarded as glorifying violence or gang culture. But he was also lauded as an inner-city chronicler, whose pen cast unrelenting social critiques of racial inequality, police brutality and other issues of the time.

“I’m as white Irish as you get,” Wilson said, but he connected with Shakur’s overarching philosophy, which Wilson described as: “Speak for the people who don’t have a voice.”

His children grew up steeped in Shakur’s legacy. One of them, 22-year-old Julian Wilson, drew a parallel to Davis’s trial and one of the first songs in Shakur’s discography that he deeply studied.

The music video for Hail Mary, a track he recorded in 1996, begins with a scene where one incarcerated man laments being wrongfully imprisoned. “Revenge has a funny, funny way of setting the score, and when it happens, you will know,” a fellow inmate consoles him.

“That’s always stuck with me. Some things may take time, but it will always come around,” Julian Wilson said. “Even then, they still had faith that justice was going to be served no matter how long it took.”

The elder Wilson felt mixed emotions about Davis’s guilty verdict. “It’s nice to have the final chapter written for the family and those that need that healing,” he said.

At the same time, Wilson called the verdict “long overdue”, adding that others who may have been more culpable have since passed away. (Authorities have long suspected Davis’s nephew, Orlando Anderson, of being the gunman. Anderson died in 2004.)

Casey Rain, a British musician, was a moderator for HitEmUp.com, a forum dedicated to Shakur that was popular in the early aughts.

“I don’t mind admitting that there was a time in the years immediately following his passing where I definitely bought into some of those conspiracy theories. A lot of people did because we didn’t have access to the information that we have now,” Rain said, referencing longstanding fan theories about who killed Shakur, or whether Shakur was secretly still alive.

“Everything surrounding his murder has kind of existed in this middle ground of historical events and folklore. For somebody to be convicted of doing it, that grounds it and makes it real,” he continued. “This isn’t a sort of hip-hop, folklore, mythology story. This is a 25-year-old man that was murdered.”

In the end, Rain was also struck by how the case against Davis relied on his own admissions regarding the deadly night.

“It finally got solved because one of the people involved in it just wouldn’t shut up talking about it. It’s a really strange kind of irony. It’s astonishing,” Rain said.

Davis is set to be sentenced in October. The 63-year-old is facing at least 40 years in prison.

title: Iran accuses US of ‘war crime’ after missile blast kills five people at wedding
excerpt:
Blast also injures 68 guests at the wedding in southern Iran, prompting fears of escalation in hostilities

Iran has accused the US of a “war crime” after a missile blast killed at least five people a...
body_text:
Blast also injures 68 guests at the wedding in southern Iran, prompting fears of escalation in hostilities

Iran has accused the US of a “war crime” after a missile blast killed at least five people and injured 68 who were attending a wedding at a private home in a coastal city of southern Iran, as the fresh exchange of strikes prompted fears of a wider renewal of hostilities.

Iranian media said that the wedding ceremony was being held in a home in the city of Kuhestak, Hormozgan province, late on Tuesday when a US missile struck, with shrapnel and debris from the strike killing and injuring people.

Among the dead was a four-year-old child, Amir-Ali Karimi, and a 16-year-old, Mohammad Mollahi.

“It’s a terrible thing. I’m extremely worried and upset about what happened – really upset,” Ali Mollahi, the father of the bride, told Mehr News.

The deputy of the provincial government, Ahmad Nafisi, said first responders had headed immediately to the scene and transferred the wounded to the hospitals.

Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson called the US attack a “war crime” and said Iran “will respond to these savage crimes with firmness”.

The chief Iranian negotiator, Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, said the attack had killed families with children, and called the US the “great Satan”.

“If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan and kills like Satan, it’s Satan. Shields a junior Satan that does the same? It’s THE Great Satan,” Ghalibaf said in a post on X.

The US attacks on Tuesday ended a month-long uneasy truce between the US and Iran and appeared to signal a resumption of another cycle of escalation. US Central Command (Centcom) said the overnight strikes focused on Iranian military targets including air defence sites, radars and maritime assets.

Iran responded by launching drones and missiles on US bases across the Middle East, including in Bahrain, Kuwait and the UAE. Iran’s military spokesperson, Lt Col Ebrahim Zolfaghari, vowed “heavier, broader, and more crushing and devestating” retaliation.

Videos of the aftermath of the strike show a caved-in roof, blown-out windows and ground riddled with debris, as well as walls pockmarked with what appeared to be holes from shrapnel. Footage from a nearby hospital showed women in wedding attire watching as injured children were being treated.

“When we arrived there, an explosion occurred. It was very intense. Bricks, stones and cement hit me in the face and head, and many others were injured,” a child who was injured at the wedding told the state-affiliated Fars news agency.

A spokesperson for Centcom, Tim Hawkins, said the US was aware of reports of civilian casualties, but the “US military never targets civilians, unlike the [Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps]”.

In February, a strike on an elementary school killed at least 156 people, including more than 120 schoolchildren. Independent investigations concluded that the US likely carried out the strike with the assistance of AI, though the US government said the incident remained under investigation.

Pictures of shrapnel collected at the site of Tuesday’s attack were published on Iranian state media, and appeared to show the internal components of US munitions. Trevor Ball, an independent weapons analyst, identified some of the remnants as belonging to the Standoff Land Attack Missile-Expanded Response (Slam-Er) missile, which is made by the US weapons company Boeing. The Slam-Er is a 1,500-pound, GPS-guided missile touted by Boeing to be “extremely accurate.”

It was unclear if the home where the wedding was being held was struck directly, or if a missile hit close to the home and debris from the strike hit the home and its occupants. CCTV footage captured at least six strikes in the area within a minute. A separate strike appeared to hit a communications tower about 150 metres away from the home.

The US has been targeting communications and radar infrastructure along Iran’s coast to try to stop its blockade on the strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint which prior to the US-Iran war was a transit point for at least 20% of the world’s oil supply. 
 Iran has virtually closed the strait since the start of the Iran war, frustrating the US president, Donald Trump, who is facing a midterm election with expensive gas prices and knock-on inflation across the board.

In recent weeks, the US has focused on trying to degrade Iran’s capacity to strike ships transiting the strait to reopen the waterway for traffic.

title: More than 900 killed in Gaza this year despite ceasefire, Hamas-run health ministry says
excerpt:
More than 900 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza this year despite the ceasefire, according to latest figures from the territory's Hamas-run Ministry of Health.

It brings the total nu...
body_text:
More than 900 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza this year despite the ceasefire, according to latest figures from the territory's Hamas-run Ministry of Health.

It brings the total number of people killed in the Strip since the 10 October ceasefire was declared to more than 1,300, including 301 children, the ministry says.

Hamas and Israel agreed to halt the war after accepting US President Donald Trump's 20-point peace plan. That plan included a suspension of "all military operations, including aerial and artillery bombardment".

Since then, BBC Verify has analysed dozens of videos which show the impact of Israeli strikes on locations including a beachside cafe, tents where displaced people have been sheltering, and a reported funeral procession in central Gaza.

Recent months have been some of the most deadly according to the figures, with more than 100 people recorded killed each month between April and August.

The health ministry attributes the deaths directly to Israeli military action, but does not distinguish between civilians and combatants.

The UN considers the figures reliable, and experts have told BBC Verify that their independent analysis is consistent with the ministry's data.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) disputes the ministry's figures. It told BBC Verify there is "no basis to assume" that all those listed were killed as a result of IDF activity.

It said it operates in "a precise manner to remove threats and protect its troops and Israeli civilians, in accordance with the agreement", and that it works to mitigate any civilian harm "to the greatest extent possible".

At the start of this year Israeli media reported that an Israeli security official acknowledged more than 70,000 people had been killed in the Gaza war, which it said included more than 20,000 combatants.

From the start of the ceasefire agreement on 10 October to the end of that month, the ministry recorded 251 deaths. Since then the deadly Israeli attacks have continued every month. The highest monthly death toll this year was recorded in July, when 152 people were killed including 21 children, according to the figures.

The IDF says five of its soldiers have been killed in combat since the ceasefire and one contractor was killed in an "operational accident".

It also says it has killed hundreds of military operatives since October.

Conflict monitoring group Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (Acled), which uses official statements, media reports and social media to verify attacks, says it has recorded around 200 Israeli strikes during the ceasefire that have reportedly killed Hamas operatives or other armed "militants" in targeted strikes.

Acled said this includes commanders involved in planning the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attack on Israel, which triggered the war and killed around 1,200 people with 251 taken hostage.

Hugh Lovatt, senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations think tank, said "Gaza has seen a ceasefire in name only" since last October. He said the Israeli military has continued its almost daily air and drone strikes, and "though it claims to be targeting Hamas or imminent threats, it is Gaza's civilians that have continued to bear the brunt".

This could now be a "central stumbling block" in international efforts to implement Trump's ceasefire deal, he added.

The IDF told BBC Verify it "remains committed" to the ceasefire agreement and that there have been "continued violations and threats posed by Hamas and other terror organizations" in Gaza.

Warning: The following segment of this story contains graphic content which some readers might find distressing.

Multiple deadly Israeli strikes in Gaza in  under 24 hours

BBC Verify has analysed dozens of videos of attacks in Gaza carried out since the ceasefire.

In one, emergency services are seen attending to people in the aftermath of a strike at a beachside cafe in Gaza City on 18 August, where six people were killed, according to the health ministry. The next day nine people, including a 13-year-old, were reportedly killed in a strike on a police headquarters in the al-Tuffah neighbourhood.

The IDF said it was targeting Hamas commanders and terrorists in the two incidents and that "steps were taken to mitigate harm to civilians".

One of the deadliest single incidents in July was a strike on a reported funeral procession in Nuseirat. Seven people were killed and 22 injured, according to the Al-Awda Hospital where casualties were taken. Several verified images show nine people covered in blood lying on the street. Two people appear to still be alive and are being treated by bystanders.

The IDF said it was targeting a "significant military operative" of the Palestinian Islamic Jihad group who was involved in the 7 October 2023 attacks.

Men assess scene of Israeli strike on high-rise block in Gaza City on 2 August

In a strike on an apartment block on the western edge of Gaza City overnight on 1 August, a pregnant woman, her husband and their young son were killed, according to local reports. Verified footage showed the body of an unborn baby in the rubble.

A man searching the ruins said he had heard a strike overnight and saw smoke coming from the building. "I broke the door and went up and I found dead bodies scattered," he said. The IDF said it had targeted an acting Hamas commander.

UN agency Unicef has also reported more than 300 children have been killed since the ceasefire. The aid organisation has been tracking all available reports of incidents affecting children in Gaza, including via UN personnel on the ground.

James Elder, Unicef global spokesperson, said the number of child deaths was "absurd and devastating".

He added that hundreds more have been injured. "A ceasefire that paints such a grim picture can only be failing children."

Unicef and other humanitarian organisations operating inside Gaza have also reported Israeli strikes on their workers since the ceasefire. This includes two water truck drivers contracted by Unicef killed in April by Israeli fire at the Mansoura water filling point in northern Gaza.

The IDF said its soldiers "identified suspects approaching" the Yellow Line area during the incident, who were later identified as UN contractors who had not "coordinated in advance". Unicef said the drivers were carrying out routine water trucking operations with "no changes in movement or procedures".

Aid Worker Security Database, whose figures have been cited by the UN and UK government, told BBC Verify it has recorded 22 aid workers killed in Gaza since 10 October 2025.

Palestinians grieve over bodies of people killed in an Israeli attack targeting a beachfront cafe in Gaza City

Independent research group Airwars works to identify civilian deaths from a range of open sources including news agencies, NGOs and social media, matching names it finds to those published by the health ministry.

Director Emily Tripp told BBC Verify the ministry's data on death tolls is consistent with its own tracking and research, and that it recorded more than 60 deadly incidents in July.

"This is the highest number of fatal incidents we've seen in a month since the ceasefire," Tripp said. "Our own findings point to an increasing number of civilian harm incidents a month."

Professor Michael Spagat from Royal Holloway, University of London, is the chair of Every Casualty Counts, a charity that studies death tolls in wars. He told BBC Verify that the figures recorded by the health ministry are "testable" because it publishes names, ages and ID numbers of the dead.

He said that since April, the monthly death toll in Gaza has been roughly double what was seen in December. "July was the worst month but even August's lower toll is still high compared with the November to March period," he added.

Additional reporting Paul Brown, Benedict Garman and Lamees Altalebi

What do you want BBC Verify to investigate?

title: Rosenberg: Putin's veiled threat to UK part of Russia's campaign against West
excerpt:
Putin warned that "if anyone tries to drag us down the food chain, to gobble us up or devour us, they might get punched in the teeth"

Russian President Vladimir Putin responded with one short sentenc...
body_text:
Putin warned that "if anyone tries to drag us down the food chain, to gobble us up or devour us, they might get punched in the teeth"

Russian President Vladimir Putin responded with one short sentence when asked at a press conference whether Moscow might strike military facilities in the UK in response to British arms supplies to Ukraine.

Military secret is not a "yes". And not a "no". It leaves us hanging.

Those two words feel like psychological pressure from the Kremlin: to keep Britain guessing - and stressing - over Moscow's intentions, as well as to encourage the UK to think twice about its staunch support for Ukraine.

It reminds me of a newspaper article I read a few days ago. Moskovsky Komsomolets had suggested that UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham should be seeing Russia, not in his dreams, "but in his nightmares".

Scary language. But short on detail about what those nightmares will look like.

We cannot conclude that Russian missiles are about to be used against targets in the UK.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham: "We will be there in Ukraine's hour of need"

But look what's happening elsewhere in Europe.

Germany now says Russia was responsible for last month's drone attack at Leipzig airport.

Putin accused Germany of "planting the evidence". But German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt described "the well-established pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe".

Could such "operations" now be stepped up in the UK?

Yet it wasn't just Britain that received veiled threats at Putin's press conference.

So did the West in general. Putin referred to Western countries as sharks.

"If anyone tries to drag us down the food chain, to gobble us up or devour us, they might get punched in the teeth," he said. "Russia is ready to do that, despite the rapidly growing appetites and teeth of these sharks."

Increasingly Russia's president is mixing the geopolitical with the zoological. He recently spoke about killer whales "tearing polar bears apart" to justify Russia's war on Ukraine.

The press conference in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, was a fascinating window on Putin's state of mind.

For forty-five minutes he took questions from Russian journalists and came across as combative, confident of victory and energised. These days Putin appears most animated when talking about the geopolitical standoff between Russia and the West and the war in Ukraine.

Even though the war has not gone to plan. Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield and the country's economy is under considerable pressure.

"I have no doubt that the enemy will crumble," he declared. Yet the war has lasted more than four-and-a-half years and Ukraine fights on.

Officially the Kremlin still calls this a "special military operation". But even Putin now is using the word "war".

"War is a brutal and unpredictable thing," he said at the press conference.

He claimed that he remained open to negotiations to end the conflict and left no doubt with whom he'd prefer to sit down with from the US administration: Donald Trump's envoys.

"We are absolutely comfortable working with those people we know well and generally trust," Putin said. "[Jared] Kushner and [Steve] Witkoff are always welcome guests. It's a pleasure working with them."

There was no such name check for the CIA director who had made a surprise visit to Moscow last week. The Kremlin says the Russian president didn't meet John Ratcliffe during that trip.

Is Putin likely to meet Witkoff and Kushner anytime soon?

But if they do head to Moscow, President Trump's envoys will encounter a Kremlin leader who remains determined that any peace in Ukraine should be on Russia's terms.

Germany says Russia behind Leipzig airport drone attack

UK 'supports Ukraine 100%', Burnham says, after Russia's drone warning

UK-made drones strike targets inside Russia

title: EU holds talks on response to Leipzig drone attack after Germany formally blames Moscow for incident – Europe live
excerpt:
Foreign policy chief says drone attack last month ‘had all the hallmarks of state sponsored terrorism’ as she prepares to lead today’s discussions

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Russia’s at...
body_text:
Foreign policy chief says drone attack last month ‘had all the hallmarks of state sponsored terrorism’ as she prepares to lead today’s discussions

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Russia’s attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport last month “had all the hallmarks of state sponsored terrorism,” as she prepares to lead talks on the bloc’s political reaction.

Kallas will host today’s informal talks between EU foreign ministers in Wicklow, Ireland, focusing on “what more we can do” after Germany formally blamed Russia for last month’s security incident.

She said the incident should serve as a “wake-up call” for those countries that have been dragging their feet on further sanctions against Russia. “If we want to end this war, we all have to focus our efforts, take it to a new level,” she said.

Separately, the EU and France have summoned top Russian officials to protest against the attack.

Kallas said the discussions will also look at how the EU can further help Ukraine when “Russia is escalating and killing the civilians and causing as much harm as they can.”

Later today, European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen will separately meet with Nato’s Mark Rutte, with the Leipzig incident and Ukraine also set to dominate their talks.

Elsewhere, Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten will host French president Emmanuel Macron today, who is then expected in Britain for talks with PM Andy Burnham.

It’s Wednesday, 2 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

Britain’s foreign secretary Ed Miliband is also taking part in today’s talks in Ireland.

“We see an attempt by Russia to divide us in Europe and to deter us from our support for Ukraine. And I say very clearly today, on behalf of the United Kingdom, this attempt will fail.”

He says that the UK “will stand shoulder to shoulder with our friends with Ukraine,” as it has since the full-scale invasion in 2022.

He says the UK knows Russia’s tactics “from the past Russian attacks on our soil,” and “these attempts to divide us will not work.”

Wadephul says he is “impressed by the strong European support” for Berlin’s decision to attribute the Leipzig attack to Russia, with “a great deal of unity” from colleagues.

“It is very important that Russia clearly sees that Europe stands together,” he says.

He says Russia “must understand” that its approach will not work.

He says the German decision to attribute the attack to Russia was “a well-founded opinion and judgment.”

“Russia must now live with the consequences,” he says, pointing to “necessary and appropriate response” proposed yesterday.

Wadephul says that in the coming weeks the EU will be working on expanding its sanctions, which would target “a large number of individuals.”

Let’s go back to Wicklow and listen to German foreign minister Johann Wadephul, who will be briefing his EU counterparts today on the latest in the Leipzig investigation and Berlin’s reasoning for formally naming Russia as responsible for the attempted drone attack.

Separately, German police are also investigating another attempt to disrupt the country’s energy grid, this time at a electricity substation in Bergheim in the west of the country.

A local police spokesperson said they are “not assuming a technical failure but a deliberate act,” without revealing more details. The region’s power supply was not affected.

Again, like with yesterday’s incident at a substation near a coal-fired power plant in Brandenburg, the issue of attribution here is not straightforward.

AFP notes that German authorities are on high alert for ​attacks on ​vital infrastructure after Berlin blamed ​Russia for an attempted drone attack on a ​Ukrainian cargo ‌plane at ​Leipzig/Halle airport ​last month and ordered a series of measures in response.

But Germany’s electricity grid has been hit by attacks before, including by suspected left-wing militants.

Again, I will keep an eye on updates on this.

Two people were injured after an unknown object exploded near a train station in the southern German city of Augsburg.

A separate suspicious object was later found nearby, prompting police to temporarily suspend train services and close the station.

But, and that’s an important caveat, local media are reporting that the incident may be linked to organised crime rather than anything else, though authorities are yet to confirm a motive.

title: Nepal floods: Father borrows $13, walks for days to search for missing son
excerpt: Kathmandu/Nuwakot, Nepal — Talka Sada’s eyes are exhausted, the wrinkles on his face deep with worry. His heels hurt after walking long miles across Nepal’s mountains. He’s hungry and angry, but as hi...
body_text:
Kathmandu/Nuwakot, Nepal — Talka Sada’s eyes are exhausted, the wrinkles on his face deep with worry. His heels hurt after walking long miles across Nepal’s mountains. He’s hungry and angry, but as his mood shifts between hope and helplessness, his focus remains on his mission: a desperate search for his son.

Sada, who is in his 50s, is from Saptari, a district in Nepal’s Terai region — the plains that stretch across southern Nepal, south of the Shivalik Hills and north of the porous border with India.

People from this part of the Himalayan nation are known as Madhesis, a distinct ethnolinguistic population with a diverse regional, cultural and caste identity. Vinod, his only son — Sada also has three daughters — has been missing since the devastating flash floods of August 26 destroyed homes, schools, bridges, power plants and everything in their path in large parts of northern Nepal.

Sada last spoke to 19-year-old Vinod a day before the floods that grew from the Bhotekoshi river. Vinod had come to the Rasuwa district, the region worst affected by the floods, a month earlier to work as a labourer at a hydropower plant. He would mix cement and take on other odd jobs. Four other young men who worked with him — all between 17 and 19 years old — are also missing since the floods.

“I can’t tell you how much my wife is howling. I am in deep pain myself and I do not know what to do,” Sada says as he wipes his tears.

Dressed in a faded white shirt and black pants, the father wears an orange polythene bag as a raincoat. He carries a grey backpack on his shoulders. With him is his brother, Sada’s companion on a long and increasingly frustrating journey.

Sada shows a dirty handkerchief in his pocket with notes amounting to less than 2,000 Nepali rupees (about $13) crumpled in it. It’s money he borrowed to be able to crisscross Nepal’s flood-affected areas in search of his son.

“I borrowed money to come all the way from Saptari to here. I have to pay an interest of 20 rupees on every 100 rupees I have borrowed,” he says. The brothers used some of that money to take a bus from Saptari to the national capital, Kathmandu. That 292km (181-mile) journey takes nine hours because of Nepal’s hilly terrain.

In Kathmandu, Sada and his brother went from hospital to hospital to look for Vinod among survivors or in the list of those declared dead — many of the flood victims were flown into Kathmandu from the northern parts of Nepal.

Outside mortuaries, the photographs displayed are often difficult to recognise. Most bodies being retrieved are decomposed or dismembered. There was no sign of Vinod — nor his name or photo at the hospitals.

So, Sada started walking towards Nuwakot (nearly 60km away from Kathmandu), closer to the location of the hydropower plant where his son was believed to be working.

After a gruelling, hours-long walk through broken roads, they reached Trishuli, a town on the way whose market now lies covered with debris, mud and slush.

“Last night when we reached here, a lodge charged us 1,500 Nepali rupees to stay the night. They gave us only one small serving of rice that did not even satisfy our hunger,” says Sada. “Now if we have to stay here another night, all my remaining money will finish and I will be left with nothing to go back home.”

Sada and his brother say they just want access to mortuaries and army camps set up to help evacuate survivors and take bodies from the disaster zone, but claim that he has been turned away repeatedly.

To the brothers, the response they’ve received to their pleas for help is a product of deep-seated ethnic and caste divisions within Nepal. Madhesis — as the people of the Terai are known — have long accused the hills-based Nepali elite of discriminating against them.

Sada’s family is from the Musahar community, a particularly marginalised community that lives in the Terai and in the Indian states of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.

“We are poor. They think of us as Madheshis and Biharis. We cannot speak Nepali fluently — which is why they are just pushing us away and making us run from pillar to post,” Sada claims, as he sobs. “Even if it is a corpse, we have a right to see it. We have registered our names everywhere – police stations to military camps. But no one is helping us.”

Nepali authorities, overwhelmed by the scale of the crisis — more than 1,000 people have been killed, and thousands are still missing — insist they are trying their best to reach and help all survivors.

The brothers try dialling Vinod’s phone number for the umpteenth time, but get no response. “We can’t talk to him. We don’t hear his voice. So everyone is heartbroken back home,” says Sada. “My wife asked me to get our son back. So we are searching all hydropower plants, but where do I find him?”

One minute, Sada is hoping for a miracle. “My son is young. He is a porter. He is daily wager. So he is agile. He could have surely walked, ran somewhere,” he wonders.

The very next moment, though, the father’s voice rings with helplessness. “I have no hope,” he says. “If Vinod was alive, he surely would have called from somewhere, even if he went to drink water.”

Yet giving up isn’t an option — not yet, at least.

So, Sada and his brother prepare to continue their trek towards the power plant where Vinod worked. As they leave, the father issues a warning that rings with a sense of betrayal and anger.

“We will have to burn down the police station if no one answers or helps us,” he shouts.

title: Ohio Supreme Court denies Mackenzie Shirilla's latest appeal bid in double murder case
excerpt: Bryan Kohberger, accused in the quadruple murder of University of Idaho students, is attempting to withdraw his previous guilty plea. Kohberger's post-conviction petition alleges ineffective assistanc...
body_text:
Bryan Kohberger, accused in the quadruple murder of University of Idaho students, is attempting to withdraw his previous guilty plea. Kohberger's post-conviction petition alleges ineffective assistance of counsel, coercion, disinformation, and false promises, seeking a new trial. Victims' families, including Kaylee Goncalves' mother, expressed disappointment but noted they were not surprised by this latest legal maneuver.

Convicted double murderer Mackenzie Shirilla suffered another legal setback after the Ohio Supreme Court denied her attorneys' request to reconsider its decision not to hear her latest appeal.

Shirilla, now 21, is serving two concurrent sentences of 15 years to life for killing her boyfriend, Dominic Russo, 20, and their friend, Davion Flanagan, 19, after prosecutors said she intentionally drove her Toyota Camry into a brick building in Strongsville, Ohio, in 2022.

Chief Justice Sharon Kennedy denied Shirilla's motion for reconsideration after her attorneys asked the state's highest court to revisit its June 23 decision declining to review her case, according to court records.

"It is ordered by the court that the motion for reconsideration in this case is denied," Kennedy wrote.

MACKENZIE SHIRILLA'S TEXTS SURFACE AS 'HELL ON WHEELS' DRIVER'S APPEAL COLLIDES WITH NETFLIX'S 'THE CRASH'

Convicted killer Mackenzie Shirilla has landed a prison job while serving a life sentence for the 2022 crash that killed her boyfriend and their friend, Ohio prison officials confirmed to Fox News Digital. (Ohio Department of Rehabilitation and Correction)

Tuesday's decision leaves intact a lower-court ruling that Shirilla's postconviction challenge was filed one day too late.

Shirilla's attorneys have argued that the missed deadline resulted from confusion over the filing timeline, including a calendar mistake involving the 2024 leap year.

The postconviction challenge sought to raise claims that Shirilla received ineffective assistance of counsel, including an argument that her trial lawyers failed to adequately investigate evidence that she suffered from Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome, or POTS.

Her attorneys have argued that the condition could have caused Shirilla to lose consciousness before the crash and potentially explain why she failed to brake before impact.

WATCH: MACKENZIE SHIRILLA’S FATHER CALLS HER ‘A DUMB 18-YEAR-OLD’ WHILE BERATING POLICE IN BODYCAM VIDEO

Mackenzie Shirilla makes a statement to the court during her sentencing in the Cuyahoga County Common Pleas Court in Cleveland, Ohio on Monday, August 21, 2023. (Law&Crime livestream)

The defense previously said the condition was only "cursorily referenced" at trial despite Shirilla and her family allegedly putting her attorneys on notice about it.

The latest court decisions, however, have focused on whether Shirilla's postconviction petition was filed on time rather than the merits of those arguments.

Under Ohio law, a postconviction petition must generally be filed within 365 days after the trial transcript is filed in the court of appeals. The court determined that the relevant transcript was filed Oct. 24, 2023, making the deadline Oct. 23, 2024.

Shirilla filed her petition on Oct. 24, 2024, the 366th day.

Shirilla argued that the clock should have started later, when juvenile bindover transcripts were filed, and also pointed to the 2024 leap year. The appellate court rejected both arguments, finding that the statute refers to the "trial transcript," not supplemental juvenile-hearing transcripts, and that the law provides 365 days, not a calendar year.

IDAHO JUDGE GRANTS BRYAN KOHBERGER TWO HEARINGS NEXT YEAR AS ADMITTED KILLER SEEKS TO WITHDRAW GUILTY PLEA

Mackenzie Shirilla is serving two concurrent sentences of 15 years to life for the deaths of her boyfriend, Dominic Russo, and their friend, Davion Flanagan. (Ohio Department of Rehabilitation and Correction)

Her attorneys later asked the Ohio Supreme Court to review the case. The state's highest court declined to accept jurisdiction June 23 before Shirilla's legal team asked the justices to reconsider that decision.

Shirilla's case has received renewed public attention following the release of Netflix's "The Crash."

Shirilla was convicted in 2023 after a bench trial of four counts of murder, four counts of felonious assault and two counts of aggravated vehicular homicide.

Prosecutors argued at trial that Shirilla intentionally drove into the building to end her toxic relationship with Russo and that Flanagan was an unintended victim who happened to be in the car.

NEW HAMPSHIRE SUPREME COURT OVERTURNS ADAM MONTGOMERY'S MURDER CONVICTION IN DAUGHTER HARMONY'S DEATH

Mackenzie Shirlla, now 19, was convicted Monday of intentionally crashing her car into a brick wall to kill her boyfriend, Dominic Russo and his friend, Davion Flanagan. Shirilla posted the photo to Russo's online obituary. (Legacy.com)

Evidence presented in the case included surveillance video, vehicle "black box" data and evidence that Shirilla's car was traveling nearly 100 mph without braking before the crash, according to WOIO.

Shirilla has maintained that the crash was not intentional.

Her convictions were upheld on direct appeal in 2024.

Fox News Digital has reached out to Shirilla's attorney for comment.

Fox News Digital's Sarah Rumpf-Whitten contributed to this report.

Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

title: Bus crash on Egypt's Red Sea coast kills 16
excerpt:
At least 16 people have been killed in a bus crash in eastern Egypt, the country's health ministry has said.

Another 28 people were injured on the road between Red Sea towns of Dahab and Nuweiba in t...
body_text:
At least 16 people have been killed in a bus crash in eastern Egypt, the country's health ministry has said.

Another 28 people were injured on the road between Red Sea towns of Dahab and Nuweiba in the South Sinai governorate on Wednesday morning.

As many as 20 ambulances were sent to the scene of the accident to provide first aid and evacuate the injured, the ministry said. The cause of the crash remains unknown.

The area is a popular tourist destination, attracting visitors from around the world.

Deadly road accidents are common across Egypt, with the authorities reporting nearly 6,000 fatalities in 2025.

Such accidents are often blamed on reckless driving and poor road maintenance.

Last month, 18 people were killed and 30 injured when two lorries collided in the north-eastern Ismailia governorate.

title: Britain is OK with public ownership, but only by foreign powers. Why?
excerpt:
Arthur Downing, author of Power and the People: A History of British Energy, says all-encompassing rapid transition will need a mutualised system

Have you ever wondered why it is that most houses in ...
body_text:
Arthur Downing, author of Power and the People: A History of British Energy, says all-encompassing rapid transition will need a mutualised system

Have you ever wondered why it is that most houses in the UK are reliant on gas boilers? Not what’s stopping more people from replacing them with heat pumps, but instead why and how the gas boiler became so ubiquitous in the first place?

Arthur Downing, the author of the new book Power and the People: A History of British Energy, can tell you exactly why. “We only have boilers in our houses because of a state-owned enterprise that went into everybody’s home and installed natural gas-suitable appliances at no direct cost,” he says. The nationalised gas industry of the 1940s to the 1980s, which oversaw this huge project, was for three decades one of the “most dynamic, innovative, efficient industries in Britain”, Downing says. Yet few of us would use these terms to describe it as such now.

Instead, Britain’s electricity and gas industries are “fragile, fragmented, comically complicated and hopelessly dependent on imported fossil fuels”, Downing writes. On top of that, as consumers, we are facing soaring energy bills amid a cost of living crisis.

Unearthing how this happened, by exploring the history of Britain’s energy industry, is the subject of Downing’s book. It’s one he lives and breathes – by day, Downing works as the director of strategy at Octopus Energy, the UK’s largest supplier of energy, but the book itself is written in a personal capacity.

Central to his argument is that this is a history a lot of us, even people working in the industry now, know little to nothing about. Yet it is instructive for the present, Downing argues, showing why we have the system we do – and, importantly, how we might change it for the better.

This summer’s string of climate crisis-driven heatwaves makes his book feel even more urgent. Although the UK has reduced greenhouse gas emissions by 50% compared with 1990 levels, Downing explains: “The second half of the journey will be much harder than the first. All the low-hanging fruits have been picked, like deindustrialising and switching from coal to gas.”

Yet debates about the energy system often happen behind closed doors, and part of his aim was to make it more intelligible. An economic historian by training and with encyclopaedic knowledge about energy, both shine through in the book, which charts how the crisis came into being.

His argument is straightforward: ownership matters. “Who owned and controlled the means of making, moving, and selling energy shaped which technologies were developed, what infrastructure got built and the extent to which citizens and consumers benefited,” he writes. Between 1926 and 1979, for instance, state-owned enterprises built huge infrastructure – from hydroelectric plants to power stations inside mountains – faster and cheaper than Britain’s private sector companies today. The system has been privatised since the start of the 1980s, and despite the mess it’s currently in, the orthodoxy tends to still be that private is always better than public ownership – cheaper, more efficient and more creative. Downing does not agree.

“I tend to view things from the perspective of political economy – the institutions, the ownership models, the organisations and the people make the system,” says Downing, who speaks with energising enthusiasm and expertise. “For me, the technology is interesting, but it is very strange to think of the [energy] system composed of inanimate objects, as if these things have agency and they don’t. They’re only there because of [human decisions].”

Downing’s book charts four phases over the last 200 years, each given a chapter of its own. In the first phase, from the late 1880s to the 1920s, ownership of Britain’s energy system was overwhelmingly public and municipal. This meant that even where private companies were involved, they were highly local, embedded in regional networks, and with municipal authorities making the decisions about how to plan and coordinate the gas and electricity system. The second phase, 1920-1945, saw government become a major owner and operator of some energy infrastructure. The third, from 1945-1979, saw energy nearly completely nationalised. And the final, before the mess of the system we have today, was characterised by almost total privatisation between 1979 and 2010.

Although 1,500 energy entities were brought into two state-owned enterprises after the second world war, nationalisation didn’t begin in the 1940s but rather started in that second phase. In fact, in 1926, it was the Conservative prime minister, Stanley Baldwin, who set up the Central Electricity Board (CEB) – a state-owned public corporation that built the first National Grid. Unlike now, this was done on time and at cost.

Downing says the energy system we have now is a zombie – a “dysfunctional hybrid” of public and private. For example, it remains privately owned but feeds off state subsidies, meaning few benefits of either model but most of the costs in that it is expensive and inefficient.

In February, Engie, the electric utility company in which the French government is the largest shareholder, bought UK Power Networks (UKPN), which owns and maintains electricity cables in the south and east of England, from a conglomerate. On that very day, Downing points out, 10-year bond borrowing rates of the French state went down and the stock value of Engie went up, meaning every French citizen got a bit richer. It didn’t play out the way the British media often claims – the bond markets didn’t blink and the government didn’t collapse.

Downing suggests Andy Burnham’s early announcement of a VAT cut on energy bills was a good first move. But if he could ask Burnham to do anything else, what would it be? “Shift the focus from producers to consumers, from investors to citizens,” he says. This would include getting bills down by taking off levies, which are added to fund environmental and social programmes. But it would also mean looking at questions of ownership.

“Public ownership was an extraordinary tool for building infrastructure at pace while delivering benefits for citizens,” Downing says. “It can be again.”

Downing doesn’t want a return to a 1940s-style system. Instead, he advocates for a mutualised system, meaning neither nationalised nor privatised. “The old labels don’t fit,” he explains. “The principle is that energy should be built around mutually beneficial relationships between capital, citizens and the state, with ownership and decision-making spread out rather than concentrated.” What does that look like in practice? “Public corporations owning the networks and part of generation, councils and community schemes taking real ownership stakes in local infrastructure, and households owning solar, batteries and electric vehicles and being paid properly for the flexibility those provide. Citizens as owners of the system, not only customers of it.”

The state would become even more involved in regulation, because regulatory institutions make the system more complex. For example, Ofgem is tasked with setting the price cap and assessing the components of bills but in many instances it doesn’t actually control the costs that are accruing.

Markets would still be involved. Natural monopolies – in networks and onshore transmission, for instance – would be publicly owned, while markets would stay for retail, electrical vehicle charging, home solar and batteries. “Public ownership and markets are not opposites,” Downing says. “The Nordic countries introduced competition in [power] generation and retail shortly after Britain and kept extensive public ownership. China is running markets at huge scale within a publicly owned system. The US has the longest tradition of private ownership and some of the least competitive markets in the world.”

To make such a change would require bold political intervention. Maybe the local aspect, which is a big part of Downing’s proposal, appeals to Burnham’s talk of devolution, nationalisation and reindustrialisation.

Energy transitions are rare and protracted, usually taking around a century, Downing says, and if this were to happen, it would be the “first all-encompassing rapid energy transition in human history”. His book suggests it is possible. We just have to reject the British orthodoxy that says the state is useless in a way private companies never are.

“We have a strange situation where we are OK with public ownership, just not by our own state,” he says.

Power and the People: A History of British Energy is published by Verso on 1 September

title: Turkiye launches search for cargo ship after vessels collide off Istanbul
excerpt:
Turkiye’s coastguard has launched a search and rescue operation after two Turkish-flagged commercial vessels collided off Istanbul and contact was lost with one vessel and its crew of 10.

The collisi...
body_text:
Turkiye’s coastguard has launched a search and rescue operation after two Turkish-flagged commercial vessels collided off Istanbul and contact was lost with one vessel and its crew of 10.

The collision took place at 3am (00:00 GMT) in the Marmara Sea a little more than 20 miles (32 kilometres) south of Silivri, a suburb of Turkey’s largest city, the Istanbul governor’s office said in a statement on Wednesday.

Contact was lost with the crew of the Tugberk Imamoglu, flagged to Turkey, after the collision with the Turkish-flagged Alsu, which appeared undamaged, the governor’s office said.

“Numerous naval units from the coast guard’s Marmara and Bosphorus Command and a coast guard helicopter were dispatched to the scene,” the office said.

title: As US seeks Gaza donor’s extradition, wife warns of ‘terrifying precedent’
excerpt: Madrid, Spain – A wealthy American donor to Palestinian causes who faces extradition from Spain to the United States over alleged financial support of Hamas is a victim of “political persecution”, his...
body_text:
Madrid, Spain – A wealthy American donor to Palestinian causes who faces extradition from Spain to the United States over alleged financial support of Hamas is a victim of “political persecution”, his wife and lawyers have told Al Jazeera.

James “Fergie” Chambers was arrested on the Spanish island of Ibiza in July while searching for a school for his son with his wife, actress Stella Schnabel.

US authorities have linked Chambers to the transfer of $7.5m to Tunisia and allege that the funds were ultimately used to provide financial support to the Palestinian armed group Hamas.

The indictment remains sealed, so the specific allegations against Chambers – who denies wrongdoing – are not yet known.

Chambers, heir to one of the richest families in the US, has supported a handful of humanitarian projects in Gaza with funds totalling more than $1m, a member of his legal team said shortly after his arrest.

The extradition effort is believed to be the first of its kind involving a US citizen accused of providing support to Hamas.

Chambers, who describes himself as a Marxist-Leninist, has been held in a Madrid jail for six weeks as Spanish authorities consider the US extradition request.

Schnabel, who is also an activist, said she was driving through the Balearic island of Ibiza with her husband to search for a school for their five-year-old son, as they were moving from Ireland to Spain, when he was arrested.

“Suddenly, several unmarked cars cut us off. Police officers got out of the cars and told us to get out of the car. I got out my phone, and they told me not to phone,” she told Al Jazeera. “They handcuffed Fergie. We said we loved each other, and he said, ‘Tell the kids I love them’. And they bundled him into a car, and he was gone. That was July 10. Over six weeks ago.”

Schnabel said US President Donald Trump’s administration was targeting her husband for being one of the largest donors to humanitarian projects in Gaza. This included supplying bread, water and medical care.

“He should be at home with his family, continuing his humanitarian work. Instead, he is facing political persecution because he has stood with the Palestinian people,” she said. “This sets a terrifying precedent for repression of the wider movement for a free Palestine, including precedent for the Trump administration exporting its repression far beyond the US borders to target the people of Europe.”

The US Department of Justice declined to comment when contacted by Al Jazeera.

The US sent the indictment and documentation to Spain last week, in time to meet the 45-day deadline after Chambers’s arrest in July.

Al Jazeera understands that the indictment is still sealed and has not been revealed to his defence team.

Spanish authorities must now assess the US request. Among the issues they may consider is whether the extradition would amount to political persecution, a circumstance that could provide grounds for refusing it.

Chambers comes from the family behind Atlanta-based Cox Communications. In 2023, he reached an agreement with his relatives under which his stake in the family business was bought back for approximately $250m, following a break with the family.

Since then, he has been funding dozens of projects in 20 countries, Schnabel has said.

On the central allegation about funding Hamas, Schnabel said this was a “trumped-up charge” for which the US has not provided a “shred of evidence”.

“My understanding is that the US appears to rely on the fact that he transferred $7.5m of his own funds from the US to Tunisia. The reality is that this money was transferred to Tunisia because we were living there, and for philanthropic activities, including supporting Club Africain [a football team],” Schnabel said.

“The money sponsored the club, helped to pay its debts and overdue salaries, rebuild its training centre and develop football fields for young people.”

The Tunisian side secured the league title in May.

Lawyers for Chambers have also pointed to his outspoken views on Israel and its genocidal war on Gaza.

In the week after the October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, Chambers posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’. There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for. No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done anything wrong. It’s simply genocide. Like it has been.”

In the wake of the 41-year-old’s arrest, FBI agents raided the rented property in Ibiza where Chambers had been staying, The Guardian reported.

Chambers is represented by Spanish human-rights lawyer Baltasar Garzon, who has argued that the case against his client is politically motivated and connected to his humanitarian work in Palestine.

“We request our client’s provisional release and to file all necessary legal actions with the courts,” he told Al Jazeera.

In 1998, Garzon sprang to international attention when he sought the extradition from London of the former Chilean dictator Augusto Pinochet. He has also acted in human rights cases in Spain and Argentina.

“We hope that Spain will not grant extradition in what we consider to be a case of political persecution based on our client’s ideas and humanitarian aid to Palestine,” he added, referring to Chambers.

title: Tyson Fury confirms Anthony Joshua fight at NYC’s Madison Square Garden
excerpt: Former world heavyweight champion Tyson ⁠⁠⁠⁠Fury has confirmed that his long-awaited heavyweight boxing showdown with fellow Briton Anthony Joshua will take place at New York City’s iconic Madison Squ...
body_text:
Former world heavyweight champion Tyson ⁠⁠⁠⁠Fury has confirmed that his long-awaited heavyweight boxing showdown with fellow Briton Anthony Joshua will take place at New York City’s iconic Madison Square Garden.

No exact date has been set for the Joshua vs Fury fight — one of the biggest in British boxing history — although it is expected to be held in November after both signed a contract with Turki Alalshikh, Saudi Arabia’s General Entertainment Authority chairman.

“What a place, what a venue, what a fight,” Fury said in a post on Instagram.

Fury called New York City “the land of opportunity”, but fans criticised him in comments on the post as they questioned why an all-British fight was being held in the US, and not at a location like Wembley Stadium in the United Kingdom.

Fury, who ⁠⁠⁠⁠turned 38 in August, has won 36 ⁠⁠⁠⁠professional bouts, suffering his ⁠⁠⁠⁠only losses in two fights with Ukraine’s Oleksandr Usyk in 2024. He announced his return to boxing in January, having retired from the sport in December 2024 after losing to Usyk in a bout for three of the four major world titles.

Joshua and Fury were unable to agree on terms in 2021, and plans for the face-off fell apart after a US judge ruled Fury had to face Deontay Wilder in a trilogy fight instead.

In the lead-up to the Joshua showdown, Fury forced Polish opponent Mariusz Wach to retire in a tune-up ⁠⁠⁠⁠bout in July attended by some 1,500 fans at the Max Muay Thai Stadium in Pattaya, Thailand.

title: ‘We had an ordinary life’: Iran fisherwoman navigates uncertainty of war
excerpt: In this first-person testimony told to Al Jazeera, Khadijeh Bandari, an Iranian fisherwoman from Hengam Island in southern Iran, explains how the United States-Israel war on her country has disrupted ...
body_text:
In this first-person testimony told to Al Jazeera, Khadijeh Bandari, an Iranian fisherwoman from Hengam Island in southern Iran, explains how the United States-Israel war on her country has disrupted her work and the lives of all the people on the island.

I am 28 years old, and for as long as I can remember, I would go out to sea with my mother, who taught me how to fish.

When I was older, I got a boat of my own and started fishing. The sea belongs to us women just as much as it belongs to men. Like my mother, I consider fishing to be a part of my life.
