title: House to vote on stopgap funding bill as lawmakers scramble to avoid government shutdown – US politics live
excerpt:
Speaker Mike Johnson to launch a floor vote designed to prevent any federal shutdown before the November midterms

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

House speaker Mike Johnson will laun...
body_text:
Speaker Mike Johnson to launch a floor vote designed to prevent any federal shutdown before the November midterms

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

House speaker Mike Johnson will launch a floor vote to pass the stopgap funding bill designed to keep the federal government fully funded through early December, removing the possibility of a shutdown before the midterm elections.

“The first thing is we’ve got to make sure this government gets funded and we don’t have another Democratic shutdown,” he told reporters as he prepared to open the chamber for business.

The short-term funding bill underwent some significant changes in the Senate, which made it more palatable for Democrats.

It delays a proposed rule from the Office of Management and Budget that would give political appointees more power over the distribution of federal grants. It also includes language to ensure the administration cannot transfer funds to the Border Patrol.

But a provision that delays for one month a federal ban on intoxicating hemp THC products has prompted criticism from many GOP lawmakers.

As a result, GOP leaders will probably place the bill on a fast-track process that avoids a separate procedural vote, bypassing any Republican efforts to block or stall the legislation.

Suspension bills require a two-thirds vote to pass, meaning a significant number from both parties need to support the measure for it to pass and advance to Trump’s desk. The funding vote will most likely take place later today.

The Supreme Court allowed Donald Trump to continue building his $400m White House ballroom project. In a 5-4 decision along political lines, the justices found that a group issuing a legal challenge against the ballroom did not have standing to bring their case. Trump celebrated with a post on his Truth Social platform while Democrats criticized the decision.

Army Secretary Dan Driscoll is stepping down from his role after 18 months on the job, leaving another top military position vacant. Driscoll and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had reportedly butted heads for some time.

Trump vowed further strikes on Iran and called it a “failed nation”. The remarks came as Washington and Tehran exchanged their first military strikes in a month.

JD Vance gave a speech in Michigan that included an attacked against Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. “There’s something about Abdul El-Sayed that is very, very evil,” Vance told the crowd.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accused Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney of turning their trade dispute into a “political shouting match”. Carney had rejected the Trump administration’s terms that would have given the US government extensive power over Canada’s trade policy.

California Governor Gavin Newsom vowed to block the appointment of election denier Tina Peters, who was convicted in 2024 in relation to a plot to chase pro-Trump election conspiracies. Newsom announced he would take measures to prevent Peters from working as an election consultant for Northern California’s Shasta county.

Thousands of American service members are about to descend on eastern Thailand, as the USS Abraham Lincoln makes a port call near the city of Pattaya.

The aircraft carrier sailed past Singapore over the weekend on its way back to the US after a lengthy deployment in the Middle East as part of the US war against Iran.

The Lincoln is expected to dock at a port in Chonburi province this week, according to Thai officials.

More than 5,000 American service members are onboard and many are expected to visit Pattaya, according to the city’s Mayor Poramet Ngampichet, who hopes the port call will boost the local economy. He said destroyer USS Frank E Petersen Jr will dock at a different port.

“For Pattaya to be seen as an important vacation spot is something that we have aimed for,” Poramet said. “We welcome more visits of the troops in the future, whether for a drill or a vacation, before they go back to the US.”

Generational ⁠change is on the ballot ⁠in Massachusetts on ​Tuesday as Democratic voters choose whether to renominate 80-year-old progressive senator Ed Markey or replace him on the ballot with 47-year-old representative Seth ⁠Moulton.

Markey, who has served in Congress for nearly 50 years, is backed by leading progressives such as senator Bernie Sanders and representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, as well ⁠as most members of the state’s congressional delegation, including senator Elizabeth Warren.

No members of the delegation have ​endorsed Moulton, a moderate US Marine Corps veteran ‌whose supporters include New Jersey ‌Governor Mikie Sherrill and the Democratic organization VoteVets, Reuters reported.

The Boston Globe’s editorial board is also behind Moulton, casting ‌him as a necessary agent of change with “proven leadership skills” and positions on key issues that align with most voters.

Markey has a nearly $2m fundraising advantage over Moulton, and Markey has led in recent polls by a double-digit margin. The primary winner is heavily favored to win in November.

Democrat Kamala Harris carried the state by nearly 25 percentage points in 2024.

A similar generational challenge is playing out in the Boston area, where moderate representative Stephen Lynch, 71, is facing progressive attorney Patrick Roath, 39.

title: London Stock Exchange to lose three more firms after takeover offers
excerpt:
Latest purchases take value of deals to leave capital’s stock market this year past $100bn

Three more London-listed companies are set to be taken over as the value of deals removing firms from the ca...
body_text:
Latest purchases take value of deals to leave capital’s stock market this year past $100bn

Three more London-listed companies are set to be taken over as the value of deals removing firms from the capital’s under-pressure stock market passes $100bn (£74bn) so far this year.

On Tuesday, Bodycote, the FTSE 250 industrials group that has been listed on the London Stock Exchange since 1972, agreed a £1.84bn takeover by the US private equity group Veritas.

The Macclesfield-based company, which offers services including heat treatment for manufacturing, metal joining and protective metallic coatings, had been the subject of a bidding war against the rival European buyout group CVC.

Veritas said Bodycote’s prospects would be better served by being taken out of public markets.

“As a private company under Veritas’ ownership, Bodycote will benefit from enhanced flexibility and long-term perspective to support continued investment in the business and pursue targeted organic and inorganic growth opportunities,” the US group said.

Meanwhile, the telecoms company Gamma Communications recommended a £1.1bn offer from the UK private equity company Epiris, days after confirming it was in possible takeover talks with the European buyout company Waterland.

Epiris first indicated its interest in a potential takeover in June. On Tuesday it said: “The additional flexibility that comes from a private company environment will enable Gamma to invest further and focus on sustainably improving the growth of its business over the long term.”

Separately, the Scottish energy company Capricorn is set to end 38 years on the FTSE all-share after striking a deal with the Norwegian rival DNO for $396m. Capricorn had recommended an offer from Genel Energy, but the company switched its recommendation after receiving a higher offer from DNO.

The takeovers put further pressure on the LSE, which has been hit by an exodus of companies so far this year in deals totalling almost $110bn, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

The flurry of dealmaking includes easyJet’s £5.7bn takeover by the US private equity company Apollo, the warehouse landlord Segro’s £14bn takeover by the US rival Prologis, and the sale of ITV’s broadcasting and streaming business to the Sky owner, Comcast, for £1.6bn.

Earlier this year the historic British asset management group Schroders agreed a £9.9bn takeover by a US investor.

Other deals include the £10bn takeover of the lab testing group Intertek by a consortium led by the Swedish private equity company EQT in June and Beazley, the specialist insurer with clients including Lloyds of London, which agreed an £8bn deal to be acquired by the larger rival Zurich in February.

title: Nepal-Tibet flood deaths pass 1,000 as police ask relatives for DNA to identify victims
excerpt:
Relatives of missing tourists asked for blood samples and photos, as efforts continue to rescue trapped hydropower workers

Visual guide: How the Nepal-Tibet flash flood unfolded

Nepali rescuers have...
body_text:
Relatives of missing tourists asked for blood samples and photos, as efforts continue to rescue trapped hydropower workers

Visual guide: How the Nepal-Tibet flash flood unfolded

Nepali rescuers have built temporary bridges to reach remote areas and dug through the ruins of hydropower projects in the Himalayas to rescue hundreds of trapped workers, as the death toll passed 1,000 nearly ⁠a week after devastating ​floods left a trail of destruction across the country’s towns and valleys.

About 600 people remain stuck in several devastated hydropower stations that have become the focus of rescue efforts. The prime ⁠minister, Balendra Shah, said more than 11,000 people had been rescued across the affected region, and power and communication lines had been restored in some areas.

“Thousands of citizens have lost their homes, families, loved ones and property,” Shah said.

Six days after the catastrophe struck the Himalayan border region, 4,400 people were still missing in Nepal and Tibet. Police in Kathmandu have urged relatives of missing tourists to provide DNA samples to assist identification efforts.

In a statement posted to social media, Nepal police on Monday asked relatives of those missing to “provide a fresh blood sample for DNA profiling and two passport-sized photographs” to the pathology laboratory at the Nepal police hospital in Kathmandu, or the nearest district police office.

Among Nepal’s list of the missing are 592 foreigners, including tourists who had come for mountain trekking and Hindu pilgrims seeking spiritual peace at Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash, from countries such as India, the US, UK, Australia and Canada.

Relatives abroad have been requested to undergo DNA profiling at an authorised laboratory and to “send a soft copy of the DNA profile to Nepal police’s official email address”.

In some of Nepal’s flood-affected areas, hundreds of unidentified bodies have already been buried because they are decomposing and there is no room left in hospitals or morgues.

At the police hospital in Kathmandu on Tuesday, more than 100 people were waiting to have their blood sampled.

Among them was Prakaiti Jurnj. Her mother was still missing, but the family had been able to identify her father’s body from a photograph on the wall outside the teaching hospital, where images of the deceased have been posted in an effort to identify the victims.

“Both my father and mother, they were in the village in Nukawot. They were both swept away by the flood,” she said. “We haven’t heard from them since Wednesday. We found my father’s body; my brother saw the photo on the wall.”

She was waiting for her two other siblings, who live in the UK, to arrive on Tuesday so they could all try to get up to the village. She said she wanted to contact her grandmother or sister-in-law, who she thinks both survived the flood because their house is further up the mountain. Their village was still in a blackout, and making contact was impossible.

“I can’t go there; the situation is very bad,” she said. “I can’t go up there alone. I am not sure if we’ll be able to get them.”

The disaster was triggered by a glacier collapse that sent a deluge of ice, rock and mud through Nepal’s border region with China, posing a massive challenge for the country’s six-month-old government.

The region is vulnerable to flooding and landslides, and extreme weather events such as intense monsoons and melting glaciers have become more common because of warming due to human-caused climate change.

In a late-night social media post, Shah said aid worth more than $42m had poured into the country, but that Nepalis were reeling. “The government understands the ​immense pain they are enduring. The path ahead is to ‌support them through this suffering and help ‌them return to normal life through rehabilitation,” the prime minister said.

Shah also said that 279 workers had so far been rescued from hydropower projects, where authorities estimated close to 1,000 people had been trapped. Days after the disaster, hope was rapidly diminisging that any of those trapped in a series of tunnels could be alive.

Pictures and videos shared by rescue teams showed earth-moving equipment digging and shovelling mud and rocks under lights in the dark of the night. Soldiers used torchlight in a big pit they had created to look for space to get into one tunnel.

Chinese state media coverage has focused largely on the official response, highlighting the deployment of firefighters, the People’s Liberation Army and instructions from top leaders. Little is known about victims on the Chinese side.

The flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming”, China’s state broadcaster said on Monday.

Shah said the ​catastrophic event signalled the growing risks that the Himalayan region faces. “The region must therefore remain vigilant. The time has come for us to strongly raise before the international community the disasters we are experiencing as a consequence of climate change,” he wrote in his post.

title: NJ boater faces homicide charge as deadly summer on the water claims another life in third fatal crash
excerpt: Jones Beach lifeguard Cary Epstein breaks down the heroic rescue of a child by 16-year-old lifeguard Ryder Williams in Santa Cruz, California. Williams braved pounding surf and massive waves to bring ...
body_text:
Jones Beach lifeguard Cary Epstein breaks down the heroic rescue of a child by 16-year-old lifeguard Ryder Williams in Santa Cruz, California. Williams braved pounding surf and massive waves to bring the struggling boy safely back to shore.

A New Jersey man faces felony charges following a late-night crash in Barnegat Bay that killed a 26-year-old passenger and left two others critically injured along the Jersey Shore in late July.

Troopers from the New Jersey State Police Marine Bureau arrested Kevin Wells, 40, of Warren, New Jersey, on Friday, charging him with vehicular homicide and two counts of assault by vessel while intoxicated.

State police said troopers responded just before 11 p.m. on July 25 to reports of a serious vessel collision along the Intracoastal Waterway in Toms River Township.

UNLICENSED NYC BOAT OPERATOR ALLEGEDLY IGNORED SAFETY WARNINGS BEFORE MOTHER, BABY DIED IN CAPSIZING: FEDS

Investigators said Wells was operating a 32-foot Boston Whaler through the waterway when the boat struck a channel marker.

Kevin Wells, 40, faces vehicular homicide and assault by vessel charges following a July 25 crash in Toms River Township. (Ocean County Sheriff's Office)

Following the impact, Wells navigated the damaged vessel to a private residence on Silver Lagoon Drive in Toms River Township, where emergency personnel arrived to render aid.

A passenger aboard the boat, Michael T. Bereheiko, 26, of Green Brook, New Jersey, was rushed to an area hospital, where he later died.

Two other passengers – 27-year-old Steven Pochick, of Green Brook, and 27-year-old Nicholas Cherasaro, of North Plainfield – sustained serious injuries and were transported to a local hospital. A fourth passenger, 24-year-old Sarah Stulh, of Bayville, suffered minor injuries.

According to his obituary, Bereheiko was a 2017 graduate of Watchung Hills Regional High School, where he played varsity football on both offense and defense. Teammates affectionately called him "Bear."

Aerial view of resort towns along the New Jersey coastline. (iStock)

He later attended Lincoln Tech, studied to become a heavy diesel mechanic and worked for Schifano Construction Corporation in Middlesex. His family noted he possessed a natural mechanical talent and loved spending time at the Jersey Shore.

TWO DEAD, INCLUDING INFANT, AFTER BOAT CAPSIZES IN NEW YORK HARBOR; 12 RESCUED

Following his arrest on Friday, Wells was booked into the Ocean County Jail. Records show he is being held without bail pending a formal court detention hearing.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

State police said the investigation into the crash remains active.

The incident marks at least the third fatal boating collision involving alleged impairment in the area this summer.

Several bayside locations remain under advisory due to elevated bacteria levels detected during recent water quality testing. (iStock)

State police charged another New Jersey boater in August for a separate fatal Memorial Day crash along the Jersey Shore. Jennifer L. Pearson, 59, of Barnegat, surrendered on Aug. 19 after authorities alleged she was intoxicated while operating a 23-foot center console vessel in Barnegat Bay near Brant Beach.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Pearson’s boat collided with a channel marker around 5:45 p.m., ejecting her 28-year-old son, Gunnar Pearson, and his girlfriend into the water. Gunnar Pearson was rushed to a hospital, where he later died, while four others were treated for minor injuries.

Pearson faces charges of second-degree death by vessel, operating a vessel under the influence, reckless operation, operating without a safety certificate and failure to keep a proper lookout.

Jennifer L. Pearson, 59, has been charged with death by vessel, a second-degree charge, operating a vessel under the influence, reckless operation of a vessel, operating a vessel without a Boating Safety Certificate, and failure to have proper lookout in the Memorial Day crash. (Ocean County Jail)

Court records show investigators smelled alcohol when speaking with Pearson, who admitted to drinking earlier that afternoon.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

In a third fatal crash this summer, authorities charged 64-year-old Stephen Schneider after a July 19 boating collision claimed the lives of his two young grandchildren in the bay near Berkeley Township, NJ.com reported.

Schneider was charged with two counts of reckless vessel homicide after his boat struck a channel marker, the outlet reported.

Police alleged Schneider was intoxicated at the time of the crash, which killed 9-year-old Mya Bella Golabek and 7-year-old Sigmund Paul Golabek.

Fox News Digital’s Sarah Rumpf-Whitten contributed to this report.

Greg Wehner is a reporter for Fox News Digital covering U.S. news and crime, with a focus on breaking developments, law enforcement, public safety and major stories shaping communities across the country.

title: Naked DoorDash driver delivers food to Texas home in shocking security camera video
excerpt:
Houston resident Kiante Matlock describes the moment he checked his security camera and discovered a "completely naked" DoorDash driver dropping off his meal before quickly leaving the property.

A Ho...
body_text:
Houston resident Kiante Matlock describes the moment he checked his security camera and discovered a "completely naked" DoorDash driver dropping off his meal before quickly leaving the property.

A Houston DoorDash customer said he was shocked when he went to fetch his food from his doorstep and saw on his security camera that the delivery driver was naked.

Kiante Matlock told FOX 26 Houston that he didn't expect the delivery driver to drop off his food while naked, "which is crazy."

"And then to handle somebody's food … is ridiculous," he said. "[There] could have been an underage child coming to the door or a woman. … It's just sick."

BURGER KING MAKES MAJOR CHANGES AFTER THOUSANDS OF CUSTOMERS SOUNDED OFF

Matlock told FOX 26 he was playing video games inside his home when his daughter alerted him to a notification on his phone, which turned out to be a notice from DoorDash that his Burger King order had arrived.

A Houston man said his DoorDash delivery took a bizarre turn when security camera footage showed the driver arriving at his home completely naked. (Kiante Matlock/FOX 26 Houston)

When he first looked at the Ring doorbell camera footage, Matlock thought the driver was wearing a onesie before realizing he was "completely naked."

By the time Matlock got to the door, the driver was gone.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Matlock said he did not eat the food the naked driver delivered and that DoorDash refunded his order.

"What this consumer experienced was abhorrent, and we've reached out directly to offer our support," a DoorDash spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

DoorDash customer Kiante Matlock, left, said he initially thought the food delivery driver was wearing a onesie. (FOX 26 Houston)

"This man's behavior was vulgar and completely unacceptable, and as soon as we were made aware, our team permanently removed their access to our platform. We do not tolerate sexual harassment or misconduct of any kind, and we stand ready to assist law enforcement with any investigation."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

DoorDash urges customers to report inappropriate or concerning delivery behavior through the app and to contact law enforcement, including 911 in emergencies, if they feel unsafe.

DoorDash told Fox News Digital that the driver's access to the app has been "permanently removed." (CFOTO/Future Publishing via Getty Images)

Houston police told FOX 26 that residents should report concerning behavior and preserve surveillance footage or other evidence. Depending on the circumstances, criminal charges could be possible following an investigation.

Matlock said he wanted to share his experience to help protect others.

"If you have the opportunity to go get your own food, go get your own food," he said. "But if you can't, I guess just be careful and get you some cameras, that's all I can say."

Teresa Mull is a freelance writer with the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: Democrats’ generational battle erupts as 80-year-old senator faces younger challenger
excerpt: Incumbent Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., and Rep. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., faced off over transgender athletes, ICE, socialism and term limits in their final debate before the Sept. 1 Democratic primary. (Cre...
body_text:
Incumbent Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., and Rep. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., faced off over transgender athletes, ICE, socialism and term limits in their final debate before the Sept. 1 Democratic primary. (Credit: WCVB)

Massachusetts is the latest battleground in the political fight between the left and the center for the future of the Democratic Party.

But in a flip of the script, progressives are supporting the longtime incumbent against a more moderate challenger as solidly blue Massachusetts holds primary elections on Tuesday.

The Senate nomination showdown between 80-year-old Sen. Ed Markey and 47-year-old Rep. Seth Moulton is also the latest faceoff in the Democratic Party's push for generational change, which was fueled two years ago by then-81-year-old President Joe Biden's exit from the presidential race amid questions over his physical and mental stamina following a disastrous debate performance against Trump.

There's a six-way scrum to succeed Moulton in the U.S. House, and four members of the state's all-Democrat congressional delegation, including House Minority Whip Katherine Clark, are facing challenges from the left. And Bay State Republicans will choose a gubernatorial nominee to challenge Democratic Gov. Maura Healey.

THE TOP FIVE MOST HEATED MOMENTS IN THE FINAL MARKEY-MOULTON DEBATE SHOWDOWN

U.S. Sen. Ed Markey and Rep. Seth Moulton stand at lecterns ahead of their debate at WWLP-22News on July 8, 2026. (Suzanne Kreiter/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)

But taking center stage on Tuesday is the battle between Markey and Moulton.

Markey, who served 37 years in the House before winning election in the Senate in 2013, is backed by progressive champions Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Bernie Sanders of Vermont, and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, who seven years ago teamed up with Markey to co-sponsor the Green New Deal.

The senator is vowing to keep fighting for a left-wing agenda that along with the Green New Deal includes Medicare for All, a Trans Bill of Rights, taxing billionaires, and slashing military spending.

WHAT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS IN THE MIDTERM RACES SHOW

U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) hugs Sen. Ed Markey (D-MA) as they speak at a news conference on the launch of the American Climate Corps outside the U.S. Capitol building on September 20, 2023 in Washington, DC. Ocasio-Cortez recently endorsed Markey's bid for re-election. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Moulton, a Marine Corps combat veteran, is backed by New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill, a Naval Academy graduate who piloted helicopters, and recently landed the endorsement of the Boston Globe, the state's largest daily newspaper

Moulton has made generational change a centerpiece of his primary challenge,

"I served with some of the most amazing leaders in my life in the Marines, but at 23 years old, they don't get to run for Congress," Moulton said at last week's final debate. "I think we should have upper age limits as well."

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

Rep. Seth Moulton, seen speaking at the Massachusetts Democratic Party convention in Worcester, on May 30, 2026, is primary challenging Sen. Ed Markey. (Boston Globe via Getty Images)

Markey responded, "I think everyone watching this debate can see that I'm more energized than I've ever been before and in my life."

"Congressman Moulton has a hard time keeping up with me," the senator added.

But Markey seemed unclear of the topic when asked whether he uses A.I. platforms like Claude or ChatGPT in his work. The senator answered that he uses "whatever is inside of my iPhone or my iPad — whatever comes up."

The two rivals agree on many issues, including abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and allowing biological males to participate in female sports. But Moulton during the primary campaign was forced to apologize for his past remarks that he did not want his young daughters "getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete."

Markey was the clear polling and fundraising frontrunner heading into the primary election.

The winner will be considered the overwhelming favorite to win the general election against attorney John Deaton, the presumptive Republican Senate nominee.

Six candidates are facing off in the battle to succeed Moulton for the Democratic nomination in Massachusetts' 6th Congressional District, including former Andover Selectman Dan Koh, financial technology executive John Beccia and state Rep. Tram Nguyen.

Koh, who served in then-President Joe Biden's administration, is showcasing endorsements from Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris.

The winner of the Democratic primary will face Republican Micah Q. Jones, who is unopposed for the nomination.

THESE 12 MIDTERM RACES WILL DECIDE WHICH PARTY CONTROLS THE SENATE

House Democratic Whip Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts is facing two longshot primary challenges from the left as she seeks renomination. (Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Among the incumbents facing primary challenges from the left is Clark, who is the second-ranking Democrat in the House. So is longtime Democratic Rep. Stephen Lynch, who is working to fend off a challenge from attorney Patrick Roath, who out-raised the incumbent.

In the race for the Republican nomination for governor, Army veteran, businessman, and former CEO Mike Minogue is facing off against Briani Shortsleeve, a Marine Corps veteran, businessman and chief administrator and a former acting general manager of the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority.

Minogue has the backing of the Massachusetts GOP.

The winner will face an uphill climb in the general election against Healey in a state dominated by Democrats but where Republicans have had success in gubernatorial showdowns.

Democrat Gov. Maura Healey, seen on August 5, 2026 signing the PROTECT Act, which keeps ICE out of courthouses, schools, child care centers, hospitals and healthcare facilities, is running for re-election this year. (Lane Turner/The Boston Globe)

Tuesday's primary could potentially be the last under the current system.

That's because Massachusetts voters will decide during the general election on a ballot initiative that would get rid of the state's current primary system and replace it with a single, all-party primary.

Under that system, the top two vote-getters would advance to the general election regardless of party affiliation.

Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

title: Trump says Iran is ‘DEAD’ — experts point to the real sign Tehran is nearing the brink
excerpt: Miad Maleki, senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, tells Fox News Digital that mounting economic pressure could push Iran to escalate in an effort to force Washington back to the...
body_text:
Miad Maleki, senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, tells Fox News Digital that mounting economic pressure could push Iran to escalate in an effort to force Washington back to the negotiating table. Photos credit: Reuters/Getty

President Donald Trump declared Iran a "Failed Nation" Monday, claiming the country is economically and militarily broken as renewed fighting with the U.S. raises questions about how much leverage Tehran still has left.

"Iran is officially a Failed Nation. IT IS DEAD!" Trump wrote on Truth Social Monday morning. "They have no Navy, they have no Air Force, they have no currency, they are not paying their soldiers or police."

Trump also claimed Iranian inflation had reached 300% and said the country's leadership was "in total disarray and incapable of properly representing the country."

Iran is facing pressure from nearly every direction — renewed U.S. military strikes, tighter sanctions and a steep drop in oil exports — raising fresh questions about how long Tehran can keep absorbing the economic pain and still maintain leverage against Washington.

COULD IRAN’S REGIME COLLAPSE? EXPERTS ASSESS BESSENT’S BID TO SEVER FINANCIAL LIFELINES

Ships are anchored in the Strait of Hormuz on August 10, 2026 off the coast of Bandar Abbas, Iran. (Ali Saeedi/Getty Images)

Official Iranian data cited by Reuters put annual inflation at 66% in July, while the IMF projects average consumer-price inflation of 68.9% in 2026.

Trump's post came amid the sharpest US-Iran military escalation in weeks. U.S. forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island Sunday after Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz, according to a U.S. official. Iran retaliated by launching ballistic missiles toward U.S. bases in Jordan, while Jordan said it intercepted eight missiles that entered its airspace.

The renewed confrontation comes as Washington ratchets up economic pressure.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Reuters Sunday that the administration expects to roll out additional secondary sanctions as frequently as every week, initially focusing on banks and potentially cutting financial institutions that continue facilitating Iranian transactions out of the U.S. dollar-based financial system.

IRAN’S DEEPEST WEAKNESS IS GETTING EXPOSED THROUGH AMERICA’S MAXIMUM PRESSURE CAMPAIGN

An Iranian navy special forces known as Takavaran stands guard near the Iranian Kharg replenishment ship docked in the Red Sea Sudanese town of Port Sudan on Oct. 31, 2012. The visit of two Iranian naval ships to Sudan reflects strong ties between the countries, Sudan's military said after Khartoum denied Iranian involvement in weapons manufacturing. (Ashraf Shazly/AFP via Getty Images)

Iran's own leaders are acknowledging growing economic strain.

President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran's exports and imports have fallen nearly 35% because of U.S. sanctions and the naval blockade, while annual inflation reached 66% in July, Reuters reported Aug. 29. The IMF projects Iran's economy will contract 5.4% this year.

Miad Maleki, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies who previously served as associate director of Treasury's Office of Global Targeting at the Office of Foreign Assets Control, told Fox News Digital that the Islamic Republic may be nearing an economic breaking point. FDD says Maleki previously helped oversee U.S. sanctions programs and served as chief and senior sanctions coordinator for Iran and the Middle East.

"I think where we stand today, it's very clear — we see very clear signs, indications of what I would call an economy that is on the verge of collapse, if it hasn't already collapsed yet," Maleki said.

Maleki argued that the critical pressure point is Iran's ability to turn oil exports into usable revenue.

US TARGETS CHINESE REFINERY IN SWEEPING IRAN OIL CRACKDOWN, SANCTIONS ‘SHADOW FLEET’ TANKERS

Oil tankers and cargo ships line up in the Strait of Hormuz as seen from Khor Fakkan, United Arab Emirates, Wednesday, March 11, 2026. (Altaf Qadri/AP Photo)

He estimates Tehran needs roughly 1 million barrels of oil exports per day to sustain itself, about 1.5 million to avoid hyperinflation and approximately 2 million to support development. Maleki said Iranian exports have fallen dramatically and Tehran is increasingly struggling to repatriate revenue from the oil it can sell.

Kpler data cited by Reuters showed Chinese imports of Iranian crude falling from an average 1.4 million barrels per day in 2025 to a provisional 534,000 barrels per day so far in August.

Maleki said Tehran is increasingly relying on money creation rather than cutting politically sensitive salaries and pensions. But there are limits.

"They can keep printing money, but they can't really print the type of commodities that they need, such as gasoline, such as wheat," he said.

The pressure, however, may create a dangerous paradox.

IRAN COULD UNLEASH ‘KINETIC’ RESPONSE AS US TIGHTENS ECONOMIC CONTAINMENT, ANALYST WARNS

An Iranian woman shops in a local market in Tehran, Iran, April 28, 2026. (Majid Asgaripour/WANA (West Asia News Agency) via Reuters)

Iran analyst Danny Citrinowicz, a fellow at Israel's Institute for National Security Studies and a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council's Scowcroft Middle East Security Initiative, told Fox News Digital that the maritime blockade, wartime losses and wider economic pressure are hurting Tehran, but argued Washington should not assume economic pain will lead to capitulation.

Citrinowicz said continued pressure could instead increase Tehran's incentive to escalate if Iranian leaders conclude the status quo is worse than renewed confrontation. He said Iran could attempt to target "U.S. economic assets in the Gulf," ports or U.S. vessels involved in enforcing the blockade, even as its missile-production capabilities have been degraded.

Maleki agreed Iran would likely attempt to escalate, but questioned how much leverage Tehran still possesses.

"They're going to try to escalate," Maleki said, pointing to the attacks of the last 24 hours. But he argued that further escalation would increasingly affect Gulf states Iran has relied upon for trade, sanctions evasion and diplomacy — potentially bringing even greater economic and diplomatic pressure.

MILLIONS OF BARRELS OF IRANIAN OIL SIT BEYOND TRUMP BLOCKADE AS HE VOWS ‘ZERO LEAKAGE’

People shop for produce at the historic Tajrish bazaar in northern Tehran on Aug. 25, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)

Asked whether Iran was losing its leverage, Maleki responded: "Absolutely."

He argued Tehran has emerged weakened from internal unrest and the external war and is increasingly isolated domestically and internationally.

What Maleki is watching next is not necessarily missed government payrolls, but shortages that could trigger another wave of domestic unrest.

"What I'm looking for is shortages of items such as gasoline," Maleki said. "Right now they're fighting a war inside Iran that is way more challenging to the regime than it is from external forces that they're facing."

Commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remained severely disrupted Monday, while Brent crude climbed more than 2% to above $90 as markets reacted to the renewed U.S.-Iran exchanges. Reuters reported Aug. 31 that Gulf oil flows have recovered from their wartime lows but remain below pre-war levels.

Maleki said he expects Iranians to return to the streets and argued Western governments should prepare now to help them communicate and organize if Tehran again shuts down internet access.

"What we need to do is to contain this regime, cut off this economic lifeline, empower the Iranian people, be prepared next time Iranians are back on the street [and] take actions to stop this regime from slaughtering Iranians," Maleki said.

The Iran internet blackout started Jan.8 and cost $1.56 million per hour amid protests. (Maria / Middle East Images / AFP via Getty Images)

"Those are the right policies — put the pressure on, be prepared to push back on the Iranian regime every time it escalates," he added. "At this point, they are the weakest they've been since 1979. Every time they try to escalate, they become weaker."

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: Judge who axed 9/11 mastermind's confession blamed military’s ‘conservative tendencies’ for rising ‘extremism’
excerpt: A military judge excluded the confession of alleged 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, ruling his statements were obtained through torture while in CIA custody. Fox News correspondent Mark Meredi...
body_text:
A military judge excluded the confession of alleged 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, ruling his statements were obtained through torture while in CIA custody. Fox News correspondent Mark Meredith reports on the ruling and its potential impact on the long-running case.

The judge who recently threw out a confession by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed: the alleged mastermind of the Sept. 11 terror attacks, previously argued that the U.S. military had a growing domestic extremism problem fueled in part by "conservative tendencies" reinforced by "extreme right-wing groups."

Lt. Col. Michael Schrama, an Air Force judge who specializes in military and environmental law, is presiding over the military commission in the 9/11 case. Last week, he tossed Mohammed’s 2007 confession on the grounds that it was not given voluntarily. The ruling could complicate what has already been a decades-long wait for the suspected plotter to stand trial. Just days before the 25th anniversary of the attacks that killed nearly 3,000 people, Schrama rejected prosecutors’ request to begin the trial in January 2027 and instead set it for June 2028.

The decision, which was not initially made public, has drawn criticism, including from journalist and author Gerald Posner, who called it a "shameful prelude to the 9/11 anniversary." Scrutiny of Schrama’s record has also resurfaced a 2023 essay he wrote titled "Creating a Codified Legal Response to Domestic Extremism in the Ranks" for the national security and foreign policy publication "War on the Rocks."

In the essay, Schrama argued for creating a new provision in the military legal code to address what he referred to as the "rising population of military members engaging in extremist activities."

NEWLY UNCLASSIFIED PENTAGON IMAGES SHOW SUSPECTED DRUG BOATS AS OFFICIAL ISSUES DEADLY WARNING

Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind of the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks, has been held at Guantánamo Bay since 2003. (AP)

Before his role on the military commission overseeing the 9/11 case, Schrama served as an Air Force trial judge at Joint Base Langley-Eustis, Virginia. He has also served as a staff judge advocate and defense counsel and was deployed in 2019 as a staff judge advocate to Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait. Between June 2017 and January 2019, he specialized in environmental law.

He wrote in his essay that "as an active-duty Air Force military judge, I have seen firsthand a rising population of military members engaging in extremist activities."

He said that "there is more than ample evidence that military members are a ripe population for extremist recruitment" and that the "rise of domestic extremism in the military ranks is a threat to national security."

To illustrate his argument, he pointed to a 2021 study by the Center for Strategic & International Studies that said military personnel were responsible for 17.6% of domestic terrorism plots and attacks.

CBC TELLS JOURNALISTS NOT TO CALL 9/11 ‘TERRORIST ATTACKS’ IN INTERNAL GUIDANCE

A U.S. soldier holds a U.S. flag during a counter-landing live-fire exercise as part of the annual Balikatan joint military drills on May 4, 2026, in Laoag, Ilocos Norte province, Philippines. (Ezra Acayan/Getty Images)

He also wrote that 12% of those charged with participating in the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot had some form of military experience, including service members on active duty.

As to the reasons for this rising extremism, he argued that "military institutions tend to become more conservative and isolated from civilian society" and that "these conservative tendencies are constantly reinforced, and young military members can be easy prey for the extreme right-wing groups that relate through similar conservative ideology."

"Unfortunately, the United States Criminal Code and the Uniform Code of Military Justice do not currently provide the tools to deal with this crisis, as they do not treat domestic extremism as a specific criminal offense," he wrote, adding, "Codifying domestic extremism as a punitive article under the military code would provide a means for commanders to adequately address the rising tide of domestic extremism."

He also noted a 2019 case in which a Coast Guard officer pleaded guilty to gun and drug charges after prosecutors said he stashed weapons and planned to murder Democratic politicians, Supreme Court justices and TV journalists.

He wrote that "despite describing Hasson as a domestic terrorist, federal prosecutors chose these more minor charges due to the fact that no domestic terrorism statute currently exists."

Two flags flutter on a fence in front of lower Manhattan and One World Trade Center at the Tear Drop 9/11 Memorial at sunset on June 13, 2026, in Bayonne, New Jersey. (Gary Hershorn/Getty Images)

Ronald Flesvig, a spokesperson for the Military Commissions Convening Authority, declined to comment on Schrama's ruling, saying it would be inappropriate to comment on the military judge's decision. He also declined to comment on Schrama's essay, saying it was published "not in his capacity as a judge for the military commissions."

In response to Schrama’s decision last week, White House senior advisor Stephen Mueller told Fox News, "Our judicial system is so badly broken it sides at every turn with predators, monsters and, in this case, a 9/11 mastermind."

title: House Republicans ramp up labor union investigations ahead of midterms
excerpt:
Inquiry come after conservative thinktanks claim unions are using member dues to support Democratic causes

House Republicans are investigating several US labor unions based on claims from far-right n...
body_text:
Inquiry come after conservative thinktanks claim unions are using member dues to support Democratic causes

House Republicans are investigating several US labor unions based on claims from far-right nonprofits alleging union dues are being used for illegal political funding.

Republicans on the House’s education and workforce committee opened the investigation this summer after multiple reports from the conservative thinktanks targeted unions and their spending, claiming that unions are using member dues to support Democratic causes.

While unions are allowed to advocate for political causes, they are prohibited from using union dues to directly fund specific candidates or political action committees (Pacs). Union members can voluntary donate to labor union’s political action committees.

The unions under investigation include the American Federation of Teachers (AFT), United Auto Workers, United Steelworkers, Smart Transportation Division (Smart-TD), Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers and Trainmen (BLET), and the Brotherhood of Maintenance of Way Employees Division (BMWED).

The allegations come from research reports by the American Accountability Foundation (AAF), a “dark money” nonprofit that counts Project 2025 architect the Heritage Foundation as a donor, and the Freedom Foundation, a conservative thinktank whose chairman once protested against Labor Day, claiming “I can’t think of a problem in society that can’t be traced in some way back to the abuses of organized labor.”

Among the AAF’s allegations toward labor unions include complaining that the BLET supported a lawsuit filed by the UAW to halt the Trump administration’s attempt to end collective bargaining. It also highlighted the BLET’s criticism of Project 2025, which advocates for several policies that would weaken labor unions and collective bargaining rights.

“The industrial unions the [House] committee is investigating have become glorified political arms of the Democrat Party,” said Tom Jones, President of the American Accountability Foundation in a statement. “When these unions care more about their friends in Congress than their members in the factories and railroads, it becomes clear they’re not serving the working men and women of America!”

In a statement, a spokesperson for United Steelworkers said the group is “working diligently on fully addressing the committee’s request”.

“Our union values transparency and annually reports our spending with the Department of Labor,” the spokesperson said.

As a part of their union probes, House Republicans are also investigating AFT president Randi Weingarten after the Freedom Foundation claimed, using speculation around the union’s annual financial filing, that union member dues funded her 2025 book, Why Fascists Fear Teachers: Public Education and the Future of Democracy.

“Perhaps Weingarten’s next book should be entitled, Why Teachers Fear Teachers Unions,” the analysis claimed.

In a letter responding to the allegations, Michael Bromwich, an attorney representing Weingarten and AFT, called the Freedom Foundation’s report “a partisan attack masquerading as investigative journalism”.

“Its claims are premised on factual inaccuracies, misleading characterizations, and a willful disregard for the complete record,” Bromwich wrote. “The documents produced to the House committee refute these allegations and demonstrate that the book project was lawfully and ethically undertaken to advance AFT’s mission, with appropriate oversight and transparent financial arrangements.”

The Freedom Foundation and House Republicans on the investigating committee did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

The House investigations follow reports that the Trump administration conducted surveillance of labor unions in Minnesota during a mass anti-immigration enforcement operation earlier this year, including the CWA and the SEIU.

Cathy Creighton, director of Cornell University’s sSchool of Industrial and Labor Relations Buffalo Co-Lab, said that union finances are strictly controlled, with disclosure requirements on how money is spent – which is how the conservative groups got the information for their reports.

Most union members vote Democrat, because the party “has a platform that supports the labor movement, the right to organize [and] the right to bargain”, Creighton said.

“The labor movement is allowed to spend money on political actions, and they do,” she said, noting that the motivation behind the reports seem political. “The Trump administration has been trying to eliminate bargaining rights and unions, full stop.”

A 2024 poll by Gallup found 62% of Americans say the Democratic party best serves the interest of union members compared to 27% who said the same about the Republican party.

US labor unions have historically supported Democrats over Republicans since Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s administration passed the National Labor Relations Act in 1935. But Republican presidents, up until Ronald Reagan in the 1980s, refrained from taking hostile positions toward labor unions and collective bargaining.

In 1976, Republican Gerald Ford’s presidential campaign stated “free collective bargaining remains the best way to insure that American workers receive a fair price for their labors.”

But under Reagan, the Republican party began to emphasize so-called “right to work” laws over collective bargaining and adopted more hostile, pro-business stances toward labor unions.

Under Trump’s second term, he issued an executive order to rescind collective bargaining rights from more than 1 million federal workers and made cuts to federal agencies tasked with enforcing labor laws.

title: Can 80-year-old Democrat Ed Markey clinch another US Senate term?
excerpt:
Age on the agenda in Massachusetts but octogenarian leftwinger leads younger rival Seth Moulton in primary poll

Democrats have spent the summer ousting long-serving incumbents in primaries across the...
body_text:
Age on the agenda in Massachusetts but octogenarian leftwinger leads younger rival Seth Moulton in primary poll

Democrats have spent the summer ousting long-serving incumbents in primaries across the country. On Tuesday, Massachusetts voters will decide whether that generational revolt extends to the 80-year-old Ed Markey, whose younger Democratic rival has argued that the incumbent is simply too old to serve another term.

But the Senate primary in this heavily Democratic state flips a central dynamic of previous contests, where youthful progressive insurgents have targeted – and in several cases, toppled – older incumbents they derided as avatars of an outmoded cautious establishment.

In something of a role reversal, it is the long-serving Markey who is positioned as the voice of the progressive left, while 47-year-old Seth Moulton, a member of the House of Representatives, has moved some of his more moderate positions closer to those of his older rival in an effort to win over a younger voting cohort.

Polls indicate that Markey – who was first elected to Congress in 1976, before Moulton was born – is poised to confound concerns over his age by winning election for a third full term, at the end of which he would be 86.

Markey’s leftwing credentials have been burnished by endorsements from other high-profile progressives, including Bernie Sanders, the leftwing independent senator from Vermont, and Elizabeth Warren, his fellow Massachusetts senator.

In a recent televised debate, Markey, who became a senator in a 2013 special election to replace John Kerry, when he resigned to become US secretary of state, attempted to tackle the age issue head on.

“I think everyone watching this debate can see that I’m more energized than I’ve ever been before in my life. I am criss-crossing the state. I’m fighting for families,” the senator said.

“Congressman Moulton has a hard time keeping up with me in the course of this campaign.”

Moulton – a former marine who later ran a private health company after military service in Iraq – called for age limits to serve in Congress and contrasted Markey’s campaign performance with his own.

“I’ve done over 50 town halls. You’ve done a couple,” he told Markey. “You’ve missed three candidate forums just in the past week. It’s a lot of work to represent this entire state.”

But it was when the debate turned to technology and the candidates’ personal use of artificial intelligence that the age question appeared to sharpen. Asked whether the senator used AI platforms like ChatGPT in his work, Markey replied that he uses “whatever is inside of my iPhone and my iPad – whatever comes up”.

Moulton seized on that response as evidence that the incumbent did not fully understand the latest technology and how it was poised to transform every sector of society.

“Senator,” he said, “if you don’t even know what you’re using on your phone or your iPad, this is why we need a new generation of leaders to regulate these technologies to make sure that they are safe.”

Moulton, who entered the House of Representatives in 2015, has embraced more moderate positions than Markey, namely on healthcare – on which he stopped short of advocating the single-payer system advocated by his opponent – and on transgender athletes. He apologized at a recent debate for previously saying in the fallout of Kamala Harris’s loss to Trump in 2024 that he did not want his daughters “getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete”.

He has said he would not vote for the Democrats’ current leader in the Senate, Chuck Schumer, if elected. Schumer, 75, has been portrayed as a symbol of what critics say is an out-of-touch and ageing establishment leadership that has left younger and left-leaning voters disenchanted.

In blue Massachusetts, the Democratic primary often decides who wins office.

An Emerson College Polling survey released on Sunday, suggested voters are willing to look past Markey’s age. In the survey, Markey led Moulton 60% to 33%, a dramatic increase from its May poll, when the senator held a five-point edge over the congressman.

“If these numbers hold, this race will mirror Markey’s successful ‘peak-late’ approach to winning in 2020,” Spencer Kimball, executive director of Emerson College Polling, said, referring to the senator’s defeat of then congressman Joe Kennedy III, a scion of the state’s best known political dynasty.

Despite Kennedy’s youth – he was 39 at the time – young progressives rallied behind Markey, painting the incumbent as the leader most willing to take on the party’s establishment.

Markey’s re-election would contradict the trend of a growing backlash against elderly leaders that critics have labelled a gerontocracy.

Joe Biden was forced to drop his presidential re-election bid in 2024 amid concerns over his mental acuity after a disastrous presidential election debate in Atlanta against Donald Trump.

Trump, who won the subsequent election against Biden’s replacement, Kamala Harris, is himself 80 and has been the subject of increasing age-related concerns about his health and ability to serve.

Mitch McConnell, 84, the former Republican Senate majority leader, has been absent from Congress for months following a fall and hospitalization that has fueled fevered speculation about his health.

On the campaign trail, Markey sought to cast his age as experience. “I’ve been standing up to the bosses for a long time, so I know no one gives it to you,” he says in one of his most prominent ads, featuring Warren and Sanders. “We have to fight for it.”

title: Press freedom advocates alarmed by $300,000 defamation verdict against Louisiana newspaper
excerpt:
Experts say ruling could undermine the ‘actual malice’ standard and make publishers more wary of critical reporting

A $300,000 jury verdict won recently by a Louisiana supreme court justice who sued ...
body_text:
Experts say ruling could undermine the ‘actual malice’ standard and make publishers more wary of critical reporting

A $300,000 jury verdict won recently by a Louisiana supreme court justice who sued the Advocate, the state’s largest newspaper, for libel over an editorial has caused concern among some US press freedom advocates.

One said the decision demonstrated a misunderstanding of a key legal principle governing such cases. And another worries the verdict could have a chilling effect on the media industry’s efforts to report on powerful people and institutions.

George Freeman, the Media Law Resource Center’s executive director, and Seth Stern, the chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation, shared those thoughts after the 24 August conclusion of a complex, days-long civil trial pitting Louisiana supreme court justice Jefferson Davis Hughes III against the state’s Advocate newspaper.

The judge maintained that a 2019 Advocate editorial whose headline included “Jeff Hughes … made a mockery of justice” libeled him – but as a US public figure, to meet his burden of proof in the dispute, he had to prove “actual malice” by the publication.

Freeman said actual malice occurs when a publisher has substantial doubts about a story’s veracity – or has a “conscious awareness” that it is probably false – and runs it anyway.

Members of an Iberville parish, Louisiana, jury that decided Hughes’ case heard testimony from two Advocate editors at the time that the outlet did everything it could to ensure the editorial was accurate – and they believed it was.

Ultimately, the entire dispute seemingly turned on a discrepancy between the editorial in question and an investigative news story published two days earlier.

The investigative news story from the Advocate and CBS affiliate WWL Louisiana quoted a woman who described helping her son fight for the custody of his five-year-old boy, Austin, in 1998 when she asked Hughes, then a lower court judge, to recuse himself from the matter. The woman told the outlets that she understood Hughes was dating a lawyer on the opposite side of the custody battle, Berkley Durbin – but that Hughes refused to step away.

The news piece reported that Durbin withdrew from the case in August 1998, days before Hughes expanded custody for Austin’s mother. But the ensuing editorial noted “in 1999 …” Hughes and Durbin were “romantically involved” and then said, “Durbin represented Austin’s mother.”

Hughes subsequently sued the Advocate for $10m, with him and his legal team claiming the publication had injured his reputation as well as unduly caused him emotional distress. The Advocate’s attorneys, among other arguments, countered that Hughes failed to establish actual malice.

Jurors who were picked for the case spent about a half hour deliberating before indicating on the plaintiff’s verdict form that the “Advocate defamed Jeff Hughes.” However, it awarded him $9.7m less than he demanded, and the verdict form made no mention of actual malice.

Advocate president and publisher Kevin Hall afterward issued a statement to the newspaper saying, “We respect the jury’s decision … [and] stand by our journalism and remain committed to strong, independent reporting that serves our communities.”

An attorney for Hughes told WWL Louisiana that “justice was served by the verdict,” allowed the judge “to clear his name from this unfortunate defamation”, and said that a large payout was never the goal.

It was the second blow in quick succession to the US press. On 21 August, an Alabama jury awarded $9.25m in damages against the New York Times for wrongly reporting, citing an anonymous source familiar with the situation, that a college basketball player named Kai Spears had been present at the scene of a fatal shooting.

But one notable factor in the Times case was that Spears – as a walk-on, or non-scholarship player – had been legally determined to be a private individual rather than a public figure. That meant Spears could win his case if he convinced the jury that the Times’ information was false and published with negligence, as the Washington Post reported.

The Times nonetheless issued a statement saying the Spears “verdict and award of damages are contrary to law and not supported by the facts”. It also said Spears’ verdict marked the first defamation case in the US that the Times had lost in 50 years.

Both the Hughes and Spears verdicts can be appealed. It was not immediately clear whether the Advocate and the Times intended to do so.

Asked to comment on the Hughes verdict and its possible implications on the actual malice standard, Stern on Monday said it “won’t improve journalism” to impose “significant monetary damages whenever the inevitable mistakes occur”.

“While [journalists] do their best to ensure that their sources and source materials are accurate, there is always a possibility that they aren’t,” Stern said. Stern added that is why the US supreme court has long held that journalists can only be held liable for defamation in cases involving public figures if they acted with “knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard of the truth”.

He said otherwise it was a real possibility that a “fear of liability” would make publishers “more timid and suppress critical reporting of wealthy, powerful or otherwise newsworthy people”.

Meanwhile, Freeman said he believed the Hughes verdict demonstrated how difficult it is to convey “what the actual malice standard requires”.

“In the mind of the publisher, you really need to believe the story is either not true or probably untrue – but you published anyhow,” Freeman said. And, in the Hughes case, he said “there is no evidence or line of proof” that had occurred.

title: Rival Ray Hadley tells Alan Jones trial that alleged victim ‘broke down and sobbed’ when detailing assaults
excerpt:
Former 2GB and 2UE broadcaster Jones, 85, has denied 22 indecent assault and sexual touching charges involving six men

Broadcaster Ray Hadley has told a Sydney court that an alleged victim of Alan Jo...
body_text:
Former 2GB and 2UE broadcaster Jones, 85, has denied 22 indecent assault and sexual touching charges involving six men

Broadcaster Ray Hadley has told a Sydney court that an alleged victim of Alan Jones confided in 2019 he’d been “sexually assaulted” by the fellow 2GB broadcaster on a number of occasions.

“He said [Jones] put his hand on my cock and kissed me,” Hadley told the Downing Centre local court on Tuesday.

Jones is on trial on 20 charges of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching against six complainants. The 85-year-old has pleaded not guilty.

“I asked him if he was homosexual and whether he was consenting to it,” Hadley told the court when giving evidence.

“He broke down and cried and said ‘No, I hated it. I’m not homosexual.’”

Hadley was questioned by the prosecutor Georgina Wright about the conversation he had with the alleged victim, known as complainant C. He was also questioned about later putting him in contact with a journalist from the Sydney Morning Herald.

Hadley said he promised C he would not reveal his identity and he would keep his disclosure secret. The conversation lasted between 30 and 40 minutes, Hadley told the court.

“At varying stages, he broke down and sobbed,” Hadley said. “I just stopped, let him compose himself, offered my support, and let him continue.”

C earlier told the court he confided in Hadley in 2019 that he had been inappropriately touched by Jones in 2008.

“I broke down and I said ‘He’s a fucking grub, he used to grab me on the cock, he used to kiss me’,” C told the court.

“Ray just listened. I just broke down sobbing. I said ‘He [Jones] is a fucking cunt, he’s just a cunt’.”

Hadley on Tuesday said: “I wanted to go across the other side of the desk and give him a hug, but I just kept telling him it wasn’t his fault. He was a victim, and he didn’t have to explain to me that he should have rejected the advances.”

Hadley told the court that C had also mentioned a luncheon where “Jones brought him to sit next to him, and during the luncheon he was touching his cock under the table”.

Hadley said C told him that two guests at the lunch, including broadcaster Jason Morrison, were “laughing and giggling at what was happening” and C said he felt “embarrassed” and “helpless”.

Jones’s defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC said in her opening address last month that the allegations against her client were “trial by media” fuelled by the hatred and jealousy of his 2GB radio rival Hadley.

“You will see evidence in Hadley’s own words of his resolve to destroy Jones and to one by one, tear his supporters apart,” Bashir said.

The court heard part of the defence case is that two SMH journalists, columnist Peter FitzSimons and chief investigative reporter Kate McClymont, were “looking for a story”.

“Unfortunately, rumours and media coverage are at the heart of more than a reasonable possibility of contamination or reconstruction in this case,” Bashir said.

Bashir alleged that Hadley “wanted to destroy” Jones and to “tear him apart”.

“Rivalry, treachery, double-dealing, money, hatred, desperation, opportunism and more” were at the “heart of this case”, Bashir said in the opening of the judge-only trial.

Bashir alleged that Hadley passed on information to the SMH about complainant C who had worked for Jones as a driver.

On Monday, a 2GB staffer told the court there was a fierce rivalry between Jones and Hadley over the coveted breakfast slot in 2019, when Jones was nearing the end of his contract and Hadley wanted to move from the Ray Hadley Morning Show to breakfast.

“My understanding is Mr Hadley had signed a secret contract to replace Mr Jones while Mr Jones was coming off contract,” James Willis told the court.

“And while this was meant to be a secret, it had spread throughout the corridors enough that our team, including Jones, had been aware of it.”

The trial before judge Glenn Walsh continues.

title: Teenager pleads guilty to planning terrorist bombing targeting Opera House and Sydney marathon
excerpt:
Boy, 16, testifies he was radicalised on TikTok before connecting to extremists on Telegram

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news...
body_text:
Boy, 16, testifies he was radicalised on TikTok before connecting to extremists on Telegram

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A school student has testified about falling down a social media rabbit hole that led him to planning to bomb the Sydney Opera House in a terrorist attack.

The 16-year-old boy, who cannot be identified for legal reasons, has pleaded guilty to planning a terrorist act over the course of more than a month in 2024.

In a sentencing hearing in the New South Wales supreme court on Tuesday, the teenager gave evidence about how he was gradually exposed to increasing levels of Islamic extremism online.

He first saw extremist material on TikTok in 2024 when aged 14 and became interested by accounts of conquests in previous centuries, the court heard.

“It was historical … the time of the Crusaders, empires a long time ago,” the 16-year-old told the court.

The aftermath of the 9/11 terrorist attacks and Islamic State propaganda were increasingly shown to him, and the videos also became more violent, the teenager said.

While he started to become more radicalised, he began communicating with other people on an encrypted app, Telegram, about his desire to learn about committing terrorism.

“Did you like talking to them?” asked the boy’s barrister, Michael Valentin.

The teen replied: “Yes, I found it interesting … [they were] a new group of people, I was trying to relate to them.”

The teenager said he then began researching how to target the Sydney Opera House with a bombing on one of its busiest days – the running of the Sydney Marathon.

The landmark serves as the finish line for the globally significant race, making it an ideal target for maximum impact on human life, the 16-year-old said. The idea came from watching videos about the 2013 Boston Marathon attack, where three people were killed and more than 500 were injured by two bombs planted at the finish line.

The teen agreed that he told someone online: “I am picking the location, places where lots of people and tourists are out.”

“I will test and then do the operation, inshallah [God willing].”

He said his justification for planning the attack was contained in a written message that said: “the country I am living in helped America evade Iraq and Afghanistan and killed many Muslims”.

Despite his detailed planning, he said he was only “50/50” about whether he would actually carry out a bombing.

He spoke of having a “little voice” in his head trying to persuade him against committing terrorism.

On Tuesday, the teen said he disavowed everything Islamic State stands for and held no extreme views.

“I’m deeply sorry for the things I did,” the boy told Justice Stephen Campbell.

His lawyer urged for a non-custodial sentence, to enable the teenager to continue his deradicalisation in the community.

Having been on bail under strict home detention since November 2024, the teen has been allowed to attend events under his parents’ supervision, including the Vivid festival and the Royal Easter Show.

“Clearly, we have before you a young man who … has seen the errors of his ways,” Valentin said.

“Thankfully he is now out of the rabbit hole.”

Crown prosecutor Sophie Callan SC acknowledged the “candid” evidence of the teenager, but said there is no other appropriate possibility than a term in custody.

“There remains a level of naivety in expressions of insight … that would leave Your Honour with a degree of caution,” Callan said.

Campbell will deliver the sentence on 29 October.
